documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Photoshop Generative Fill

documents.t: Generative Fill is Photoshop's native selection-to-fill feature. Make a selection, open Generative Fill from the Contextual Task Bar, pick an Adobe or partner model, prompt or leave it blank, and generate. Firefly fills return as a set of variations to choose from in the Properties panel. Reference images guide Firefly Fill & Expand with an object or whole-image scope; for partner models, a reference panel accepts up to 8 images for Gemini and up to 3 for Flux. Partner models use the account terms attached to Creative Cloud. Adobe's generative credits FAQ explains current usage, reset, and refund behavior. Each user must accept a partner-model confirmation before first use, availability "may vary by country or region," and enterprise administrators can define which generative models each user may use. Adobe draws a line between its own model and its partners'. Firefly is the model it calls commercially safe; for partner models, its FAQ says you decide which to use and are responsible for judging whether one is appropriate. Its Firefly product description (27 August 2026) excludes capabilities "denoted in the user interface as being powered or provided by non-Adobe trained models" from the Firefly IP indemnity, and its partner-models security fact sheet (March 2026) notes that "Partner models may store generated content before returning it to Adobe." That is the boundary Adobe itself sets around Nano Banana and Flux inside Photoshop.
documents.s: What Photoshop Generative Fill is

documents.t: The Astria plugin is a CCX/UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (version 26 and later) on macOS and Windows. Six hosted models sit in one dropdown: GPT Image 2 (OpenAI, mask-aware, 1K/2K/4K), Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1), Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro), Seedream 5 Pro, Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro. Flux Kontext was retired in favor of these. The workflow is three steps. Select with the marquee, lasso, brush or color range. Prompt in short, specific language, dropping reference images into the panel as visual instructions. Generate, and the result lands as a new layer. Mask-aware models read the selection directly. The model is chosen per task, and keys are switched inside the panel. Two things separate it from a browser round trip. Each generation is placed as a Smart Object that holds the model's full returned resolution, so a 4K result placed into a small selection still carries the 4K pixels and can be re-transformed, masked and re-edited later without resampling. And the panel's model list is served by the Astria platform, so a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches, with no plugin update or re-download. The platform already carries GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image as of 13 September 2026. Billing runs two ways. An Astria key covers every model on pay-as-you-go, with no subscription and no minimum, and Astria abstracts the Google, OpenAI, fal and ByteDance APIs so quota, auth and retries stay invisible. Or paste a Google AI Studio key and the Gemini models run against your own Google quota, billed by Google. A consumer Gemini subscription cannot be used by any plugin; Google only authorizes external apps through API keys. No GPU is needed. Per-image rates are on the pricing page.
documents.s: What the Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is

documents.t: Adobe's proof is the release train. Its blog post of 20 November 2025 announced Nano Banana Pro powering Generative Fill on the day Google announced the model, and Photoshop 27.6 added Nano Banana 2 on 28 April 2026 (CG Channel, secondary). Adobe's forum holds the counter-evidence: a quality thread reports softer Photoshop results than Gemini web; a bug thread reports intermittent failures; and a content-flag thread collects reports of ordinary prompts returning a guidelines violation. These are user reports, not benchmarks. Astria's proof is first-party: 16,000 sales and 187 ratings on the landing page, and seven production reels covering fashion edits with references, bridal retouching, sketch and CAD to photo, product design, real estate, hair and clothing swaps, and packaging. Treat all of it as vendor-published.
documents.s: Public proof, with provenance

documents.t: The job: a campaign hero of a model on a stone step. The client wants the shoes swapped to the new-season style from a product reference, the background extended for a 4:5 crop, and a phone removed from the model's hand. Final delivery is a 4,000-pixel print file and a web crop.
documents.s: A realistic workflow: one campaign hero, then forty SKUs

documents.t: Select the shoes, open Generative Fill, choose Gemini 3 (with Nano Banana Pro), attach the product shot in the reference panel, prompt, and generate. Extend the canvas for the delivery crop with Firefly Fill & Expand or Nano Banana 2. Select the phone and hand, then run the partner model again with a reference of the empty hand. Check current Adobe usage terms before estimating the job, including retries. Adobe publishes no partner-model output size, and the forum thread above is the only public data point. If the shoe fill is soft against a large delivery file, Adobe's route to more pixels is Generative Upscale with Topaz Gigapixel.
documents.s: In Photoshop Generative Fill

documents.t: Lasso the shoes, drop the product reference into the panel, choose Nano Banana Pro at 4K, short prompt, generate. The result lands as a Smart Object carrying the full 4K return, so scaling it to the selection loses nothing and the layer mask does the blend. Extend the canvas, marquee the new area, and switch the dropdown to GPT Image 2 for a mask-aware fill, or Seedream 5 if the extension needs a longer structural prompt. Select the hand, reference the empty-hand frame, generate. Three Smart Objects, each re-editable when the client wants the step a shade warmer. Cost is per image against the Astria balance, or your Google key for the two Gemini calls.
documents.s: In the Astria plugin

documents.t: Here the two products stop being comparable. Photoshop's answer for volume is the Firefly web app and Boards on the same credit pool, still one document and one selection at a time. The Astria plugin is one door into the Astria platform. The same key and balance drive Astria workspaces, templates and the API, so the approved hero treatment becomes a template that runs the remaining 40 SKUs while the retoucher stays in Photoshop for the hero and the fix. The AI fashion photoshoot guide covers that side.
documents.s: And the other 40 SKUs

documents.t: Adobe's Photoshop generative AI FAQ, last updated 23 February 2026, states that the Firefly model returns 1024×1024 pixels to Photoshop. It states no size for partner models. The community quality thread reports Nano Banana Pro output in Photoshop as far below the same prompt on Gemini web, with no fix timeline published. The Astria plugin returns each generation as a Smart Object holding the model's full output, up to 4K on GPT Image 2 and the Gemini models. That is the difference between a fill that survives a print crop and one that needs an upscale pass.
documents.s: Returned resolution, winner: Astria

documents.t: Adobe and Astria use different billing systems, and model terms change. Price the same representative job—including retries—using Adobe's current generative credits information and Astria's current pricing page. Astria also supports a Google AI Studio key for Gemini calls. This article does not claim a universal cost winner.
documents.s: Billing flexibility, compare current terms

documents.t: Adobe lists GPT Image 2 and both GPT Image 2.5 variants for Firefly, Boards and Illustrator, not Photoshop. Seedream is absent from Adobe's stack. Inside the Astria panel, GPT Image 2 reads the selection as a mask and Seedream 5 Pro handles long, structured edit prompts, alongside the two Gemini models and Flux 2 Pro. A retoucher who knows which model handles surgical replacement and which handles long structural prompts gets that choice in one dropdown. That choice opens workflows the picker does not address. Generative Fill returns a generated region for the selection you made; it is not built to take a finished, flattened layout apart. Pulling a flat poster back into editable pieces, the product, the typography and a rebuilt background each on its own layer, is a sequence of extractions against an editing model. We tested what that actually delivers, and where it falls short, in AI layer separation in Photoshop.
documents.s: GPT Image and Seedream inside the document, winner: Astria

documents.t: Photoshop offers one billing path: Adobe generative credits. On enterprise plans, the Admin Console decides which models a seat can see, and Adobe notes availability may vary by region. The Astria plugin accepts an Astria key or a Google AI Studio key, switched inside the panel, and one Astria key authenticates every model. Install the CCX, paste a key, and the roster is available to that key.
documents.s: Bring your own key, and no organizational gate, winner: Astria

documents.t: Nano Banana Pro reached Photoshop on launch day, the best case for Adobe's partnership model; Nano Banana 2 waited for a point release, and GPT Image 2.5 reached Firefly web but not Photoshop. The Astria panel reads its model list from the platform, so a model added to Astria is in the dropdown the same day with no plugin update.
documents.s: Zero-day models, winner: Astria

documents.t: This is the genuine advantage, stated once and plainly. Generative Fill is already in the Contextual Task Bar of every current Photoshop. There is nothing to install, no key to create, and Firefly fills return a set of variations to choose from. For Firefly output, Adobe offers a commercial-safety framing and, where a customer's agreement includes it, an IP indemnity. Partner outputs are excluded from that indemnity, so this advantage applies to Firefly work rather than to Nano Banana work. Astria offers no equivalent framing; treat both products' partner-model outputs on the same footing.
documents.s: Zero install and Firefly's commercial-safety framing, winner: Photoshop Generative Fill

documents.t: Most of your generative work is Firefly fill and expand, and you want Adobe's commercial-safety framing for it. Your current Creative Cloud terms comfortably cover the occasional Nano Banana or Flux fill. Your organization requires that every model in use be enabled through the Adobe Admin Console. Installing a third-party panel is not an option on your machine.
documents.s: Choose Photoshop Generative Fill if...

documents.t: Fills must hold up at delivery resolution, with the full returned pixels kept inside a Smart Object. You need GPT Image 2 with a mask, or Seedream, without leaving the document. Your current Adobe plan is not a practical fit for sustained partner-model work. You want to bill per image through one key, or run Gemini calls on your own Google key. You want new models on launch day without waiting for a Photoshop release or a plugin update, and a production route behind the panel for the rest of the collection.
documents.s: Choose the Astria plugin if...

documents.t: Photoshop Generative Fill with partner models is the right default for Firefly work and for the subscriber who wants an occasional Nano Banana fill with nothing to install. Its advantages are real and narrow: zero install, Adobe's commercial-safety framing for its own model, and Nano Banana Pro on launch day. The Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is our recommendation for professional retouching. It extends Photoshop with the models Adobe does not put in the picker, keeps every result at full returned resolution inside a Smart Object, bills per image or on your own key, and picks up new models the day they land on the platform. Photoshop for the hero and the fix; the Astria platform for the other forty SKUs.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Run one fixed PSD through both routes with the same selection, reference and short prompt. Measure the returned pixel dimensions of the Nano Banana Pro fill in each, then check whether the layer can be re-transformed later without resampling. Count the credits or balance consumed by the full job, retries included. On a Photoshop single-app plan, check your allowance and reset date in the Generative Credits Usage panel first; on enterprise Creative Cloud, confirm which partner models your Admin Console exposes. Then decide which fills are Firefly work that benefits from Adobe's framing and which are partner-model work, because the indemnity line falls between them.
documents.s: What to test before choosing

documents.t: For a Photoshop professional who needs current partner models at full returned resolution, the Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is our recommendation. Photoshop Generative Fill is the right default when the work is primarily Firefly fill and expand and the native Adobe workflow matters most.

documents.t: Aiuta's core business is shopper-facing virtual try-on for enterprise retail. Shoppers upload a photo and see themselves in an item in seconds, building single looks or complete outfits. It deploys via SDK or API and is designed to slot into existing ecommerce infrastructure with minimal engineering lift. The customer list is the strongest part of the story: ASOS, About You, Alice + Olivia, adidas Originals, Namshi, HEMCO, Tanya Taylor, and Leset. Aiuta Studio is the second product and works differently from most tools in this comparison. A brand supplies basic product images; the platform returns studio-grade outputs with custom backgrounds and lighting, including flat-lay conversion from model shots. Two details define the experience: every output passes human QA before delivery, with a stated 95% first-pass acceptance rate, and turnaround is quoted at 24–48 hours. That QA guarantee is a real differentiator against pure self-serve generators, and it is also the shape of a service. You submit, you wait, you receive. Neither Aiuta page we reviewed publishes pricing for Studio.
documents.s: Aiuta: try-on infrastructure, with a studio attached

documents.t: Astria puts the creative decision inside the brand. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored, editable, and reusable by the people who own the brand's look. The immediate consequence is iteration speed. A creative director who wants a warmer background, a tighter crop, or different casting changes the treatment and re-runs; there is no submission and no return cycle. The second consequence is coverage: templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Aiuta's evidence is enterprise retail try-on, and it is genuinely impressive at that: recognizable global retailers running its shopper experience. We found no named customer references specifically for Aiuta Studio in the material reviewed, and no published performance metrics on the shopper-experience page beyond capability claims. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases. The relevant question is which body of evidence matches the job you are buying for.

documents.t: Consider a retailer already running Aiuta try-on across its apparel catalog. The ecommerce director likes the vendor, the integration is stable, and Studio promises catalog imagery from the same contract. Consolidating suppliers is a legitimately good instinct. Here is how the season plays out. Product images go in; polished outputs come back within 24–48 hours, QA-checked, and the acceptance rate is high. Then the creative director sees the first batch and wants the crop 15% wider and the light cooler. That is a new submission and another cycle. Two weeks later a campaign brief lands that needs editorial framing rather than catalog framing, and that is outside what the studio product is aimed at. The lookbook needs a different answer again. The consolidation saved a vendor relationship and did not save the production. With Astria, the crop change is an edit to the approved treatment, applied instantly across everything already produced and everything still to come. The campaign frames and lookbook come from the same treatment rather than a different supplier. And the try-on integration—if the retailer wants it—stays exactly where it is, doing the job it is genuinely good at.

documents.t: This is Aiuta's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Rendering a specific shopper into a garment in seconds, deployed at ASOS and adidas Originals scale, with SDK and API integration paths, is hard infrastructure that Astria does not build. Retailers whose bottleneck is fit confidence at the point of purchase should evaluate Aiuta on those merits and not expect a production tool to substitute.
documents.s: Enterprise shopper-facing try-on — winner: Aiuta

documents.t: A QA-checked delivery pipeline is dependable precisely because it is standardized, and standardization is the opposite of art direction. In Astria the treatment is the brand's object: editable by the brand's creative director, visible to the brand's team, and applied on the brand's schedule.

documents.t: A 24–48 hour turnaround is excellent for a service and slow for a decision. Creative work converges through rapid, cheap iteration; a delivery cycle makes each iteration a scheduled event. This is the single biggest practical difference between buying finished images and running production.
documents.s: Iteration speed — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta Studio is aimed at product photography. A season also needs lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, all sharing one visual language. Astria produces those from a single approved direction, which is both fewer suppliers and a more coherent result.
documents.s: Coverage of the season — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta advertises diverse AI models intended to reflect a brand's customers, which is the right ambition. Astria's reusable library goes further into production requirements: ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that persist across seasons.
documents.s: Casting depth — winner: Astria

documents.t: Aiuta's team surface is technical integration. Astria's is creative review: private brand workspaces, a multiplayer Board with named cursors, and live voice over the actual canvas, with the photographer, in-house studio, and agency all inside the same workspace.
documents.s: Collaboration and review — winner: Astria

documents.t: Studio throughput is bounded by the QA and delivery cycle, and no pricing is published, so a brand cannot model a season before entering a sales process. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—import the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive, run it against the approved setup—with brand pricing scoped to usage: pay for what you create. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper. The point is that a delivery cycle you cannot price is hard to plan a season around; model a full collection, including revisions, before comparing.
documents.s: Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria

documents.t: After a year with a delivery service, a brand has a large set of finished files. After a year with Astria, it has the files plus the casting, references, templates, and approvals that produced them—and the next season starts from those.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

You want the creative recipe at the end of the season, not only the files.

Aiuta is a serious enterprise try-on vendor, and its studio service is a reasonable convenience for retailers who want finished catalog files—just not a substitute for owning production. Consolidating vendors is sound procurement. Consolidating your art direction into a delivery queue is not.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Ayna

documents.t: Ayna positions itself as an AI photoshoot platform for fashion ecommerce brands. Upload a flat-lay, mannequin, or existing on-model photo, pick a model from an attribute-built library, choose a background, pose, and accessories, and Ayna generates the on-model shot—then rounds out the listing with a short product video, AI-written titles and descriptions, and a direct push to Shopify. Marketplace tooling is a real strength: compliant crops, ghost mannequins, platform-specific ratios, and bulk runs across large SKU batches. Ayna's own materials are candid about the job it does: it replaces the studio, the videographer, and the copywriter for routine catalog and marketplace work. That is a precise description of both the value and the boundary. The model library is deep—Ayna advertises over 1,000 attribute-built AI models, with brand-locked custom models on higher plans—and the categories skew toward marketplace-driven segments such as kidswear, ethnic wear, and plus-size.
documents.s: Ayna: listing automation from a single flat-lay

documents.t: Astria approaches the same category from the brand's side rather than the marketplace's. It gives fashion teams a workspace where products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together, so an approved look becomes a reusable recipe rather than a one-off generation. Templates cover fashion-specific categories beyond standard apparel PDPs—beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial—and brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic. Teams operate the approved workflow without becoming prompt experts, and creative decisions survive personnel changes because they are encoded in the workspace.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Ayna's case-study library is genuine adoption evidence, concentrated in marketplace-first fashion: customer stories describe Zucchini scaling catalog throughput on Myntra, Aditya Birla Fashion cutting per-SKU photoshoot spend, and D2C labels launching without a physical shoot. Ayna also reports 3,000+ brands and over a million images generated as self-reported platform data. These are vendor-written accounts rather than independent benchmarks, but they show real listing-volume adoption, including at enterprise brand houses. Astria's public materials show a professional production base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. This is also vendor-published evidence, but the signal points toward brand-directed production—lookbooks, campaigns, and social—rather than listing automation alone.
documents.s: Public proof: marketplace throughput versus professional production

documents.t: Imagine a brand launching 60 garments needing four PDP images per SKU, a small lookbook, paid-social variations, and a late colorway addition. With Ayna, the team uploads flat-lays, picks models and scene presets, and generates listings quickly—including marketplace variations and AI-written copy pushed straight to the store. Use Ayna pricing to budget for the full shot list and additional attempts. Each listing is also an independent generation: the lookbook, the social variants, and the late colorway each start from menu choices again, and image corrections route through an edit queue measured in working days. With Astria, the team defines casting, styling, lighting, and format once, approves the treatment, and runs the collection against it. The late colorway inherits the approved setup automatically. Campaign crops and video extend the same direction instead of restarting it, and reviewers work on the same board rather than trading screenshots.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: a seasonal drop

documents.t: Ayna's menus—models, scenes, poses, accessories—make each listing fast, and custom templates on higher plans add some reuse. But the unit of work remains the individual listing, and a menu of presets is not the same as encoding a brand's casting, styling, and art direction. Astria makes the approved direction itself the reusable asset: it persists across SKUs, channels, and contributors, and compounds over a season.
documents.s: Creative direction and repeatability — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna advertises fashion-grade realism and photoreal models, and its marketplace acceptance evidence suggests the routine case works. Its correction workflow, however, is metered: plans include one to three regenerations per image, and photoshoot edits carry a one-to-three-working-day turnaround depending on tier. Astria treats refinement as part of the workflow: a dedicated face-inpainting and refinement pass improves facial detail, skin, hair, and texture inside the production loop, without consuming a capped correction budget or waiting on a queue.
documents.s: Natural-looking people and corrections — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna's video product generates 10-second catalog and reel clips, metered per second of generation and capped per plan. That covers PDP motion. Astria offers a choice of current video-generation options so an approved still can be animated without leaving the workspace, alongside campaign, editorial, and social formats drawn from the same source assets.
documents.s: Stills, motion, and formats — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Ayna's genuine edge, and the one concession that matters: no other tool in this comparison turns a flat-lay into a complete, publishable listing—image, video, title, description, marketplace-compliant crops—and pushes it to Shopify in one flow, from a self-serve plan a team can start on today. It is a listing-operations advantage, not a creative-production verdict: the same pipeline that automates the routine listing standardizes it, and the brand's creative direction lives outside the tool.
documents.s: Listing automation and marketplace publishing — winner: Ayna

documents.t: Ayna's bulk runs produce marketplace variations at volume, but the commercial model meters the work: yearly image allowances, per-image credits, capped regenerations, and seat limits by plan. At collection scale the bill and the caps track every SKU, colorway, channel, and retry. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, the approved setup runs across it—and brand pricing is scoped to usage: pay for what you create, sized to the production engagement. A per-image allowance is not a production budget; model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria

documents.t: Ayna offers team seats—one on the entry plan, up to ten on the highest published tier. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: teammates see named cursors, talk over the actual canvas with live voice, and resolve looks together. And the work accumulates: products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs carry from the collection into campaigns, video, and social, so the photographer, in-house studio, and social agency share one source of truth instead of a folder of exported listings.
documents.s: Collaborative production and compounding value — winner: Astria

documents.t: Your catalog lives on marketplaces and you need routine listing imagery, video, and copy automated end to end. A self-serve start with published per-seat plans matters more than owning the creative direction. Your inputs are flat-lays or mannequin shots and the standard on-model treatment is acceptable. Listing enrichment and direct Shopify publishing are the core of the job.

Casting, styling, and scene decisions must survive team changes and late colorways. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through exported files. Video, campaign, and social work should extend the collection, not restart it.

documents.t: For professional fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it converts art direction into infrastructure that compounds across the season. Ayna is a capable, honestly positioned listing-automation platform—and the right answer when the entire job is routine marketplace content. Do not decide from hero images. Test the second SKU, the difficult garment, and whether a teammate can reproduce the approved look without help.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Run five representative SKUs—including one sheer, knit, or layered garment—through both products. Require PDP, detail, and campaign crops, then add a colorway after approval. Count the credits, regenerations, and queue days the round trip actually consumes. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction from scratch. That last test separates listing generators from production systems.

Users choose a Botika model and background, generate, review, and bulk-download results. Its onboarding guide documents corrections. This is convenient, but convenience is the product's ceiling: selecting generic options is not the same as directing styling, casting, garment behavior, lighting, and composition for a fashion brand.
documents.s: Botika: generic preset transformations

documents.t: Astria's broader fashion and ecommerce workflow moves from reusable templates and product inputs to ecommerce, lookbook, social, and campaign assets at scale. Templates move creative decisions upstream: define the treatment once, approve it, and reuse it across a drop. The templates gallery provides fashion-specific starting points, while brand references keep the result from collapsing into a generic AI aesthetic. Teams can operate the approved workflow without becoming prompt experts.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Botika's case-study library includes named examples from Jordache, Get Dressed Collective, BLVCK, Nil+Mon, and JUAN & ME. These are vendor-written first-party accounts rather than independent benchmarks, but they show real ecommerce adoption of Botika's transformation workflow. Astria's homepage and fashion materials show a broader production base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and professional photographers building client workflows on Astria. This is still vendor-published evidence rather than an independent benchmark, but the signal is materially broader: Astria is used by brands and the professionals who create for them, not only as an image-transformation app.
documents.s: Public proof: Botika's ecommerce cases versus broader professional adoption at Astria

documents.t: Imagine a brand has 60 new garments and needs four PDP images per SKU, a small lookbook, and social variations. The campaign should use the same casting direction and visual language, but the team expects late colorway changes. With Botika, the team prepares supported product photography, chooses models, poses, and backgrounds, and generates. Its flat-lay flow can combine garments and accept front and back views; eligible plans include corrections. The workflow processes the queue, but every new creative requirement remains bounded by the available presets. Botika's help documentation describes beta pose limits, while a newer guide documents back views. Confirm current behavior with representative garments. With Astria, the team establishes the casting, styling, scene, lighting, crop, and format once, then applies that direction across products. A late colorway, campaign crop, or video can reuse the approved setup. For a 60-SKU collection, that is the more capable production model.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: a 60-SKU drop

documents.t: Botika standardizes the job: upload, choose prepared options, and generate. That is practical for routine PDP refreshes, but it can also produce a generic template result—familiar AI polish, weak garment behavior, or styling, poses, and lighting that are not specific to the brand. Paid correction can address marked defects; it does not replace fashion art direction. Astria keeps fashion context in the workflow. Teams can draw from models—including children and extended-size casting—locations, poses, and other references. Templates extend beyond basic apparel PDPs into beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial treatments.
documents.s: Fashion direction — winner: Astria

documents.t: Botika's answer to synthetic-looking people is a manual service: on eligible plans, users flag an output and a human corrects or retouches it. That turns realism into a post-production queue, with turnaround and consistency dependent on manual intervention. Astria handles the problem as a professional technology layer. Its face-inpainting and refinement pass rebuilds facial detail, skin, hair, eyes, and texture—especially in full-body and wider fashion frames where generic generation can produce an obvious AI look. Human creative review still matters, but the finishing layer operates inside a repeatable production workflow rather than being outsourced as a correction request.
documents.s: Natural-looking people — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both products offer fashion video. Astria provides a choice of current video-generation options, allowing a team to animate an approved still without rebuilding the job elsewhere. Astria's Describe tool can turn a rights-cleared reference image into usable creative direction while accounting for product and model references already loaded. Its Agent can help reconstruct an existing brand treatment as a reusable AI setup. For a team with campaign material it already owns, that shortens the path from “make something like this” to a repeatable template. We could not verify an equivalent reference-to-workflow feature in Botika's public material reviewed for this article.
documents.s: Stills, motion, and existing brand material — winner: Astria

documents.t: Botika advertises team collaboration on its Advanced plan. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: teammates can arrange references, products, templates, and results on the same canvas, see named cursors, and start a live voice conversation over the work—closer to a creative review huddle than a file handoff. That distinction matters when art direction, merchandising, and production need to resolve a look together.
documents.s: Collaborative production — winner: Astria

documents.t: Astria becomes more valuable as the team uses it. Bring the full SKU set into one workspace from Shopify or Google Drive, create reusable avatars and templates, review together on the multiplayer Board with chat and voice, and run the collection. The approved products, casting, direction, and outputs can then move into campaigns and editorials, video, and social content. That keeps a photographer or freelancer, the in-house studio, and the social media agency on the same assets and approvals. Each stage builds on the last instead of duplicating uploads, recreating briefs, or restarting production in another tool.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: Botika publishes self-serve subscription tiers, which makes the first purchase simple. But those tiers meter per-image credits, so the bill grows with every SKU, variant, channel crop, and regeneration—and plan-dependent corrections sit on top. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage and the production engagement, and the approved setup is reused rather than re-prompted, so the commercial conversation matches how a brand actually produces. A per-image price is not a production budget—model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Commercial model — winner: Astria

documents.t: You need a standardized on-model PDP transformation from existing product photos. You are willing to trade category-specific fashion direction for generic preset choices. A correction queue is sufficient; you do not need to own a reusable creative workflow. Published credit pricing matters more than a distinctive, cross-channel visual system.

A creative director, photographer, educator, or studio will define a workflow that other people should reuse. The brand needs its casting, styling, scene, crop, and campaign direction to carry across a collection. Your briefs span different casting needs, category templates, stills, and video. Creative review should happen with the team on the shared canvas, not through exported screenshots. The durable deliverable should include the creative recipe, not only the exported images.

documents.t: For professional fashion brands, Astria is the clear choice. Botika handles a narrow product-photo transformation; Astria provides the fashion direction, breadth, finishing, motion, and team workflow needed to produce the collection and its channels. Do not decide from a polished hero image. The revealing test is the second SKU, the late colorway, and whether another team member can reproduce the approved direction.

documents.t: Run the same five representative SKUs through both products. Require PDP, detail, and campaign crops; add a colorway after approval. Have a senior fashion creative review the outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, lighting, brand fit, and visible AI artifacts. Then ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction. The final step reveals the difference between generating individual images and operating a repeatable workflow.

documents.t: Browzwear and Astria are adjacent, not interchangeable, and any honest comparison has to start there. Browzwear is 30 years of 3D apparel design and development: fabric physics, virtual twins, fit validation, tech packs, fewer physical samples. Astria is a production system for the brand's imagery. The real question buyers ask is narrower and more useful than "which one"—it is whether an existing 3D investment can also produce the catalog and campaign. The short answer: for producing on-brand imagery across a collection, Astria is the clear winner, and that is the decision this page addresses. For designing and validating garments before manufacture, Browzwear is the right tool and Astria does not compete with it. Plenty of brands should run both. documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Browzwear

documents.t: Browzwear's platform is built around a serious idea: if a virtual garment behaves like the physical one, most of product development can happen before anything is cut. VStitcher creates what the company calls accurate virtual twins of physical garments, combining AI-driven fit intelligence with true-to-life 3D simulation. Designers work across 2D drafting and 3D draping, fit on customizable avatars, grade across sizes, use tension and pressure mapping, and export tech packs with detailed specifications. Fabric Analyzer measures real fabric properties so the simulation is grounded in the actual material. Stylezone handles collection collaboration; the Open Platform handles integrations. The claimed outcomes are the ones a product development director cares about: 50–80% fewer physical samples, 95% first-time-right samples, double the development speed, 35% total cost reduction. The company cites over 1,000 apparel companies and 10 million digital garments created, with brands including Nike, Puma, Under Armour, Target, Walmart, and VF Corporation. These are vendor-published figures rather than independent benchmarks, but the adoption base in this space is not in question. Browzwear also states that the platform generates technical and ecommerce assets. That is true, and it is the sentence that brings buyers to this comparison.
documents.s: Browzwear: getting the garment right before it exists

documents.t: Astria starts where Browzwear's job ends. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—becomes the reusable unit that produces the season's imagery. The inputs are the difference. Astria works from the product photography a brand already has, not from a digital twin built to manufacturing tolerances. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same approved direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion. The people operating it are the brand's creative and ecommerce team, or the photographer or agency they work with—not a 3D department.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Browzwear's proof is deep and industrial: a thousand-plus apparel companies, household-name brands, and three decades of digital product creation. Read it for what it demonstrates—that 3D design and development works at scale in real supply chains. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Neither set of evidence transfers to the other's domain, which is the honest summary of this whole comparison.
documents.s: Public proof: development adoption versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a sportswear brand that adopted 3D development two years ago. Roughly half its styles have digital twins. The ecommerce team asks the obvious question: can we skip the photoshoot? Rendering from Browzwear is possible, and for the styles that have production-ready twins it can look excellent, because the garment geometry and fabric behavior are real rather than inferred. But the path has costs that do not appear on a license: only half the line qualifies, so the other half needs a different solution anyway; each render needs a 3D artist to build the scene, light it, and produce the frames; the avatars are fit avatars rather than cast models with a brand's point of view; and a request for a warmer campaign crop is a rendering job, not an edit. Producing 400 SKUs across four channels this way is a studio operation staffed with specialists. With Astria, the same team works from the product photography it already produces. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get approved once, the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, and the collection runs against that treatment. The styles with digital twins and the ones without are handled identically. Campaign and social extend the same direction, and motion animates stills that already passed review. The two are not in conflict. The 3D investment keeps paying for itself upstream—fewer samples, better fit, faster development—while imagery production stops depending on which styles happen to have twins.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the brand with 3D already in the building

documents.t: This is Browzwear's genuine edge and the one concession that matters, and it is a large one. True-to-life fabric physics, tension and pressure mapping, size grading, and tech pack generation solve problems that no image-generation product addresses, including Astria. If your objective is fewer physical samples, better first-fit rates, or a shorter development calendar, Browzwear is the answer and this comparison should not talk you out of it.
documents.s: Digital product creation, fit, and sampling — winner: Browzwear

documents.t: Producing imagery from 3D requires a production-ready digital twin, a specialist to render it, and a scene built per treatment. Producing imagery in Astria requires a product photo and an approved template. For a design team with twins for every style and 3D artists on staff, the first path is viable. For everyone else, the prerequisite is the obstacle.
documents.s: What it takes to produce one image — winner: Astria

documents.t: Browzwear's ecommerce output is a by-product of a development pipeline: accurate, technical, and centered on the garment. Lookbooks, campaign frames, editorial treatments, social-native crops, and motion are not what the software is for. Astria treats those as expressions of one approved direction, which is what a season actually requires.
documents.s: Coverage of the channels that sell — winner: Astria

documents.t: A fit avatar exists to test how a garment sits across sizes. A cast model exists to express who the brand is talking to. Astria's reusable library covers ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references—and it holds styling and composition decisions, not just body geometry.
documents.s: Casting and creative direction — winner: Astria

documents.t: Browzwear's collaboration is built for collections in development, which is the right shape for its users. Astria's multiplayer Board is built for the creative review: named cursors, live voice, and the actual production canvas shared by the photographer, the in-house studio, and the agency.
documents.s: Collaboration on the creative decision — winner: Astria

documents.t: Browzwear's imagery scale is bounded by digital twin coverage; a style without a production-ready twin cannot be rendered, and building one is development work, not marketing work. Astria imports the whole SKU set and runs it against the approved setup regardless of how each style was developed.
documents.s: Collection scale for imagery — winner: Astria

documents.t: Browzwear does not publish pricing in the material reviewed, and the real cost of imagery through a 3D pipeline is not the license—it is the specialist headcount that operates it. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage: pay for what you create. This article makes no claim about which is cheaper overall; it notes that the imagery cost in a 3D pipeline is mostly people, and asks you to model a full collection, including the styles without twins, before comparing.
documents.s: Commercial shape — winner: Astria

documents.t: Your objective is fewer physical samples, better first-fit rates, or a faster development calendar. Garment construction, fabric behavior, grading, and tech packs are the work. You have or want technical design and 3D specialist capability in-house. Imagery is a welcome by-product rather than the goal.
documents.s: Choose Browzwear if...

documents.t: The goal is producing the season's catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion assets. You want to work from product photography rather than build a digital twin per style. Your creative team, photographer, or agency should operate the workflow — not a 3D department. One approved creative direction must carry across the collection and its channels. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through rendered files.
documents.s: Choose Astria if...

documents.t: These two products belong in different parts of the year, and the most common right answer is both. For designing garments, validating fit, and cutting samples, Browzwear is a mature and well-proven investment. For producing the imagery that sells the finished collection, Astria is the stronger choice: it works from what the brand already has, covers every channel from one approved direction, and does not make marketing output depend on the state of the 3D pipeline.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: If you already run 3D, take five styles—ideally a mix with and without production-ready twins—and produce a full channel set for each: PDP, detail, campaign, and social. Track two numbers honestly: elapsed time and specialist hours. Then change the creative direction after approval and measure the cost of that change in each path. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask what happens to the styles that will never get a digital twin.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Caimera

documents.t: Caimera positions itself as an AI photo studio for ecommerce brands. Its Fluid tool transforms a single product shot into editorial-style imagery, while its Click tool swaps models and backgrounds on existing on-model or mannequin photos. A bulk catalog flow converts flat lays to on-model shots at volume, and the company advertises upscale quality suitable for billboard use. The workflow is deliberately prompt-light: upload a product, pick a template or describe a scene, generate, and refine with editing tools. A campaign ideas tool can read a brand's website or Pinterest board and propose moodboards. Caimera's own help documentation notes that Fluid works best when garment accuracy is not the top priority and recommends Click for delicate fabrics, textures, and sheer materials—an honest boundary that matters for demanding fashion work.
documents.s: Caimera: fast self-serve fashion imagery

documents.t: Astria approaches the same category from the opposite direction. Instead of optimizing a single transformation, it gives fashion teams a workspace where products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together. An approved look becomes a reusable recipe rather than a one-off generation. Templates cover fashion-specific categories beyond standard apparel PDPs, and brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic. Teams can operate the approved workflow without becoming prompt experts, and creative decisions survive personnel changes because they are encoded in the workspace, not in someone's chat history.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Caimera's case-study library is genuinely useful evidence: Adore Me, BlissClub, Floafers, Ioni Swim, and Maggie the Label describe measurable outcomes—higher click-through rates, lower CPAs, and large production-cost reductions. These are vendor-written accounts rather than independent benchmarks, but they show real commercial adoption, particularly for advertising imagery. Astria's public materials show a broader professional base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. This is also vendor-published evidence, but the signal points toward professional production use rather than purely self-serve image generation.
documents.s: Public proof: two credible adoption stories

documents.t: Imagine a brand launching 60 garments needing four PDP images per SKU, a small lookbook, paid-social variations, and a late colorway addition. With Caimera, the team uploads products, runs the bulk catalog flow, uses templates and the campaign ideas tool for social variants, and generates VooDoo videos for ads. Credit consumption is predictable and the queue moves fast. Each image, however, is largely an independent generation: changing the colorway or extending the campaign means re-entering prompts and re-checking consistency manually. With Astria, the team defines casting, styling, lighting, and format once, approves the treatment, and runs the collection against it. The late colorway inherits the approved setup automatically. Campaign crops and video extend the same direction instead of restarting it, and reviewers work on the same board rather than trading screenshots.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: a seasonal drop

documents.t: Caimera's templates and moodboard tool accelerate ideation, but the unit of work remains the individual image. Astria makes the approved direction itself the reusable asset: casting, styling, scene, crop, and format persist across SKUs, channels, and contributors. That distinction compounds over a season.
documents.s: Creative direction and repeatability — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both platforms take garment accuracy seriously, and Caimera's Click tool preserves garments well when starting from fitted product photography. But Caimera's documentation concedes Fluid's limits on intricate and sheer garments, and realism depends on which tool fits the input. Astria adds a dedicated face-inpainting and refinement pass that improves facial detail, skin, hair, and texture inside the workflow—a finishing layer rather than a manual correction request.
documents.s: Product fidelity and realism — winner: Astria

documents.t: Caimera's VooDoo agent produces short fashion videos, which covers many ad needs. Astria offers a choice of current video-generation options so an approved still can be animated without leaving the workspace, alongside campaign, editorial, and social formats drawn from the same source assets.
documents.s: Stills, motion, and formats — winner: Astria

documents.t: Caimera supports team collaboration from its Starter plan and human Photoshop requests on higher tiers. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: teammates see named cursors, talk over the actual canvas, and resolve looks together—closer to a studio review than a ticketing queue.
documents.s: Collaborative production — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Caimera's genuine edge, and the one concession that matters: self-serve onboarding mean a team can start the same day, without a sales conversation. It is an onboarding advantage, not a production-cost verdict—those plans meter per-image credits, so at collection scale the bill tracks how many generations, and regenerations, the work actually takes.
documents.s: Self-serve onboarding — winner: Caimera

documents.t: Caimera's bulk packshot flows produce images at volume, but each output remains an independent generation, and per-image credits accumulate with every SKU, colorway, channel, and retry. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work: the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive, the approved setup runs across it, and brand pricing is scoped to usage and the production engagement rather than metered image by image. A per-image price is not a production budget—model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Collection scale and commercial fit — winner: Astria

documents.t: In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate: the photographer, in-house studio, and social agency work from the same source of truth. In Caimera, value accumulates mostly as a library of generated images. Both models deliver ROI; only one builds an owned creative capability.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: You need product or ad imagery quickly, without a sales cycle. Published per-seat pricing and credit rollover matter for budgeting. Your inputs are already well-shot product photos suited to swap or bulk flows. You want API access, DAM integrations, or bulk packshots. Ad-creative velocity matters more than owning a repeatable brand production system.

documents.t: One approved creative direction must carry across a collection and its channels. A creative director or photographer needs to install a workflow other people can reuse. Casting, styling, and scene decisions must survive team changes and late colorways. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through exported files. Video and social should extend the campaign, not restart it.
documents.s: Choose Astria if...

documents.t: For professional fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it converts art direction into infrastructure. Caimera is a capable, honestly positioned tool for fast self-serve product and ad imagery—and the right answer when that is the entire job. Do not decide from hero images. Test the second SKU, the difficult garment, and whether a teammate can reproduce the approved look without help.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Run five representative SKUs—including one sheer, knit, or layered garment—through both products. Require PDP, detail, and campaign crops, then add a colorway after approval. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction from scratch. That last test separates image generators from production systems.

documents.t: Creator MAX (formerly Banana MAX) is the most fully featured bring-your-own-key panel on Adobe Exchange. It runs Google's Nano Banana models, OpenAI's GPT Image 2 and xAI's Grok Imagine inside one Photoshop panel, returns up to four variations per prompt, tracks usage, and puts no third-party server between you and the provider. It expects you to hold your own API keys. The verdict: the Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is the better buy for most Photoshop professionals. It bills every hosted model through one key, carries Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro that Creator MAX does not, picks up new models on launch day without a plugin update, and lands each result as a Smart Object at the model's full returned resolution. Choose Creator MAX if you already run funded provider accounts and want no server in the request path. documents.t: Five criteria, all from the retoucher's chair. First, the model roster and how quickly new models reach the panel. Second, output fidelity: the resolution that comes back, whether the result is a Smart Object or a flattened raster, and how the selection is honoured. Third, the editing workflow inside the document. Fourth, the commercial model: entry price, per-image cost, subscription or pay-as-you-go, and bring-your-own-key options. Fifth, maintenance and longevity. We also asked what happens when the job outgrows one document, because that decides whether the panel is the whole answer or the first step. We read both vendors' public material on 13 September 2026 and did not run Creator MAX.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Creator MAX

documents.t: Creator MAX is a UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (v26.0) and later on macOS and Windows, published by Bielfor LLC. It sells on Adobe Exchange and aescripts. The Exchange listing was first published on 27 February 2026 as a Gemini-only panel. The July 2026 v2.0.0 rebuild renamed it from Banana MAX, added OpenAI and xAI as providers, and brought the variations, spend dashboard and multi-document features. Version 2.1.2 followed in September 2026. Check the vendor listing for current commercial terms. The workflow is the familiar one: make a selection, type a prompt, pick a model, and the result lands as a new layer. Around that core Bielfor has built more than any other bring-your-own-key panel we reviewed. Up to four variations per prompt come back as grouped layers. Reference images can be dragged from disk, pasted from the clipboard or pulled from any open layer, up to 14 on Google models, 15 on OpenAI and 2 on xAI. Lock Edges keeps a selection border untouched during inpainting. Prompt Enhance rewrites a rough idea for the provider in use. Nano Banana 2 exposes a thinking level and Google Search grounding. Visual Prompt History stores thumbnails, prompts and the cost of each generation with one-click re-run, and a Usage and Spend dashboard tracks cost per model over time. Generations are recorded to the Actions panel, and results route back to the document they started in. The commercial and privacy design is the other half of the pitch. You bring your own Google, OpenAI or xAI API key; one is enough to begin, and each further provider needs its own account. Bielfor charges nothing per image and, in its own words, "no Bielfor server sits in the request path": prompts and images go straight from Photoshop to the provider, and history stays local. For a privacy-first retoucher that is the strongest reason to pick Creator MAX.
documents.s: What Creator MAX is

documents.t: The Astria plugin is a CCX/UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (v26 and later) on macOS and Windows, with no GPU required. The panel carries six models today: GPT Image 2 (OpenAI, mask-aware, 1K/2K/4K), Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1), Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro), Seedream 5 Pro, Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro. Flux Kontext was retired in favour of these. Three things separate it from Creator MAX. The model list is served by the Astria platform, so a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches with no plugin update. Every result is placed as a Smart Object that holds the model's full returned resolution. And billing has two paths. Pay-as-you-go against one Astria key that authenticates every model, with Astria abstracting the Google, OpenAI, fal and ByteDance APIs so quota, auth and retries are invisible. Or your own Google AI Studio key for the Gemini models, billed by Google. No subscription, no minimum; you top up only what you need. Per-image rates are on the pricing page. The workflow is the same three steps. Select with marquee, lasso, brush or colour range; prompt in short, specific terms, with reference images dropped into the panel read as visual instructions; generate, and the result lands as a new layer. Mask-aware models read the selection directly, keys switch inside the panel, and the model is chosen per task from one dropdown. Behind the panel sits the Astria platform, where the same key and balance drive workspaces, templates and the API.
documents.s: What the Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is

documents.t: Astria's landing page reports substantial adoption and shows production reels covering fashion reference edits, bridal retouching, sketch and CAD to photo, product design, real estate, hair and clothing swaps, and packaging. Those are first-party claims. Users of the older JSX script received the CCX build as an upgrade, and the script still supports Replicate-backed workflows. Creator MAX's public proof is its two listings, a dated release history on bielfor.com going back to February 2026, and a walkthrough video. Bielfor publishes no sales or user counts in the material reviewed. Neither vendor publishes an independent benchmark.
documents.s: Public proof, with provenance

documents.t: The brief: a campaign hero of a model on a studio cyclorama. The client wants the shoes swapped for the new-season pair from a reference photo, the background extended for a 4:5 crop, and the phone taken out of the model's hand. Then the same treatment across the other forty SKUs in the drop.
documents.s: A realistic job: one campaign hero, three fixes, then forty SKUs

documents.t: You paste a Google AI Studio key into the panel; for GPT Image 2 as well, you open an OpenAI account and paste that key too. Lasso the shoes, pull the reference pair in from disk or from a layer, write the prompt or run Prompt Enhance, choose Nano Banana Pro, and submit up to four variations. They arrive as a group of named layers cropped to the selection, with Lock Edges keeping the border untouched. Pick the best, mask the rest. For the 4:5 crop you extend the canvas, select the empty band and prompt for a continuation of the backdrop. For the phone, select the hand and inpaint. Visual Prompt History shows what each attempt cost in dollars, and the spend dashboard totals the day. What is not public is what those layers hold. Bielfor says output is up to 4K depending on the model and that results are cropped to the selection. Whether the layer keeps every returned pixel when the selection is smaller than the output, and whether it is a Smart Object, is not stated. The forty SKUs stay in Photoshop: Actions recording replays a generation and results route back to the right file, but each document is still opened, selected and submitted by hand, on your own provider quota.
documents.s: In Creator MAX

documents.t: You sign up, generate an Astria key in one click and paste it in; no Google, OpenAI or ByteDance account is involved. Lasso the shoes, drop the reference pair into the panel, and prompt: "swap the shoes for the reference pair, keep the stance and the floor shadow". GPT Image 2 reads the lasso directly, so the edit stays inside it; Nano Banana Pro is the alternative when identity and material matter more than the mask. The result lands as a Smart Object at the resolution you chose. Extend the canvas for 4:5, marquee the empty band, and ask Seedream 5 or Nano Banana 2 to continue the cyclorama with the same light direction. Brush the hand and ask GPT Image 2 to remove the phone. Generate the hero at 4K, scale it down for the comp, and scale it back for print; the Smart Object still holds every returned pixel. Every generation bills against one balance, whatever the model. Then the forty SKUs leave Photoshop. The same Astria key and balance drive Astria workspaces and templates, where the approved treatment runs across the rest of the drop, and the API if you want it automated. Photoshop keeps the hero and the fixes; the workspace does the volume. That route is described in the AI fashion photoshoot guide.
documents.s: In the Astria plugin

documents.t: Creator MAX covers Google, OpenAI and xAI. The Astria plugin covers OpenAI, Google, ByteDance and Black Forest Labs. Seedream 5 Pro, Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro are in the Astria panel and not in Creator MAX; Grok Imagine is in Creator MAX and not in the Astria panel. For retouching, Seedream's handling of long, structured prompts and GPT Image 2's mask-aware replacement matter more often than a second general-purpose generator.
documents.s: Which models you can reach — winner: Astria

documents.t: Creator MAX adds models in plugin releases, "once they clear our quality bar". Its release notes date GPT Image 2 to the July 2026 rebuild and Grok Imagine Image 2.0 to 27 August 2026; each arrived as a download. Astria's landing-page changelog dates GPT Image 2 in its panel to April 2026. Its model list is served by the platform, so a model added to Astria shows up in the dropdown with no plugin update. On 13 September 2026 the Astria platform banner listed GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image; none appears in Creator MAX's listing. Retirements cut the same way: Creator MAX still lists the original Nano Banana, which Google shuts down on 2 October 2026.
documents.s: How fast a new model arrives — winner: Astria

documents.t: The Astria plugin places every generation as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned pixels, so a 4K result dropped into a small selection can be re-transformed, masked and re-edited later without resampling. Creator MAX describes results as named layers cropped to the selection; its layer type and retained resolution are not publicly verified, so we do not assume either way. For a retoucher who delivers layered files, this is the row to test first.
documents.s: Smart Objects at returned resolution — winner: Astria

documents.t: Creator MAX's model is honest and simple: your keys, your bills, no middleman. The cost is set-up. To reach its full roster you open and fund a Google AI Studio account, an OpenAI account and an xAI account, and you handle quota, errors and retries with each. The Astria plugin offers the same Google key path for the Gemini models, and adds a hosted path where one Astria key authenticates every model and the platform handles the provider APIs. A studio can hand a junior one key and one balance. We do not claim Astria's hosted rate beats Google's direct rate; compare per-image rates on the pricing page.
documents.s: One key versus one account per provider — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both use a one-time plugin licence with generation usage billed separately. Creator MAX depends on the provider accounts you fund; Astria offers hosted top-ups or a Google key for Gemini. Compare current terms on the Creator MAX listing and Astria pricing page using the same representative workload.
documents.s: Cost to start — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Creator MAX's genuine edge, and it is wide. Four variations as grouped layers, reference images from any layer, Lock Edges, Prompt Enhance, thinking level, Search grounding, usage history, a spend dashboard, Actions recording and multi-document routing are all shipping today. The Astria plugin does not advertise variations per generate, a cost preview, a spend dashboard or Actions recording. Add the no-server design, and a retoucher whose client contracts forbid a third-party relay has a clear reason to choose Creator MAX.
documents.s: Depth inside the panel — winner: Creator MAX

documents.t: Creator MAX ends at the Photoshop window. The Astria plugin is one surface of a platform: the same key and balance run workspaces, templates and the API, so the forty SKUs behind the hero do not have to be forty Photoshop sessions. See the ecommerce production page.
documents.s: Beyond the document — winner: Astria

documents.t: You already hold funded Google, OpenAI or xAI API keys and want your generation spend on those invoices. A client or compliance rule requires that no third-party server sits between Photoshop and the model provider. You lean on variations, layer-sourced references, a spend dashboard or Actions recording every day. Grok Imagine is part of your toolkit. You want a trial before paying and are buying through aescripts.
documents.s: Choose Creator MAX if...

documents.t: You want GPT Image 2, Nano Banana, Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro in one hosted panel. You would rather paste one key and top up a balance than open and fund up to three provider accounts. Layered deliverables matter, and you want each result as a Smart Object at the model's full returned resolution. You want the next model in the dropdown on launch day, not after the next download. The hero is in Photoshop but the rest of the collection needs a workspace or an API.
documents.s: Choose Astria if...

documents.t: Creator MAX is the best-built bring-your-own-key panel we reviewed and the right buy for a retoucher who already runs provider accounts and wants the request path to themselves. For everyone else, the Astria plugin is the better decision. It brings a wider hosted roster, one key for every model, Smart Objects that keep the returned pixels, and launch-day models with no re-download. When the job leaves the document, the platform behind it runs the volume.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Take one PSD, one lasso selection about a quarter of the canvas, one reference image and one prompt, and run it in both panels at 4K on Nano Banana Pro and on GPT Image 2. Record the returned pixel dimensions and the layer type. Scale the result down by half, then back up, and check whether detail survives. Count the accounts you had to open and fund to run both models, and time each generation. Then price a realistic week of edits on both, using each provider's published rates for Creator MAX and the Astria pricing page for the hosted path. If layered delivery is your business, the Smart Object test decides it.

documents.t: DRESSX and Astria both put clothes on people with AI, and there the overlap ends. DRESSX builds the experience a shopper has at the moment of decision: a fitting room on the product page, an AI stylist, an interactive mirror in the store. Astria builds what fills that page in the first place—the catalog imagery, the lookbook, the campaign, the social cutdowns. The short answer: for producing a brand's imagery, Astria is the clear winner, and that is the decision this page addresses. For adding a shopper-facing fitting room to a product page or a store, DRESSX is the specialist and Astria does not compete for it. A brand with budget for both is not making a mistake. documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs DRESSX

documents.t: DRESSX has been in digital fashion since 2020 and has converged on a clear enterprise proposition: an AI suite for fashion and luxury brands, sold as modules. Virtual try-on is the flagship, answering the question the company puts at the center of its pitch—whether an item will actually look good on the shopper. It handles single items, full looks, and mix-and-match, integrates through an API, a white-label option, or a Shopify plugin, and the company advertises very fast integration. Around it sit adjacent products: an AI customer assistant, an AI stylist for retail, and DRESSX Mirror, a human-sized interactive screen for stores, pop-ups, window displays, and events. Named implementations include Victoria Beckham and Farfetch. The published outcome claims are aimed squarely at ecommerce leadership: a 40% reduction in return rate, a 3.2× conversion lift, 68% higher engagement, and up to 75% fit certainty. These are vendor-published figures without disclosed methodology, and a buyer should ask how they were measured and over what baseline. But they are the right metrics for what DRESSX sells, and they are not metrics a content production tool should be claiming.
documents.s: DRESSX: the experience at the point of decision

documents.t: Astria's job starts earlier in the funnel and further back in the calendar. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—becomes the reusable unit that produces the season. That covers the assets a try-on experience cannot: the PDP images a shopper sees before deciding to engage, the lookbook that frames the collection, the campaign that drives traffic, the social cutdowns, and the motion. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial alongside apparel, and the same approved direction runs across the whole SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: DRESSX publishes brand implementations and conversion-oriented statistics. Read them as evidence that the experience layer gets deployed by serious retailers, and probe the methodology in a demo. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Neither company's evidence speaks to the other's domain, which is the accurate summary of this comparison.
documents.s: Public proof: storefront metrics versus production adoption

documents.t: Trace a single customer journey for a spring dress. She sees a paid-social video, clicks through to a campaign landing page, browses the collection grid, opens the product page, scrolls the four PDP images and a detail shot, then taps "try it on." DRESSX owns the last step of that journey and does it well. Everything before it—the social video, the campaign frame, the collection grid, the five PDP images—is content the brand had to produce. If the answer to producing it was a photoshoot, DRESSX has not changed the brand's production economics at all; it has improved the conversion rate on assets that still cost what they always cost. With Astria, that entire upstream chain comes from one approved treatment: the campaign frame, the grid, the PDP set, the detail crop, and the social video all derive from the same casting, styling, and direction, run across the collection. The try-on button at the end is a complementary purchase, not an alternative one.

documents.t: This is DRESSX's genuine edge and the one concession that matters. Rendering a specific shopper into a specific garment, at request time, on the product page or an in-store mirror, is a hard problem with direct commercial consequences—and Astria does not attempt it. Brands whose live problem is return rates or fit hesitation should evaluate DRESSX on that basis, ask hard questions about how the published lift figures were measured, and not expect a content production tool to substitute.

documents.t: A fitting room improves the last click. It does not make the campaign, the grid, or the PDP set. Astria produces all of them from a single approved direction, which is why the collection reads as one shoot rather than a series of separately commissioned jobs.

In Astria the direction is the stored, reusable thing: casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format, editable by the brand's own team and applied to everything downstream.

documents.t: DRESSX scales with catalog coverage on the storefront, and its commercial model is an enterprise integration rather than published pricing. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—import the SKU set, run it against the approved setup, extend into campaign and motion—with brand pricing scoped to usage: pay for what you create. The two are not substitutes on cost, and this article makes no claim that one is cheaper; they buy different things.

documents.t: Every season, Astria's workspace holds more: products, avatars, templates, approvals, outputs. A try-on integration does not compound in the same way—it performs the same function on whatever catalog it is pointed at, which is exactly what it should do.

An AI stylist or customer assistant fits your retail experience roadmap. Your content production is already solved.

A creative director, photographer, or agency needs to install a workflow other people can reuse. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through exported files. Your production cost, not your conversion rate, is the constraint.

documents.t: If content production is the bottleneck, Astria is the answer and try-on will not help. If content is handled and conversion is the bottleneck, DRESSX is the answer and a production system will not help. Most brands discover, in order, that they have the first problem — because the fitting room is only as good as the collection page that got the shopper to it.
