documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Emilia AI Studio

documents.t: Emilia's promise is compact and well executed: upload a product photo, pick a style, get campaign-ready images in seconds. Three output types anchor the experience—clean packshot, with presenter, and lifestyle scene—and six category libraries supply the style presets. Campaign kits produce ready-made sets of four images, applied all at once or chosen individually. The editor is the part that stands out. Users draw on an image to mark a region, then describe the change or drop a reference image; there are move and remove operations, a proper filter set spanning instant film, teal and orange, high-key and low-key, bleach bypass, rim light, noir and more, plus background removal, simple and advanced expand, aspect-ratio resizing across eight ratios, and AI super-resolution up to 4K. That is more genuine editing craft than most self-serve generators in this category offer. Practical touches are sensible too: a WooCommerce plugin and CSV upload for catalog import, bulk upload, a true free tier, and an interface available in English, Hebrew, and Spanish. The company describes itself as built by a digital agency, and it reports 150,000+ images generated, 5,000+ active businesses, 42+ countries, and around forty seconds per image. Two things a fashion buyer should read carefully. The first is what "Lookbook" means here: up to three variations of one product from different angles or focal points. Useful, and not what a fashion team means by a lookbook. The second is the plan structure, discussed below.
documents.s: Emilia AI Studio: breadth across the shelf

documents.t: Astria narrows to fashion and spends the depth there. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces a season. That means casting is a library rather than an entitlement, references accumulate rather than expiring against a storage cap, and templates encode the conventions of apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work as production disciplines. Campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion all derive from the same approved direction, and review happens on a multiplayer Board with named cursors and live voice, with external photographers and agencies inside the same workspace.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Emilia publishes volume statistics—images generated, active businesses, countries, average generation time. Those describe reach, and in the material we reviewed we found no named customer, case study, or testimonial. That is common for a self-serve product at this stage; it also means a buyer has nothing specific to verify. Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published too, and at least checkable by looking.
documents.s: Public proof: aggregate figures versus named brands

documents.t: Consider a womenswear label with 60 styles going live, needing four images per style at 4K, plus campaign assets and social crops. The team evaluates Emilia against that complete brief. The first week goes well. The editor is pleasant, packshots and lifestyle scenes look good, and the WooCommerce import saves real time. Then three constraints arrive together. Casting: the brand wants three recurring models for different segments of the line, so it needs to check that the plan supports its casting requirements. Credits: use current Emilia pricing to budget for every required image and rejected attempt. Storage: the plan caps stored images, so a season's output has to be managed against a ceiling. Then the campaign brief lands. Campaign kits give four ready-made images per category, which is a starting point rather than a brand's campaign. A real lookbook is not three angle variations. Motion for social is not something we could verify the product does at all. With Astria, casting is a library the brand builds and keeps, the 60 styles run against one approved treatment, the campaign and editorial frames come from that same direction, and motion animates stills that already passed review. Nothing in the season is rationed by a plan tier.

documents.t: This is Emilia's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Region-select editing with a reference-image drop, a real filter set, expand, background removal, and super-resolution gives an operator direct manual control over a finished frame, and several larger competitors in this category offer less. If your work is a modest number of images that each need individual attention, that toolkit is a real advantage.

documents.t: A product serving food, furniture, and apparel optimizes for what they share: a clean subject, a pleasing background, a consistent light. Fashion's hard parts are not shared—drape on a knit, how a sleeve breaks, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention held across a collection. Emilia's jewelry and beauty categories are style presets for those product types; Astria's are production disciplines with their own casting, lighting, and framing logic.

For a seller shooting one product line that is generous. For a fashion brand, casting is not a feature allowance: a womenswear line, a kids range, and an extended-size offer are three casting requirements before anyone discusses campaigns. Astria treats casting as a reusable library, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Eti Image

documents.t: Eti Image is a CCX/UXP panel built by Pouya Eti for Photoshop 2023 or later on macOS and Windows. Its product page lists seventeen generation and editing models and ten enhancement and analysis tools, twenty-seven entries in all, spanning Seedream, Nano Banana, GPT Image, Flux, Qwen and WAN plus Magnific, Topaz and other upscale, relight and expand tools. None of it runs on a hosted Eti Image account. You bring a Replicate, Kie.ai or Google AI Studio key, and the page maps each model to its provider. Replicate serves most of the roster; Kie.ai serves GPT Image 2 at 4K, WAN 2.7, Qwen 2.0 and Nano Banana 2 Lite; Google serves Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro only. The Magnific tools need a paid Magnific subscription on top. Eti Image offers tiered licensing. The higher tier adds fast actions on Seedream 5 Pro, premium upscalers, the Magnific skin, relight and expand tools, and a prompt library. The panel also runs one prompt across several models in parallel, places results as layers masked to the selection since version 3.0.0 (August 2026), and includes a Product Views generator. Check the vendor page for current licence and refund terms.
documents.s: Eti Image: the widest bring-your-own-key menu in a Photoshop panel

documents.t: The Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is a CCX/UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (version 26 and later) on macOS and Windows. It carries six current models: GPT Image 2 from OpenAI, mask-aware at 1K, 2K or 4K; Nano Banana 2 on Gemini 3.1; Nano Banana Pro on Gemini 3 Pro; Seedream 5 Pro; Seedream 5; and Flux 2 Pro. Three things separate it from a bring-your-own-key panel. The model list is served by the Astria platform, so a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches, with no plugin update or re-download. GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image are already on the platform. The workflow is three steps: select with the marquee, lasso, brush or colour range, prompt, generate. Mask-aware models read the selection directly, references dropped into the panel act as visual instructions, and the model is chosen per task from one dropdown. And each generation is placed as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution. The Astria plugin uses a one-time licence with hosted usage billed separately. One key authenticates every model, and Astria abstracts the Google, OpenAI, fal and ByteDance APIs so quota, authentication and retries are invisible. Or paste a Google AI Studio key into the panel for the Gemini models. No GPU is needed. Check the Astria pricing page for current terms.

documents.t: Take a footwear campaign hero. The art director wants the shoes swapped for the new colourway from a reference shot, the background extended so the frame survives a 4:5 crop, and a phone removed from the model's hand.

documents.t: First, decide which provider serves the models you want and fund it. Nano Banana Pro for the shoe swap runs on Replicate or a Google key; GPT Image 2 runs on Replicate, or through Kie.ai for 4K; Magnific Expand for the background needs the Pro tier and a Magnific subscription. With the keys in, the edit is what you would expect: select the shoes, drop in the reference, prompt, and the result returns as a layer masked to the selection. The parallel mode can run the same swap across Seedream 5 Pro, Nano Banana Pro and GPT Image 2 at once so you pick the best. Whether the returned layer is a Smart Object, and whether it holds more pixels than the selection covers, is not stated on the product page.
documents.s: Running it in Eti Image

documents.t: Sign up, generate an Astria key, top up, paste it into the panel. That is the whole provider setup, for every model. Lasso the shoes, drop the colourway reference into the panel, pick Nano Banana Pro from the dropdown for its subject consistency, and generate; the new shoes land as a Smart Object at the model's full returned resolution. Enlarge the canvas to 4:5, marquee the new band, and generate the extension with a mask-aware model that reads the selection directly. Select the phone and the hand around it and prompt the removal; the bridal reel on the landing page shows that exact job. Short prompts win.

documents.t: The campaign has forty more shoes that need the same treatment, and this is where the two products stop resembling each other. Eti Image ends at the panel, so every SKU is another Photoshop session. The Astria key that paid for the hero also drives Astria workspaces, templates and the API, so the approved look runs across the rest of the collection outside Photoshop while the panel is kept for the hero and the fix. documents.t: This is Eti Image's real advantage, stated once and plainly. Twenty-seven entries in the panel, including families Astria does not carry (Qwen, WAN, Flux 2 Max and Klein, Flux Kontext), upscalers to 16×, Magnific relight and expand for Pro owners, a Product Views generator, and one prompt fired at several models in parallel. It also runs on Photoshop 2023, two major versions below Astria's floor, and comes with a 14-day refund where Astria offers none. If those are the things you would use every day, and you already hold the provider accounts to feed them, Eti Image is the more capable toolbox.

documents.t: Eti Image's breadth is paid for in accounts. Its provider map sends different models to Replicate, Kie.ai and Google, and its Magnific tools to a fourth subscription. Each is a sign-up, a payment method, a balance and a key to paste, and a model whose provider you have not funded sits in the dropdown unusable until you do. Astria collapses that to one key and one balance: GPT Image 2, the Gemini models, Seedream and Flux all authenticate through it, and the plugin handles the upstream APIs so a quota error at Google or a retry at fal never reaches you.

Scale a 4K swap into a small selection today and re-transform it larger tomorrow, and the pixels are still there. For a hero re-cropped for three channels, that is one generation instead of three.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs FashionLab

documents.t: FashionLab positions itself for brand and marketing teams producing on-brand AI content, and its core flow is a clean five-step batch: select garment references as flat lay or on-body, assign models, choose pose, choose background, then generate dozens of looks with consistent models and backgrounds. Generation times are quoted around ninety seconds, and the company is unusually candid about disclosing the underlying generation model it uses. Its casting options are broader than most small competitors: a free library of diverse AI models, custom brand-specific models, and the option to hire authorized digital twins of real models and influencers. Its published use cases include kids fashion—explicitly framed around avoiding the complexity of photoshoots with minors—and size inclusivity, both of which are real production needs that many tools in this category ignore. Credit where it is due: that is a thoughtful use-case set. The genuinely novel part is the Creative Marketplace. Brands can hire specialized talent for creative direction, prompting, retouching, and project management; creators can find paid projects from brands. A separate in-built professional retouching service handles polished finishing at scale. No other product in this comparison bundles a labour market with the software. Check the vendor’s current pricing page for brand, project, seat, and token terms. Published proof is early: one named testimonial from a brand and marketing manager at Bruun Steengade, plus a reference to top Scandinavian brands.
documents.s: FashionLab: generation plus a talent layer

documents.t: Astria's answer to the same problem is to make outside expertise less necessary each season. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored so the next person runs it rather than rebuilding it. That extends across categories and channels. Templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct disciplines; the casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references; and campaign, editorial, social, and motion all derive from the same direction. When a brand does bring in an outside photographer or art director, that person works inside the workspace and leaves the treatment behind.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: FashionLab's public evidence is a single named testimonial and a regional claim. That is honest for a young product and it gives a buyer little to verify. Its marketplace, if it reaches liquidity, may become its strongest proof—brands returning to hire talent is a hard signal to fake. Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and broader across brand size and contributor type.

documents.t: Consider a brand with three lines—womenswear, a kids range, and a small accessories capsule—producing roughly 200 SKUs a season. On FashionLab, the batch flow handles the womenswear and kids imagery well, and the kids use case is a real strength. Where the model shows its shape is in the account structure and the economics of expertise. Check the current pricing page for the brand, project, collaborator, and generation capacity required by the full collection, including rejected frames. If the brand does not have a strong prompt-fluent operator, the marketplace answer is to hire one—which works, and which means the brand's creative consistency is a contractor relationship rather than a stored asset. On Astria, each line gets a brand workspace, the treatment is approved once per line, and the 200 SKUs import from Shopify or Google Drive and run against it. The accessories capsule uses jewelry templates rather than being forced through an apparel flow. Motion for social comes from the same approved stills. When the brand hires an outside art director, that person works in the workspace and the direction stays after the invoice is paid.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: buying expertise versus keeping it

documents.t: This is FashionLab's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Hiring vetted creative directors, prompt engineers, retouchers, and 3D artists from inside the platform—plus a professional retouching service for polished finishing—solves a real problem: most brands adopting AI production do not yet have the skills in-house. Astria does not offer a labour marketplace. Brands that know they need people as much as software should weigh this seriously.

documents.t: The marketplace solves the skills gap by supplying a person. Astria solves it by making the output of that person durable: once a treatment is approved, running it does not require the expert. Both are legitimate strategies; only one of them costs less next season than it did this one.

documents.t: Price the whole shape of your business, not the entry plan: count brands, projects, seats, and a realistic annual generation volume including rejected frames. Ask for social motion derived from an approved still. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask what remains yours if you stop paying.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs FASHN

documents.t: FASHN describes itself around a single clear promise: realistic images of your clothes, worn by anyone. It ships that promise in two forms. The app gives brands, agencies, and creators a set of tools—product to model, model swap, AI model creation, background removal, editing, reframing, 4K upscaling, face swap, and short video. The endpoint suite offers the same capabilities to other software: try-on at up to 4K, product to model, model swap, image to video, and more, with published latency ranges and language SDKs. The customer signal is worth reading closely. On the app side, FASHN publishes testimonials from fashion-adjacent businesses and marketplaces. On the endpoint side, the logos are largely other AI products and tools rather than fashion brands. That is not a criticism—it is an accurate picture of what FASHN sells best. It is a capability that other people build products and workflows around, and it is good enough at that job to have become infrastructure for a chunk of this category. FASHN also does real work on consistency. A face reference can anchor a specific look across generations, and model creation exposes control over age, body type, expression, and styling. A brand that needs the same face on 200 PDPs has a supported path.
documents.s: FASHN: a capability, packaged two ways

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is not the image; it is the treatment. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together in a brand workspace, so an approved look becomes something a team runs rather than something one operator recreates. The practical consequence is what carries forward. A face reference keeps a face consistent; an Astria template keeps the casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format consistent, then applies that whole treatment to the next SKU, the next colorway, and the next channel. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work, and Astria's Describe tool can turn a rights-cleared reference into usable creative direction while accounting for products and models already loaded.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: FASHN's published proof points to genuine traction in its own lane: named app testimonials from fashion businesses and a roster of software products building on its endpoints, alongside open-source model releases that earned it technical credibility. These are vendor-published signals rather than independent benchmarks. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: recognizable names including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, plus studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and also an adoption signal rather than a quality proof—but it points at a different buyer. FASHN's strongest evidence is that developers ship with it. Astria's is that fashion teams produce with it.
documents.s: Public proof: developer adoption versus brand production

documents.t: Consider a small creative agency producing seasonal content for three fashion clients: catalog imagery for one, a lookbook and campaign for another, social-first content for the third. Different casting, different visual language, different approvers. With FASHN, the agency works tool by tool. Product to model for the catalog shots, model swap where a client supplies existing on-model photography, a face reference per client to hold casting steady, then editing and reframing for channel variants. It works, and for individual assets it works quickly. But each client's visual language lives in the operator's head and in a set of remembered settings; seats are capped by plan; and automating the catalog client's volume means building against the endpoints, which is an engineering project, not a production feature. With Astria, each client gets a private brand workspace. The agency defines the treatment once per client, approves it, and runs the collection against it. Client approvers join the multiplayer Board and review the actual canvas with voice rather than receiving a folder of exports. When the catalog client adds a colorway in week six, it inherits the approved setup instead of restarting it—and when the agency hands the workflow back to the client's in-house team, the recipe goes with it.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: an agency running three client brands

documents.t: FASHN is organized around operations. You pick a tool, supply an input, get an output. That is the right shape for try-on, and it is a poor shape for a season, because nothing above the individual image is durable. Astria is organized around the treatment: the approved combination of casting, styling, scene, crop, and format that a brand wants repeated. Once that exists, running the next SKU is an execution step rather than a fresh creative decision.
documents.s: Unit of work: operation versus treatment — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is FASHN's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. If the requirement is try-on—shopper-facing, inside your own product, at 4K, with documented latency and language SDKs—FASHN is built for exactly that and Astria is not. Teams whose roadmap item is "add try-on to our app" should choose FASHN and stop reading. That is a real and well-executed job; it is simply a different job from producing a brand's campaign and catalog imagery.
documents.s: Virtual try-on as an embeddable capability — winner: FASHN

documents.t: Check FASHN pricing for current team access and plan terms. Astria treats review as part of production: private brand workspaces, a multiplayer Board with named cursors, and live voice over the actual looks. For work that passes between a photographer, an in-house studio, and an agency, the question is not how many logins exist but whether the next person inherits the decisions.
documents.s: Collaboration, review, and handoff — winner: Astria

documents.t: Scaling FASHN to a full catalog is possible and well documented, but the path runs through its endpoints: someone writes the integration, manages the queue, and reassembles the outputs. That is a reasonable trade for a product team and an unreasonable one for a brand's creative department. Astria imports the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive and runs it against the approved setup as a normal operation.
documents.s: Collection scale — winner: Astria

documents.t: FASHN's app plans are per-seat with monthly and daily credit allowances, and credits are consumed by every generation, including the frames a creative director rejects. That is a sensible model for individual operations and an awkward one for a collection push, where rework is the norm and seats multiply across contributors. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create, sized to the production engagement. A per-credit rate is not a production budget; model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria

documents.t: In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate, and each stage of the season keeps what the last one approved. With FASHN, what accumulates is a library of finished images plus, if you built one, an integration. Both have value. Only one of them is the brand's creative capability.

documents.t: Run five representative SKUs—including one sheer, knit, or layered garment—through both products. Require PDP, detail, and campaign crops, then add a colorway after approval. The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for fashion brands producing catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social imagery. documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Figma Weave

documents.t: Figma acquired Weavy on October 30, 2025 and relaunched it as Figma Weave. The product's premise, in Figma's own framing, is that the first prompt is a creative starting point rather than a final destination—so generation and hands-on craft belong in the same place. In practice that means a node-based canvas where outputs from many current models can be combined, branched, and refined, with professional editing operations—inpaint, outpaint, relight, upscale, crop, masking, color work—applied as part of the graph rather than in a separate tool. Model coverage is deliberately broad across image, video, and 3D. Workflows are reusable: a author builds the graph once, and Figma Weave can generate a simplified interface so teammates can run it without touching the nodes. Since 2026 a set of Weave tools and community workflows has been reachable directly inside Figma Design. It is genuinely excellent software. It is also, by intent, a general creative environment—the published examples span ad generation, product photography, illustration, storyboarding, and 3D rendering. Nothing in it is specifically about fashion.
documents.s: Figma Weave: a canvas for building creative pipelines

documents.t: Astria makes the opposite trade. Instead of a canvas that can express any workflow, it supplies a workflow that already understands fashion: products, casting, references, templates, and outputs in a brand workspace, with the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—as the reusable unit. The practical difference is what you start with. A fashion template for footwear, jewelry, beauty, or editorial work already encodes the conventions of that category. A casting library already spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting. The SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive rather than being wired up. Astria's Describe tool can extract usable direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for products and models already loaded. None of that is a node graph anyone had to author.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Figma Weave's evidence is its adoption across creative disciplines—independent creatives, startups, and enterprise teams including architects, VFX artists, marketers, and designers—and the credibility of the Figma platform around it. That is a strong signal for general creative production and says nothing specific about fashion catalogs. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published, and narrow on purpose.
documents.s: Public proof: creative breadth versus fashion production

documents.t: Consider a brand with 200 SKUs, a small creative team, and a design lead who is fluent in Figma. The Figma Weave path is attractive because the design lead can build exactly what the brand wants: a graph that takes a product photo, places it on a generated model, applies the brand's lighting treatment, produces four crops, and upscales. Once built, the team can run it behind a simplified interface. The costs are real but easy to overlook. Someone has to design that graph and keep it working; the fashion judgment inside it—how this brand casts, how a knit should fall, what crop convention the PDP uses—is knowledge the graph author supplies, not knowledge the tool contributes; and every new category, a jewelry capsule, say, is a new graph. When the design lead leaves, the pipeline becomes an artifact nobody fully understands. The Astria path starts further along. The team picks a fashion template appropriate to the category, loads the products, sets casting and styling, approves the treatment, and runs the SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive. What the brand maintains is a creative decision, not a piece of software. When someone new arrives, they inherit an approved treatment rather than a graph.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: who builds the pipeline

documents.t: This is the whole comparison. A node canvas is infinitely expressive and completely uninformed: it will happily build a beautiful pipeline that gets a garment's drape wrong, because nothing in it knows what drape is. Astria's templates, casting library, and product-reference handling exist because fashion has conventions worth encoding once. Flexibility is valuable when your outputs are unpredictable; supplied domain knowledge is valuable when they are not.
documents.s: Supplied knowledge versus built knowledge — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Figma Weave's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Combining many current models with professional editing operations—relight, inpaint, matte work, compositing—inside a single node graph, reachable from the design environment a team already uses, is a real capability advantage for creative work in general. Teams whose output spans ads, illustration, motion design, and product imagery will get more from that breadth than from any fashion-specific system, and they should choose accordingly.
documents.s: Model breadth and editing craft on one canvas — winner: Figma Weave

documents.t: Figma Weave's answer is thoughtful: workflow authors can publish a simplified UI so teammates run the graph without editing nodes. But that still divides the team into people who can change the workflow and people who cannot. In Astria, changing the crop convention or the casting is an edit to the treatment, made by the person who owns the creative decision.
documents.s: Who can run it without help — winner: Astria

documents.t: A season is catalog, detail, lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion, produced consistently across a collection. Figma Weave can produce every one of those as an individual asset. Astria produces them as expressions of one approved direction, which is what makes them look like a collection rather than a set of executions.
documents.s: Coverage of a fashion season — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both scale, differently. Figma Weave scales a workflow once the workflow exists. Astria scales a creative decision: import the SKU set, run it against the approved treatment, extend into campaign and motion. The distinction matters most when the direction changes mid-season—an edit to a template versus a revision to a graph.
documents.s: Collection scale — winner: Astria

documents.t: Figma Weave consumption sits inside Figma's credit and plan structure, which is designed for a design organization rather than for a collection's production budget. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create, sized to the production. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper; the point is that credits inside a design-seat subscription are a hard thing to map onto 200 SKUs across four channels. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.
documents.s: Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria

documents.t: In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate in a workspace shared by the photographer, the studio, and the agency. In Figma Weave, what accumulates is a library of workflows—valuable, and dependent on the people who authored them.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: Your team produces many kinds of visual work, not primarily fashion collections. You want access to many current models with professional editing on one canvas. You have someone who enjoys building and maintaining node-based pipelines. Deep integration with Figma Design is a meaningful advantage for your workflow.

documents.t: You are producing a fashion collection and want the fashion knowledge supplied, not built. One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion. Casting across ages and body types, and category-specific templates, matter to your work. The people who own the creative decision should be able to change it themselves. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, alongside your photographer and agency.

documents.t: For fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it starts where a node graph would need to be built, and it keeps the creative decision editable by the person who made it. Figma Weave is exceptional general-purpose creative software, and for a design team with broad output it may well be the better investment—just not the faster route to a season's catalog.

Add a second category—jewelry, footwear, beauty—and see what each requires. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask whether the person who owns the brand's look can make a change without the person who built the pipeline.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs FLORA

documents.t: FLORA describes itself as the AI-powered canvas for designers, brand teams, and agencies, and it has built a genuine fashion solution on top of that foundation. The pitch for fashion teams is end to end: from a sketch to a render, through colorways and fabrics, to on-model and campaign imagery, with batch application of one approved look across every SKU. It splits the experience into a Fashion Studio for everyday work and a Canvas for deeper ideation where models and steps chain together into reusable workflows. The platform breadth is real: FLORA advertises access to 50+ models spanning image, video, and multimodal reasoning under one subscription, with recognizable video models available for cinematic work. It reports venture backing, and its published references include Pentagram, Lionsgate, Base Design, and Hebbia. That reference list is the most useful signal for a fashion buyer. Pentagram is a design consultancy; Lionsgate is entertainment; Hebbia is enterprise software. They are impressive names and they attest to FLORA's quality as a creative environment. What the fashion solution page offers instead of brand case studies is credits to individual designers. For a brand evaluating who has actually run a season on the platform, that is a thinner evidence base than the platform's overall profile suggests.
documents.s: FLORA: a creative canvas that reaches into fashion

documents.t: Astria is deliberately less ambitious in scope and more specific in depth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces the season. Depth shows in the assets. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season. Templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories rather than variations on apparel. And the collaboration model assumes the work crosses company boundaries, because in fashion it almost always does.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: FLORA's evidence establishes that serious creative organizations choose it. That matters, and it is not the same as evidence that fashion brands produce collections on it. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Both sets are vendor-published adoption signals rather than independent benchmarks. The difference is which industry they come from.
documents.s: Public proof: creative credibility versus fashion production

documents.t: Consider a contemporary label developing a 120-piece resort collection. The design team explores silhouettes and prints in the autumn; the production team needs catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social assets in the spring; a freelance photographer sets the visual direction; an agency handles paid social. FLORA is genuinely strong in the autumn half. Sketch-to-render, colorway exploration, and print and pattern replacement are exactly the design-stage problems a creative team has, and having 50+ models on one canvas makes exploration cheap. The spring half is where the shape of the product starts to matter. Batch across SKUs exists, but the casting depth is shallower, category templates outside apparel are thinner, and—most practically—every additional collaborator is a seat. Check FLORA pricing for current seat and usage terms when adding the photographer, agency collaborators, and merchandiser. Astria inverts the emphasis. It contributes little to the autumn exploration, and it is built for the spring: the approved treatment runs across the 120 pieces imported from Shopify or Google Drive, campaign and social extend the same direction, motion animates approved stills, and the photographer and agency work inside the brand workspace rather than against a seat count.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the season, from sketch to shipped

documents.t: This is FLORA's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Sketch to render, colorway and fabric exploration, print and pattern replacement, and very broad model access make it a strong environment for developing what a collection should look like before it exists. Astria does not compete for that work. Design teams whose central problem is exploration should weigh this heavily.
documents.s: Design-stage ideation — winner: FLORA

documents.t: Beyond apparel, fashion production is beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial, each with its own conventions of lighting, crop, and styling. Astria treats those as first-class templates. Casting depth matters just as much: age range, body type, children's and extended-size casting are production requirements, not preferences, and a general on-model capability does not cover them.
documents.s: Fashion-specific depth — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is where per-seat licensing quietly shapes the work. Fashion production is collaborative across company lines—photographer, in-house studio, agency, merchandiser—and a model that charges per seat and caps self-serve teams at eight makes each additional participant a cost decision. Astria's brand workspaces are built for that cast of collaborators, with a multiplayer Board, named cursors, and live voice over the actual looks.
documents.s: Who gets to be in the room — winner: Astria

documents.t: Both companies publish first-party proof. FLORA's strongest names come from design and entertainment; Astria's come from fashion brands and the studios that serve them. Neither is an independent benchmark, and a buyer should discount both accordingly—but when the question is "has anyone run a fashion season on this," the relevant evidence is the fashion evidence.
documents.s: Evidence in your own industry — winner: Astria

documents.t: FLORA batches one approved look across SKUs, which is the right idea. Astria imports the SKU set directly from Shopify or Google Drive and runs the approved treatment across it, then extends the same direction into campaign, editorial, social, and motion. The difference is how much of the season comes out of one decision.
documents.s: Collection scale — winner: Astria

documents.t: FLORA's shape is a creative-suite subscription: per seat, per month, with metered usage credits layered on and enterprise options for larger teams. That is coherent for a design department with stable headcount, and awkward for a production that expands and contracts around a season and pulls in outside collaborators. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it observes that seats plus credits is not a production budget. documents.t: Graswald describes itself as the AI production studio for fashion brands, and the workflow matches: a team establishes brand standards—custom avatars, lighting, studio scene, poses—then generates across the catalog, including batch runs driven by CSV upload. Supported output spans PDP on-model imagery, packshots, lookbooks, lifestyle content, and video, with 4K resolution and PIM/DAM integrations. The customer evidence is genuinely strong for this category. The VAUDE case study reports 50% lower content production costs and 30% more content published live, with the brand generating from flat-lays and factory sample photos on two custom avatars that replicate its studio scene digitally—work the internal team now runs in-house. The PUMA case study describes something more unusual: adapting central global creative to individual US retailer specifications for wholesale, so partners receive imagery that meets their guidelines without a round of rework. Two caveats a buyer should carry into a demo. The PUMA story, unlike the VAUDE one, publishes no quantitative outcomes. And the homepage headline figures—90% cost reduction, 10x faster, 100% brand consistency—are vendor absolutes. "100% brand consistency" is not a testable claim; your own difficult garments are.
documents.s: Graswald: enterprise brand standards, configured once

documents.t: Astria shares the configure-once thesis and diverges on who the system is for. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace that a creative director, an in-house team, an outside photographer, or an agency can all work in. The approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit, and it is designed to be handed over rather than maintained by one party. Coverage is the other divergence. Astria's templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work alongside apparel, so a brand with an accessories line or a beauty extension is not routing those categories elsewhere. Astria's Describe tool can turn a rights-cleared reference into usable creative direction while accounting for the products and models already loaded, which is a faster path from "match our last campaign" to a template than commissioning a new avatar build.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Graswald publishes named enterprise stories—VAUDE with real numbers, PUMA on wholesale localisation—plus a strategic partnership with Orendt Studios. That is a serious set of references for large-brand catalog work, and it is vendor-published rather than independently verified. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. Also vendor-published. The distinction worth noting is the shape of the base: Graswald's evidence concentrates in large enterprises with internal content teams, Astria's spans brands and the external creatives they hire.
documents.s: Public proof: enterprise logos versus production breadth

documents.t: Consider a mid-size brand whose visual direction comes from an outside photographer it has used for six seasons. The brand wants to produce most of its catalog and campaign imagery with AI, but it wants that photographer's eye encoded in the result, and it wants its own two-person ecommerce team running the work by spring. With Graswald, the path runs through the vendor: an enterprise conversation, then a collaboration to build custom avatars and replicate the studio scene and lighting digitally. That produces a strong result—VAUDE's story describes exactly this and the outcome was good—but the brand's photographer is not naturally a participant in it, and the configuration lives in an enterprise engagement rather than in a workspace the brand's creative partner can operate. With Astria, the photographer works directly in the brand's workspace: sets the casting, builds the templates, uses Describe to pull direction out of a rights-cleared reference from a previous season, and reviews with the ecommerce team on the multiplayer Board with live voice. When the season starts, the two-person team runs the approved treatment across the SKU set imported from Shopify or Google Drive. The photographer's judgment is now the brand's asset, and the handoff happened inside the tool rather than as a document.

Astria is used by brands and by the creatives who serve them, which changes who can put the system in place.

Producing imagery that satisfies each retail partner's format, dimension, and background specifications—out of the box, from one central creative—is a specific and unglamorous problem that large wholesale brands actually have, and Graswald has a named enterprise reference for solving it. Paired with PIM/DAM integration, that makes it a strong fit for brands whose content pipeline is an operations function. It is a distribution-compliance advantage rather than a creative-direction verdict.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Higgsfield

documents.t: Higgsfield has grown past the one-feature category. Its Product Photography workflow starts from one or several product photos and advertises studio, lifestyle, on-model, detail, multi-angle, colorway, batch, 4K upscale, and channel-resizing outputs. Marketing Studio keeps products in a reusable library, can import them from a site or social link, and applies templates across product shots, UGC, ads, marketplace images, posters, and motion graphics. Products and avatars persist, and layered poster elements remain editable. The image side is not merely utilitarian. Soul 2.0 is positioned as a fashion-aware foundation model with reference images, moodboards, color transfer, editorial composition, and Soul ID for consistent characters. AI Stylist lets a creator change a look by category — outerwear, base, pants, footwear, accessories — then choose pose and background presets. That makes Higgsfield unusually credible at both fashion aesthetics and fast content variation. Motion is where the distance opens. Canvas connects prompts, references, images, and video models into a node-based pipeline on a shared board. Cinema Studio adds the language of production — cameras, lenses, focal lengths, movement, cast, locations, and multishot sequences — rather than reducing video to “animate this image.” Higgsfield also aggregates current third-party models and advertises native connections to the editing applications where filmmakers finish the work. That breadth is Higgsfield's advantage and the main buying caution. Product Photography, Marketing Studio, Canvas, Cinema Studio, Soul, the Apps catalog, and Supercomputer are several different surfaces. A capable team can connect them into a pipeline. A fashion brand should test whether the exact product, casting, and art-direction decisions it approved are recalled as one reusable production setup, or whether its operator is responsible for rebuilding that context across tools.
documents.s: Higgsfield: a broad creative suite with real fashion and film depth

documents.t: Astria starts with a narrower question: how does a brand produce one season so that the catalog, lookbook, campaign, editorial frames, social crops, and motion all look as though the same team directed them? Products, casting, locations, poses, references, templates, and outputs live in one brand workspace. The reusable object is the approved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format together — so it can be run against the next SKU and recalled next season. The SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive rather than being assembled asset by asset. That is also where Astria spends its category depth. Templates encode different conventions for apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work. Casting spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes. A campaign frame and a PDP are different outputs from the same direction, not unrelated generations that happen to use the same product. Astria's Board is an infinite production canvas with multiplayer cursors and live voice. A photographer or agency can build the workflow with the client inside the same brand workspace, then leave the approved template behind. The public API and fine-tuning system are available without requiring an enterprise contract.
documents.s: Astria: the collection is the operating model

documents.t: Higgsfield publishes better production evidence than most general AI suites. In its first-party case study, Istanbul studio Sinecera describes using Cinema Studio, AI Cast, Soul ID, AI Locations, and Multishot in an approval-gated workflow, with an approved still before motion. The same story names a full-AI Lacoste × SuperStep film and a hybrid production model where several artists work inside one project. A separate first-party profile of director Sasha Kasiuha describes using Soul 2.0 and Cinema Studio for selected AI-assisted B-roll around Dolce & Gabbana and Madonna projects. The most persuasive point is the modesty of the use case: generative work extends an authored visual world instead of pretending that access to a model replaces direction or post-production. Astria's public materials name fashion brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers producing client work. Those are vendor-published references too. Higgsfield has the stronger published film-production detail; Astria's evidence is closer to the collection-production decision this article addresses.
documents.s: Public proof: Higgsfield deserves to be taken seriously

documents.t: Consider a fashion brand launching 80 styles. It needs five ecommerce frames per style, a 24-image lookbook, eight campaign hero images, and twelve short social clips. A creative director has approved the casting, warm directional light, a low camera position, and a particular balance between clean PDPs and slightly imperfect editorial movement.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: one drop, two operating models

documents.t: The team can get surprisingly far. Product Photography supplies the catalog shot types and batch claim. Marketing Studio turns products into ad and social formats. Soul creates the editorial keyframes. Canvas connects references to still and video branches. Cinema Studio gives the motion team more model choice and more explicit camera language than Astria offers, and the Adobe, DaVinci, and Figma integrations reduce export friction. The critical test happens after the first ten styles. The creative director asks for the light to move cooler, keeps the same casting, and changes only the campaign crop. The buyer should watch whether those decisions update one reusable fashion treatment that can be run across every remaining SKU, or whether an operator has to update several products, templates, nodes, or projects. Higgsfield has the components; the question is how much production logic the brand must supply. The meter should be tested at the same time. Higgsfield charges credits according to the chosen model, resolution, and duration. Individual subscription credits expire at renewal, while add-on credits expire after their stated period. Selected Unlimited access applies only to manual generation on the main website: Canvas, MCP, CLI, and Supercomputer always spend credits. A workflow designed around Canvas or automation must therefore be costed in credit mode even when a pricing card advertises Unlimited models.

documents.t: The brand imports the SKU set, keeps the products and trained casting inside its workspace, and runs the approved treatment across the catalog. The cooler-light revision changes that treatment; it does not start a separate product-photo job. Lookbook and campaign frames derive from the same product, casting, and visual references, and approved artboards carry those decisions into motion. The photographer, ecommerce lead, and agency review together on the Board. Astria has fewer filmmaking surfaces and less model choice. It does not replace a dedicated finishing stack. What it removes is the work of turning a broad set of generation tools into a fashion production system every season.

A large current model catalog, Cinema Studio, camera and lens language, multishot generation, VFX presets, audio-capable models, and integrations with editing software make it the more capable environment for filmmakers. A fashion film whose central problem is the shot rather than the catalog should be tested in Higgsfield first.

The difference appears after approval: whether the casting, garment references, scene, crop, light, and channel format become one production asset that can be applied to the next SKU and recalled next season. For a brand, that repeatability matters more than the number of models behind a generation button.

documents.t: Both platforms now cover far more than on-model apparel. Higgsfield is broader across general products and marketing formats, with packshots, UGC, posters, ads, marketplace assets, and motion graphics. Astria is deeper across fashion disciplines and connects ecommerce, lookbook, campaign, editorial, social, and motion around one collection. The correct winner depends on whether “breadth” means more media formats or more of the fashion season.

documents.t: Higgsfield's Canvas is a real shared production surface, not a token team folder: prompts, models, outputs, and versions live together, and business plans pool credits and assets. Astria's Board adds named cursors and live voice inside the brand workspace, with photographers and external agencies treated as participants in the production. Test the people who actually cross company boundaries, not just two coworkers on the same account.

Some protections are explicitly reserved for Enterprise, so buyers should read the tier boundary carefully. Astria's advantage is different: its public API and fine-tuning are not held behind an enterprise sales process.

The complication is that the rate changes with the model and settings, and web-only Unlimited access does not cover Canvas or automated workflows. Astria's brand model is usage-scoped rather than a flat monthly credit allowance. Neither structure is automatically cheaper. documents.t: Lookgen's three-step flow is deliberately unglamorous: upload items in whatever form you have them—flat lay, hanger shot, ghost mannequin, straight off the rack—pick a virtual model, and generate. From there a stylist adjusts poses, swaps accessories, and fine-tunes, then extends the look to more camera angles and different sceneries before publishing. Two things distinguish it. First, the emphasis on complete outfits rather than single products: accessories can be added in one click, from the brand's own collection or generated, and the customer testimonials repeatedly describe showing shoppers styling options rather than individual garments. Lookgen says it was built in collaboration with professional stylists so that expertise sits inside the product, and the framing rings true. Second, the publishing path: Lookgen connects to a PIM and DAM to import, code, and publish automatically, which for a European multi-brand retailer is often the part that decides whether a tool gets used at all. Its published proof is a wall of named-person testimonials—WE Fashion, NAADAM, Esqualo, The English Hatter, Suitable, Arthur & Willemijn—which is a more checkable form of evidence than aggregate statistics, even though it remains vendor-published. Access is through a booked demo; no pricing is published.

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is not the look but the treatment behind it. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved combination of casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format becomes the reusable thing. That is a superset of look-building in practice. Astria produces the styled on-model shots, and it also produces the campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion from the same direction. Categories go beyond apparel plus accessories into beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, and luxury as full template disciplines, and the casting library spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes.

documents.t: Lookgen's testimonials name individuals at recognizable European retailers, which makes them unusually verifiable for vendor content—you can look those people up. documents.t: Consider a menswear retailer with 300 SKUs that merchandises by outfit: a jacket shown with the right shirt, trousers, and shoes, so shoppers buy three items instead of one. Lookgen is well aimed at this. A stylist builds the looks, swaps accessories, generates angle variants, and the results publish into the PIM without a manual handoff. For catalog merchandising of styled combinations, that is a tight, purpose-built loop, and the retailer's ecommerce team gets exactly the assets it needs. The gaps appear at the edges of the season. The spring campaign needs imagery with a point of view rather than a scenery swap. Social needs motion. The accessories line has a jewelry capsule that needs macro treatment, not one-click placement. A new hire needs to produce looks consistent with what the stylist established, and the direction lives in the stylist's choices rather than in a stored treatment. And the brand's freelance art director cannot join the work without a demo and a contract. With Astria, the styled looks come from an approved treatment that also produces the campaign, the editorial frames, the social crops, and the motion. Jewelry and beauty have their own template categories. The art director works inside the brand workspace, reviewing on the multiplayer Board with live voice, and what the stylist decided is stored rather than remembered.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Looklet

documents.t: Looklet has been doing this since 2009, and its architecture reflects that lineage. The workflow starts in a studio: garments are shot in a Looklet setup, with the company describing up to 100 items per day handled by one or two operators. Captured items are processed with automated quality control and a human check, with turnaround stated in hours. Only then does the styling step happen, in software where a team composes looks on digitized models—mixing garments shot at different times without reshooting—and exports with metadata for the storefront. The model library is the part competitors cannot easily replicate. Looklet's digitized models are real people captured with a large range of facial expressions and body movements, alongside a smaller set of AI-generated models. For a retailer with licensing sensitivities, digitized real models are a meaningfully different proposition from synthetic faces. The customer evidence is correspondingly serious. Looklet's Saks Fifth Avenue case study describes deployment across five studios, single-operator shoots replacing eight-person crews, and looks live within 6–24 hours. It is vendor-written, but the operational detail is specific enough to be checkable, and it describes exactly the buyer Looklet is built for.
documents.s: Looklet: digital styling on top of a capture operation

documents.t: Astria removes the capture step from the equation. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the inputs are the product photographs a brand already has. An approved look becomes a reusable treatment rather than a styling session repeated per item. The consequence is reach. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work rather than catalog PDPs alone, and brand references keep results anchored to the brand's visual language. The same approved treatment extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion, so the season's assets come from one direction instead of several disconnected production tracks.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Looklet's proof is enterprise retail: Saks Fifth Avenue, Holt Renfrew, and Stockmann, with outcomes framed around staffing, turnaround, and cost per look. That is credible evidence of industrial catalog production and it should be read as such. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Both sets are vendor-published adoption signals rather than independent benchmarks. They describe different jobs: Looklet's customers are running a photography operation more efficiently; Astria's are producing a brand's creative output.
documents.s: Public proof: retail operations versus brand production

documents.t: Consider a growing contemporary brand with roughly 500 SKUs a year. It needs catalog imagery, a seasonal lookbook, campaign assets, and social content, and it currently books a photographer twice a season. Choosing Looklet means choosing an operating model. Garments must reach a studio and be shot there; the enterprise tier bundles the hardware to make that possible in-house. Once that pipeline exists, catalog throughput is genuinely excellent and the per-look styling economics improve with volume. But the brand has taken on a capture operation—space, equipment, sample logistics, and operators—to solve what was, for it, a creative problem rather than a throughput problem. The lookbook, campaign, and social work still need a separate answer. Choosing Astria means the product photos the brand already produces become the input. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get defined once and approved; the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive and runs against that treatment. The lookbook and campaign extend the same direction, motion animates stills that already passed review, and there is no sample-to-studio logistics chain in the middle.

documents.t: This is the decisive difference and it comes before any image quality discussion. Looklet's workflow assumes a capture step you operate; Astria's assumes product photography you already have. For a retail group amortizing five studios across tens of thousands of SKUs, Looklet's assumption is sound. For most brands, installing a capture operation to produce catalog imagery is a larger commitment than the problem warrants.

documents.t: This is Looklet's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Nothing else in this comparison combines a licensed portfolio of digitized real people, hundreds of expressions and body movements, quality-controlled processing, and same-day delivery at retailer volume. If your requirement is thousands of consistent catalog looks per season with real-model likeness rights already handled, Looklet is built for precisely that and Astria is not competing for it. It is a throughput and licensing advantage, not a creative-direction verdict.

They are not campaign frames, editorial spreads, jewelry or beauty treatments, or social-native crops. Astria treats all of those as expressions of one approved direction, which is why a brand can run the season from a single setup instead of routing each channel to a different supplier.

It is efficient and repeatable, but the reusable unit is the model and the template, not the brand's point of view. Astria encodes casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, and format as an approved treatment that another operator can run without being told what the brand wants.

When merchandising, art direction, and an outside agency need to agree before a drop, that is where the time goes.

documents.t: Lumoo's product page shows a source image branching into model shots, detail views, and video. It lists cropping, colour controls, template packages, and live collaboration; Basic and Pro also list Shopify integration. The page names brands including GANT, Gina Tricot, Holebrook, NEUW, and Nikben. Those are vendor-published references, not independent evidence of image quality. Our assessment: the appeal is keeping adjacent tasks in one place. If the team currently passes each image between a generator, an editor, and a crop tool, test whether a connected flow reduces that work. The public feature list alone does not establish how much time it will save or how reliably casting carries from one item to the next. A generated back view needs particular care. A single front photo cannot document unseen construction. Supply the actual back and detail references when they matter; reject plausible inventions. The preparation checklist in flat lay to on-model applies here too.

The useful question is what the team can reproduce, not which homepage has the more ambitious promise. See the AI lookbook guide for that approval sequence.

Use product photography cost per SKU to turn that into a useful budget. The same accounting applies to Astria. Ask for a price against the identical output list, and include preparation and review. documents.t: Medicraft sells the plugin on aescripts and Adobe Exchange as a single-user licence, with a floating server licence and a trial on aescripts. The Exchange package is a compact UXP plugin, published 19 September 2025 and at version 2.3.0 since July 2026. The pitch is generation without a separate hosted balance. In practice you create a Gemini API key in Google AI Studio, paste it in, and Google bills you under its current API terms. The listing notes that an "exceeded quota" error can mean billing is not configured. Check Google's pricing page for current availability and terms. The model list is the Gemini image line and nothing else: Nano Banana 1, Nano Banana 2 (added 27 February 2026, with Search grounding and a thinking-level control), Nano Banana Pro, and Nano Banana 2 Lite (added 2 July 2026). Nano Banana 2 has a resolution override of auto, meaning match the selection, or 1K, 2K and 4K. Inside the document, Medicraft has built useful things: references from the active layer or a file, output as a new layer or into the original, an edge-feather helper, an editable prompt library with history, and Actions recording on Photoshop 25 and later. The version floor is low: Adobe Exchange lists Photoshop 22.2 or higher and the aescripts description says 24.2 (2023) and above. Support runs through a ticket portal, and the readme's advice for "Internal API Error" is to click Generate again.
documents.s: Medicraft Nano Banana Generative Fill: a Gemini-only panel on your own Google key

documents.t: The Astria plugin is a CCX/UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (version 26 and later) on macOS and Windows. Select with the marquee, lasso, brush or colour range; type a short prompt, dropping reference images into the panel if the edit should follow a look; generate. Mask-aware models read the selection directly, and the result lands as a new layer. Six hosted models sit in one dropdown: GPT Image 2 from OpenAI with mask-aware editing at 1K, 2K or 4K; Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1); Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro); Seedream 5 Pro; Seedream 5; and Flux 2 Pro. Flux Kontext was retired in favour of these. Because the model list is served by the Astria platform, a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches, with no plugin update. The platform already carries GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image, listed on the site banner on 13 September 2026. Each generation is placed as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution. A 4K result placed into a small selection still carries the 4K pixels, so it can be re-transformed, masked and re-edited later without resampling. Billing has two paths in one panel. An Astria key authenticates every hosted model with pay-as-you-go top-ups; Astria abstracts the Google, OpenAI, fal and ByteDance APIs so quota, authentication and retries stay invisible. Or paste a Google AI Studio key and run Nano Banana calls on your own Google account. Keys switch inside the panel. Current terms are on the Astria pricing page; the workflow is in the Nano Banana Photoshop guide.

documents.t: Medicraft's evidence is its two listings and a version history from 28 September 2025 to 2.3.0 on 2 July 2026. Adobe Exchange reviews are mixed; the critical ones cluster around key and quota errors rather than image quality, which matches the vendor's own notes about connecting a payment method. In our September 2026 search checks the aescripts page sat at the top of results for the plugin query. Astria's evidence is first-party: the landing page reports 16,000 sales and 187 ratings, and shows seven production reels covering fashion edits with references, bridal retouching, sketch and CAD to photo, product design, real estate, hair and clothing swaps, and packaging. Both vendors' numbers are adoption signals, not quality benchmarks.

documents.t: A footwear brand sends a retoucher one campaign hero. The shoes need swapping for the new colourway from a product reference, the background needs extending for a 4:5 crop, and a phone in the model's hand has to go. Then the brand mentions forty more SKUs.
documents.s: One campaign hero, then forty SKUs: the same job in both plugins

documents.t: Setup first: a Google AI Studio key and a payment method connected to Google, because Nano Banana 2 and Pro are paid-tier models. Then select the feet, add the colourway reference from its layer, prompt the swap, and generate to a new layer with Nano Banana Pro. Feather the edge with the helper. Enlarge the canvas, select the empty band, and generate with Nano Banana 2 at 4K. Select the phone, prompt its removal, and write the result in place. On an "Internal API Error", the readme says to click Generate again. That is a workable hero. For the forty SKUs the plugin offers only repetition: an Action can replay a fixed prompt on Photoshop 25 and later, but each file still needs its own selection and generation on your Google account.

documents.t: Select the feet, drop the colourway reference into the panel, pick Nano Banana Pro for identity consistency, and generate. For a surgical replacement inside a brushed selection, switch to GPT Image 2, which reads the mask directly. The result arrives as a Smart Object at full returned resolution, so the shoe can be re-transformed later without resampling. For the 4:5 extension, send the empty band to Seedream 5, which handles long structural prompts, or to Nano Banana 2 at 4K. For the phone, GPT Image 2 reads the brushed selection directly. Every call runs on one Astria balance, or on your Google key for the Gemini steps. For the forty SKUs, the same key and balance drive Astria workspaces and templates, where the approved colourway, crop and background become a reusable setup. Photoshop for the hero and the fix, Astria workspaces for the other forty.

documents.t: This is where Medicraft's design choice bites. Before your first Nano Banana 2 or Pro generation you need a Google AI Studio key, a payment method connected to Google, and a billing relationship you monitor yourself. The vendor's listing documents the "exceeded quota" error that greets users who skip that step. Google's pricing page, updated 11 September 2026, shows no free tier for any image model and marks the original Nano Banana as deprecated with shutdown on 2 October 2026, so the free path narrows further next month. The Astria plugin offers the same Google-key route for Gemini models and adds a hosted path: one key, one balance topped up when needed, and quota, authentication and retries handled across every model. A BYOK-only design removes the hosted intermediary, which may suit a Gemini-only user who already runs Google billing. Compare the same representative workload on Google's pricing page and the Astria pricing page before deciding.
documents.s: Billing path and the Google setup step — winner: Astria

documents.t: Medicraft's changelog shows care here: a resolution override for Nano Banana 2, gamma correction for 32-bit documents, and support for colour spaces such as ProPhoto RGB. It also notes that large images are compressed before upload. Its public material does not state the layer type of the result, so we report it as not publicly verified. The Astria plugin places each generation as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution, which is what a retoucher needs when a 4K result must be repositioned or masked a week later.

documents.t: Credit where it is due, once. Medicraft's edge-feather helper, editable prompt library, in-place output option and Actions recording are real conveniences the Astria plugin does not advertise. Its Photoshop floor is also lower, at 22.2 on Exchange or 24.2 per aescripts, against Astria's Photoshop 2025 requirement. If you are pinned to Photoshop 2023 or 2024, Medicraft is the panel you can actually run.
documents.s: In-document helpers and older Photoshop — winner: Medicraft

documents.t: Medicraft's public material describes no web app, workspace or API. The Astria plugin is one surface of the Astria platform: the key that runs a generation in Photoshop also runs Astria workspaces, templates and the API, which matters the moment a job becomes a collection.
documents.s: Production beyond the document — winner: Astria

documents.t: Medicraft is an independent developer with a ticket portal. The Astria plugin has a company and support desk behind it, a dated changelog, first-party adoption claims, and a platform that absorbs upstream failures instead of asking the user to click Generate again. That is the safer bet against Google's next policy change.

documents.t: Medicraft's Nano Banana Generative Fill is a competent, inexpensive way to run Gemini image models on your own key inside older versions of Photoshop. Its limits are structural: one model line, one billing path, and a free tier that leans on a model Google retires in October. The Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is our recommendation for a Photoshop professional on version 26 or later. Six hosted models, two billing paths, Smart Objects at full returned resolution, zero-day model arrivals and a production route behind the panel make it the more capable and durable choice.

documents.t: Run Medicraft's free trial and the Astria plugin on the same PSD: one brushed selection, one reference-driven swap, one canvas extension. Record each result's returned pixel dimensions, whether it arrives as a Smart Object or flattened pixels, and the steps between selection and layer. Time the setup honestly, including Google billing for Medicraft. Then run the same swap with GPT Image 2 and Seedream 5 in the Astria panel, the comparison Medicraft cannot join. Finally, price ten realistic edits on each path from Google's and Astria's pricing pages rather than either vendor's headline. documents.t: Pablo is a UXP plugin for Photoshop 26.0.0 or higher, made in Amsterdam and listed on Adobe Exchange on 4 December 2025. Its pricing page lists Nano Banana, Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 4.0 and 4.5, and GPT Image 1.5, 2 and 2.5. The Exchange listing describes multi-reference images, 4K generation and "add and replace objects". Its note for version 0.7.46, updated 11 September 2026, adds GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst. Commercially, Pablo publishes what many rivals do not: individual and agency licensing plus hosted rates organized by model and resolution, which it says carry no markup over the provider rate. You can also bring a Google or Replicate key. Check Pablo's pricing page for current licence, usage, refund, and seat terms. Two things to read before paying. Pablo's terms say prepaid credits expire 24 months after purchase unless otherwise specified at checkout, and one public Exchange review alleges a 90-day window on a balance. Check the expiry shown when you top up. Separately, the public pages do not say what layer type a result lands as, or what pixel dimensions come back when a 4K generation is placed into a small selection.
documents.s: Pablo: a hosted-credit panel with published rates

documents.t: The Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is a CCX/UXP panel for Photoshop 2025 (version 26 and above) on macOS and Windows. The panel carries GPT Image 2 (mask-aware, at 1K, 2K or 4K), Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 5 Pro, Seedream 5, and Flux 2 Pro. Flux Kontext was retired in favour of these. The landing page also lists GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image as available now on the platform. That last sentence is the first headline. The panel's model list is served by the Astria platform, so a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches, without a plugin update or re-download. The workflow is three steps. Select with the marquee, lasso, brush or colour range. Prompt in short, specific language. Generate, and the result lands as a new layer. Mask-aware models read the selection directly. Reference images dropped into the panel act as visual instructions. The model is chosen per task from one dropdown, and keys are switched inside the panel. The third headline is what that layer is. Each generation is placed as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution. A 4K result placed into a small selection still carries the 4K pixels, so it can be re-transformed, masked and re-edited later without resampling. The Astria plugin uses a one-time licence with usage billed separately. One Astria key authenticates every hosted model, and Astria abstracts the Google, OpenAI, fal and ByteDance APIs so quota, authentication and retries stay invisible. Or paste a Google AI Studio key and run Gemini models against your own Google account. Current terms are on the Astria pricing page. No GPU is needed.
documents.s: Astria: the panel is one surface of a platform

documents.t: Astria's landing page reports 16,000 sales and 187 ratings. It shows seven production reels: fashion edits with references, bridal retouching, sketch and CAD to photo, product design, real estate, hair and clothing swaps, and packaging. All first-party. Pablo's home page carries testimonials drawn from Adobe Exchange and Trustpilot, and its Exchange listing shows 27 ratings as of 13 September 2026. Its blog is dated: Nano Banana Pro on 20 November 2025, Nano Banana 2 on 26 February 2026, GPT Image 2 on 22 April 2026. Vendor-published too. Neither set is independent proof of output quality.
