documents.t: Take a footwear campaign hero shot on location. The art director wants three edits: the shoes swapped for the new colourway from a product reference, the background extended for a 4:5 crop, and the phone in the model's left hand removed. Then the colourway has to appear on the other forty SKUs in the drop.
documents.s: One campaign hero, then forty SKUs

documents.t: Drop the product reference in, lasso the shoes, and prompt the swap on Nano Banana Pro. Extend the canvas, select the empty band and prompt the fill. Brush over the phone and prompt its removal. Each result returns as a layer, and the cost of every generation is knowable from the published rate card. What the public material does not say is whether the swap layer holds the full 4K return or only the selection's pixel count, or whether it re-transforms later without loss. Test that before committing the hero.
documents.s: In Pablo

documents.t: The same three edits, with a model chosen per task. GPT Image 2 with mask is the natural pick for the shoe swap: it reads the lasso as a mask and is built for clean replacement inside a brushed selection. Seedream 5 handles the 4:5 extension from a longer structural prompt. Nano Banana Pro removes the phone while keeping the hand and sleeve consistent. Each result is a Smart Object at the model's full returned resolution, so when the crop changes next week the swap layer is scaled, re-masked and re-edited without resampling.
documents.s: In the Astria plugin

documents.t: Pablo is a plugin; forty more SKUs are forty more documents and forty more selections. With Astria, the key in the panel is the same key and balance that run Astria workspaces, templates and the API. Photoshop is for the hero and the fix. The workspace runs the rest of the collection from the same product reference. The AI fashion photoshoot guide covers that side of the job.

documents.t: Pablo is quick. Its Nano Banana Pro how-to went up on Google's launch day, its GPT Image 2 post followed OpenAI by one day, and GPT Image 2.5 arrived three days after OpenAI's 8 September 2026 release. The difference is not speed but mechanism. Pablo's newest model is tied to plugin version 0.7.46. A user who has not updated does not have it, and the roster is bounded by what the plugin build knows about. The Astria panel reads its list from the platform. A model added to Astria appears in the dropdown with no plugin update, which is why GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image are already listed as available.

documents.t: Both products advertise 4K. Only one says what happens to those pixels afterwards. Astria places every result as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution. Pablo's layer type and returned pixel dimensions are not stated in its public material, so a buyer has to measure them. For a retoucher who re-crops, re-lights and re-masks a hero across a campaign's life, that is the whole reason to care about the layer type.

documents.t: Both products offer a one-time plugin licence and let a Gemini-heavy user route calls through a Google key. Compare Pablo's pricing page with the Astria pricing page using the models, resolution, seat count, and retry rate you actually expect.

documents.t: This is Pablo's real advantage and it deserves a plain statement. Pablo publishes pass-through rates, offers centralized agency licensing, and runs both hosted and bring-your-own-key paths, with Replicate as a second key option. An agency buying seats in bulk, whose finance team wants the usage model documented before the first generation, will find Pablo's commercial pages easier to sign off.

The balance you top up for Photoshop produces the forty SKUs, from the same product reference used for the hero. For a studio whose Photoshop work is the visible tenth of a larger production, the panel is the entry point and the ecommerce workspace is the rest.

documents.t: Both products are maintained. Pablo has a dated public record, a support desk and a company behind it, which is more than most Exchange listings in this category can say. Astria's panel was rebuilt as a CCX/UXP plugin in 2026, carries a dated changelog and reports 16,000 sales. It is one surface of a platform company rather than a company's only product. If the question is which panel is still current in eighteen months, the one that needs no release to see a new model has the structural edge.

documents.t: Published, no-markup per-image rates are a purchasing requirement. You are buying ten to fifty seats and want one licence with centralised billing. You prefer a Replicate key to a Google key or need centralized agency licensing. You are content to update the plugin when a new model ships and to measure the returned layer yourself.

Your heroes get re-cropped and re-lit for months, and every generation should be a Smart Object at full returned resolution. You want a hosted top-up balance without a recurring subscription. The rest of the catalogue should run from the same key in Astria workspaces or through the API.

documents.t: Pablo is the rival to take seriously. Its rate card, agency licence and free allowance are the clearest commercial pages we reviewed, and its release cadence is measured in days. If the decision turns on those three things, buy it. For everyone else, the Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop is our recommendation. It can receive the next model without a plugin release, keeps every returned pixel in a Smart Object, and is the front door to a production platform rather than a plugin that ends at the document. It is a technology-enabled production company: you send product images, expert retouchers and automated steps finish them, and files come back on a guaranteed turnaround. Astria is the opposite arrangement—a production system your own team operates, where the brand's creative direction becomes a reusable asset instead of a specification held by a supplier. The short answer: Astria is the clear overall winner for fashion brands that want to own a repeatable production capability. Choose Pixelz when you specifically want expert human retouching delivered on an SLA and have no internal team to run production. documents.t: Pixelz describes itself as one place to scale ecommerce content, and the offering is broad: PDP image retouching, editorial and campaign retouching, video post-production, image-to-video, AI-generated content, and AI models and digital twins. What holds it together is the delivery model. Pixelz's own terms describe the standard service as human-assisted hybrid editing—expert retouchers combined with automated AI-driven steps—which is an honest description of a service rather than a product. The operational apparatus is real and mature. Customers get a cloud platform for review, markup, order tracking, and dashboards; the Professional plan publishes next-morning turnaround with a three-hour expedite option and plan-dependent capacity; the Enterprise plan offers turnaround from three hours with custom capacity. Editorial work is quoted at 48 hours standard, video at 24. Brand logos on the site include large retailers such as Zalando, Mango, ASICS, and Bestseller. Check Pixelz pricing for current subscription, per-image, add-on, and service terms. Use Astria pricing for Astria rates. Include every required service in the production budget.
documents.s: Pixelz: outsourced finishing, industrialised

documents.t: Astria puts the same capability inside the brand. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a workspace the team controls, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored as a reusable recipe rather than a brief sent to a supplier. That changes what a season looks like. Templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work alongside apparel, so campaign and catalog needs come from one setup. Motion extends the same approved stills rather than becoming a separate order. And review happens on a multiplayer Board with named cursors and live voice, where the people making the creative decision are looking at the same canvas rather than annotating returned files.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Pixelz's evidence is enterprise retail scale: recognizable logos and a published case study with luxury retailer Luisa Via Roma. As with every vendor in this comparison, these are first-party materials rather than independent benchmarks. They do establish that large operations trust Pixelz with volume, which is the relevant proof for a service business. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. The two point at different buyers: Pixelz's customer has outsourced production and wants it run well; Astria's customer wants production capability in the building.
documents.s: Public proof: service references versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a brand three weeks into a 400-SKU season. The catalog imagery is half delivered when the creative director decides the crop is wrong: the products need more headroom and a warmer background, across everything shipped so far and everything still to come. With a managed service, this is a commercial event. The specification is revised with the supplier, the delivered assets are re-ordered for correction, and the remaining queue is updated. The turnaround is contractually good—next morning on the Professional tier—but the volume doubles for the affected batch, per-image charges apply again, and the brand's own team spends the week coordinating rather than creating. The decision was made in-house; the execution of it was not. With Astria, the change is an edit. The approved treatment is updated once, the affected SKUs re-run against it, and the same change automatically applies to everything still to come—including the campaign frames and social crops derived from the same direction. The cost is generation, not re-procurement, and the correction happens in the room where the decision was made.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the mid-season direction change

documents.t: This is Pixelz's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Skilled retouchers working to a documented specification with a contractual delivery time is a service Astria does not offer. For brands with complex finishing standards, legacy imagery to correct, or no internal production capacity at all, that is a real answer, and the published SLAs and expedite options make it a dependable one. It is a service-delivery advantage rather than a production-capability verdict—you are buying finished files, and that remains true after the hundredth order.
documents.s: Expert human retouching on a guaranteed turnaround — winner: Pixelz

documents.t: With a service, the brand's visual standard becomes a specification the supplier maintains. It works well, and it is not portable: leaving means rebuilding it, and changing it means renegotiating scope. In Astria the standard is a template in the brand's own workspace, editable by the brand's own people, and it carries into every channel that starts from it.
documents.s: Where the creative direction lives — winner: Astria

documents.t: Pixelz covers a lot: PDP retouching, editorial finishing, video post, AI content. But each is a service line with its own quote, turnaround, and intake. Astria produces catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion from a single approved treatment, which is why the season reads as one shoot rather than four workstreams that were separately briefed.
documents.s: Coverage across catalog and campaign — winner: Astria

documents.t: Pixelz's platform offers review, markup, and order tracking, which is exactly right for approving work someone else produced. Astria's multiplayer Board is for producing it together: named cursors, live voice, and the actual production canvas, with the photographer, the in-house studio, and the agency in the same workspace.
documents.s: Collaboration and review — winner: Astria

documents.t: Pixelz's scale is throughput through a production queue, bounded by plan capacity and turnaround windows. Astria's scale is the collection as the unit of work: import the SKU set from Shopify or Google Drive, run it against the approved setup, extend it into campaign and motion. No intake form, no queue position, no per-asset ticket.
documents.s: Collection scale — winner: Astria

documents.t: Pixelz's per-image rate is transparent, and it is only one component: the monthly platform subscription, module add-ons, and onboarding services stack on top, and every revision is billable volume. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create, sized to the production engagement. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; the point is that a per-image rate plus a subscription plus onboarding is not a production budget. Model a full collection, including the mid-season change, before comparing costs.
documents.s: Commercial model for brands — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is the whole argument in one line. After a year with a managed service, a brand has a large archive of finished images and a supplier relationship. After a year with Astria, it has the images plus the casting, references, templates, and approvals that produced them—and the next season starts from those rather than from a purchase order.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: You need expert human retouching to a complex standard, with a contractual turnaround. You have no internal production team and do not intend to build one. Legacy image correction at volume is a significant part of the work. Buying finished files is the outcome you want, and owning the workflow is not.
documents.s: Choose Pixelz if...

documents.t: You want production capability inside the brand rather than a supplier relationship. One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion. Mid-season creative changes should be an edit, not a re-order. A creative director, photographer, or agency needs to install a workflow other people can reuse. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not on returned files.
documents.s: Choose Astria if...

documents.t: For fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it converts art direction into infrastructure the brand owns, and it makes the next season cheaper in effort rather than in invoices. Pixelz is a mature, well-run outsourced finishing operation—and the right answer when buying finished files, rather than building capability, is genuinely the goal. The honest test is not image quality. It is what you have at the end of the year.
documents.s: The bottom line

documents.t: Take five representative SKUs and run them through both paths, then deliberately change the creative direction after approval. Measure what the change costs in each: money, elapsed time, and your own team's hours. Price the full commercial picture for the service option—subscription, per-image charges, add-on modules, onboarding—not just the headline rate. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask what you would keep if you switched vendors tomorrow.
documents.s: What to test before choosing either platform

documents.t: They solve the same business problem in opposite ways. Pixelz is a managed service: you send assets and receive finished files on an SLA. Astria is a production system your team operates, where the creative direction and the outputs stay in-house.

documents.t: With a managed service, a direction change means revising a specification and re-ordering affected assets through the queue. In Astria, you edit the approved treatment and re-run the collection against it.

documents.t: Pletor's framing is deliberate: production infrastructure, not a generative toy. It orchestrates models—Flux, Seedance, Kling, Veo, Sora, and language models among them, with new ones added continuously—alongside brand context and marketing data, so a team can produce product imagery from a catalog, performance ads at campaign pace, and AI-generated UGC. The clearest statement of intent is its promise to turn one campaign into every version it needs to be: languages, formats, markets, seasons. Use Pletor pricing for current plans, credit allowances, rollover, and team access. For Astria rates and terms, see Astria pricing. Its published references—an agency, a creative director, a global consumer electronics brand—describe marketing organizations rather than fashion brands. That is consistent with the positioning. Pletor is not claiming to be a fashion product, and a fair comparison should not pretend otherwise.
documents.s: Pletor: an engine for campaign versions

documents.t: Astria produces the source material. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that generates the collection's imagery. That includes fashion knowledge a general marketing engine has no reason to carry: category templates for beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work; a casting library spanning ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting; product references and a refinement pass aimed at how garments and faces actually read. Campaign frames and social crops extend the same approved direction, and motion animates stills the brand already signed off.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Pletor's evidence points at marketing teams and agencies, with a named agency case study and a consumer electronics reference. Read as evidence for ad production infrastructure, that is reasonable and on-point. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published in both cases, from different industries.
documents.s: Public proof: marketing adoption versus fashion production

documents.t: Consider a fashion brand launching a 90-piece spring collection with a significant paid-social budget. The growth team needs dozens of ad variants across three markets and two languages. The ecommerce team needs PDP sets. The brand team needs a lookbook and campaign imagery. Pletor is excellent at one third of this, and it is the third that comes last. Versioning a campaign across formats, markets, and languages is precisely its design goal, and its credit pricing makes high variant counts affordable. But every one of those variants derives from source creative: a cast model wearing the garment, shot in a treatment the brand approved. If that source does not exist, no amount of versioning infrastructure creates it, and generic product imagery generated from a catalog is not the same as a campaign image a brand would run. Astria produces the source. Casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format get approved once and applied across the 90 pieces imported from Shopify or Google Drive; the lookbook and campaign frames come from the same treatment; motion extends approved stills. The growth team then has something worth versioning—and can version it in Pletor, or anywhere else, without conflict.

Producing many versions of an approved campaign across languages, formats, markets, and seasons is a real operational problem for growth teams, and Pletor is built for it with pricing and rollover that suit bursty demand. Astria is not competing for that job, and a brand with a large paid-social operation may well want both.

Astria imports the whole SKU set and runs it against the approved treatment, then extends into campaign, editorial, social, and motion.

documents.t: Credit tiers with rollover are a sensible fit for campaign bursts and an awkward one for a season's production, where volume is predictable but revision-heavy and the unit that matters is a finished collection rather than a variant count. Astria's brand pricing is scoped to usage—pay for what you create. No claim is made here that Astria is cheaper; the two meters measure different work. Model a full collection, including rework, before comparing.

documents.t: In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate, and next season starts from them. In Pletor, what accumulates is a library of campaign variants — valuable while the campaign runs, and superseded when the next one starts.

documents.t: Your bottleneck is ad variant volume across formats, markets, and languages. You are a marketing or growth team rather than a production team. Published credit pricing with rollover suits your bursty demand. Your source creative already exists and needs multiplying, not making.

One approved creative direction must carry across catalog, lookbook, campaign, social, and motion. Your photographer, studio, and agency should work in the same brand workspace. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not in a marketing workflow tool.

documents.t: These two are complementary far more than they are competitive, and the honest advice is to be clear about which problem you have. If you cannot produce enough ad variants, Pletor solves that well. If your ads are constrained by not having enough good source imagery of your own collection, a versioning engine will not help — and Astria is the stronger choice.

documents.t: Ask one question first: do we lack variants, or do we lack source creative? Then test accordingly. For Astria, run five representative SKUs through a full channel set — PDP, detail, campaign, social — and add a colorway after approval. For Pletor, take one approved campaign image and count how many usable market and format versions come out of it. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Rawshot

documents.t: Rawshot positions itself as an AI photo studio for fashion, built explicitly for garment people rather than prompt engineers. The interface replaces the text box with controls: lens choices from 35mm to 135mm, framings from full body to close-up, lighting from studio softbox to golden hour, a large background library, and a catalog of synthetic models configured across body attributes covering womenswear, menswear, plus-size, kidswear, and infant. Two things deserve credit. First, Rawshot does support repeatability within its own vocabulary: the product describes reusing the same face, styling logic, and framing across a large assortment so a catalog stays coherent. Second, and more distinctive, Rawshot publishes a provenance and disclosure stack—C2PA signing, visible and cryptographic watermarking, and stated alignment with EU AI Act Article 50, California SB 942, and GDPR. For a brand whose legal team has AI-labelling obligations on the roadmap, that is a concrete, checkable capability rather than a marketing line. The site itself is the other signal. Rawshot's public surface runs to thousands of programmatically generated pages—one per feature, solution, and comparison permutation. It is an effective way to capture search demand. It is not evidence of production adoption, and we did not find named customer case studies or testimonials on the public site in the material reviewed.
documents.s: Rawshot: removing the prompt, one menu at a time

documents.t: Astria starts from the brand rather than the interface. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together in a workspace, so an approved look becomes a reusable recipe rather than a configuration a single operator remembers. That difference shows up in what a team can encode. Templates cover fashion-specific categories well beyond standard apparel PDPs—beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial—and brand references anchor results to the brand's own visual language rather than a generic AI aesthetic. Astria's Describe tool can extract usable creative direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for the products and models already loaded, which shortens the path from "make something like our last campaign" to a template the team can run.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Astria's public materials show a professional production base: recognizable brands including Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work on the platform. This is vendor-published evidence rather than an independent benchmark, and it should be read as an adoption signal, not a quality proof. Rawshot's public evidence is different in kind. The company publishes extensive category and comparison content and clear technical specifications, but in the material we reviewed on August 23, 2026, we could not find a named customer story, testimonial, or case study. Absence of published proof is not proof of absence—Rawshot may well have customers who prefer not to be named—but a buyer evaluating a production commitment has less to check.

documents.t: Consider a knitwear label with 24 styles, each in three colorways, needing PDP and detail shots, a small lookbook, and paid-social crops. With Rawshot, an operator configures the first look—model, lens, framing, lighting, background—and generates. The result arrives in well under a minute, labelled and cleared for commercial use. Reusing that face and framing across the assortment is supported, so the catalog can stay coherent. Use Rawshot pricing to budget for the full collection, model creation, and rejected attempts. With Astria, the team defines casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format once, approves the treatment, and runs the collection against it. Colorway two and three inherit the approved setup rather than repeating the configuration. The lookbook and social crops extend the same direction instead of restarting it, and the reviewers work on the shared board rather than passing exports around.

documents.t: This is the heart of the comparison. Rawshot's menus are broad and genuinely well organized, and for a designer who has never written a prompt they remove a real barrier. But a menu is a fixed vocabulary. It can describe a 50mm lens and golden-hour light; it cannot describe why this brand shoots its knitwear cropped at the collarbone with the sleeve pushed back, or that its casting skews older than the category norm. Astria lets a creative team encode those decisions—casting, styling, pose, composition, references—and then hand the result to someone else to run.

Astria's reusable library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting, alongside locations, poses, and other production references that accumulate in the brand's workspace.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Rewarx Studio

documents.t: Rewarx Limited, based in San Francisco, positions Rewarx Studio as an AI production suite for commerce content. The promise is compact: upload a product photo, choose a scene or model, export a 4K asset. Eight tools anchor the workspace — AI Photography Studio, Lookalike Creator, Model Studio, Ghost Mannequin, Mockup Generator, Group Shot Studio, Product Page Builder, and Commercial Ad Poster — plus a Virtual Model Try-on tool and a REST API. The apparel-specific work is real. Ghost Mannequin fills a neckline and removes the mannequin. The company describes a Geometry-Lock approach it says preserves a product's dimensions and logo placement, and a texture engine intended to hold stitching and material grain. Model Studio offers archetypes across ethnicities, ages, and body types, and its Lookalike technology can carry one face and body across a production — a meaningful capability, and one a fashion buyer should test rather than assume. The commercial plumbing is sensible too: assets formatted for Amazon, Shopify, Etsy, and eBay, a Shopify app, batch generation, exports up to 4096 pixels, stated commercial ownership of generated assets, and self-serve onboarding. The company also states that uploads are not used to train public models. Two things a fashion buyer should read closely. The first is what the fashion page means by standardizing a lookbook: applying the same studio lighting setup consistently across a large catalog. That is useful, and it is catalog standardization rather than what a fashion team means by a lookbook. The second is the plan structure, discussed below.
documents.s: Rewarx Studio: breadth across the catalog

documents.t: Astria narrows to fashion and spends the depth there. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format — is the reusable unit that produces a season. Casting is a library rather than an entitlement, covering ages and body types including children and extended sizes, alongside locations, poses, and brand references that accumulate season over season. Templates encode apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work as production disciplines with their own casting, lighting, and framing logic. Campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion all derive from the same approved direction, and review happens on a shared production canvas with named cursors and live voice, with external photographers and agencies inside the same workspace.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Rewarx publishes headline statistics — an 85% reduction against studio and retouching fees, a 34% average conversion increase, and a 10x time-to-market improvement — alongside a 5.0 G2 rating. Its testimonials carry first names and a last initial with generic role labels, and we found no named customer brand or case study in the material reviewed. The reach figures are also inconsistent between pages: the homepage invites you to join "5M+ Sellers and Creators" while the about page says "10,000+ brands." Both are vendor-published; a buyer has nothing specific to verify. Astria's public materials name fashion and retail brands including Gant, Nine West, Lee Cooper, Nununu, Renuar, Fox, and Terminal X, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published too, and at least checkable by looking.

documents.t: Consider a contemporary womenswear label with 60 styles going live: four images per style at 4K, a campaign set, social crops, and a handful of short clips for Reels. The team evaluates Rewarx’s batch tools against that complete brief. The first week goes well. Ghost mannequin on the knitwear is fast and clean, background removal saves the offshore clipping-path budget, and the Shopify export is genuinely convenient. Then three ceilings arrive at once. Budget for all required images, clips, and rejected attempts using current Rewarx pricing. Check capacity for the complete drop before choosing a plan. Collaboration: the stylist wants to review with the ecommerce lead and the freelance photographer. Multi-user account access is an Agency-tier entitlement, so a workflow question becomes a billing question. Direction: the brand wants its own recurring look held across the season. Custom style training also sits on the Agency tier. Until then, direction is re-selected per generation by whoever is at the keyboard. Then the campaign brief lands. An ad poster puts typography over a product focal point, which is a listing asset rather than a campaign. A real lookbook is not one lighting setup applied consistently. Include the social calendar alongside the catalog when checking current Rewarx pricing. With Astria, casting is a library the brand builds and keeps, the 60 styles run against one approved treatment, the campaign and editorial frames come from that same direction, motion animates stills that already passed review, and the photographer is in the workspace rather than outside the account. Nothing in the season is rationed by a plan tier.

documents.t: This is Rewarx's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. Ghost mannequin, group shots, pattern mockups, eight-image product page sets, and ad posters, all exporting into Amazon, Etsy, eBay, and Shopify formats, cover a marketplace seller's asset list without anyone having to decide what a listing should look like. If your job is to put correct, consistent, well-lit images against many SKUs across a mixed catalog, that toolkit is a real advantage, and self-serve onboarding supports an initial evaluation. Check Rewarx pricing for current trial terms.

documents.t: A product serving hand tools, beverages, eyewear, and apparel optimizes for what they share: a clean subject, a pleasing background, consistent light. Fashion's hard parts are not shared — drape on a knit, how a sleeve breaks, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention held across a collection. Rewarx's twenty verticals are material-physics and lighting profiles for those product types; Astria's categories are production disciplines.

documents.t: Style and scene are chosen per generation in Rewarx, and custom style training is an entitlement on the top tier. Astria stores the approved treatment itself, so the tenth SKU is produced the same way as the first by someone who was not there for the decision. That is the difference between a tool that repeats an operation and a system that repeats a decision.
documents.s: Direction that survives the session — winner: Astria

documents.t: Rewarx's Lookalike reference holding one face across a production is a real capability, and it solves the single-model consistency problem well. A fashion brand's casting problem is usually plural: a womenswear line, a kids range, and an extended-size offer are three casting requirements before anyone discusses campaigns. Astria treats casting as a reusable library spanning ages and body types, sitting alongside locations, poses, and brand references that carry into the next season.
documents.s: Casting that scales with the collection — winner: Astria

documents.t: One lighting setup across 500 SKUs is not a lookbook, and typography over a product shot is not a campaign. Editorial framing, social-native crops, and motion are separate disciplines. Astria produces them as expressions of one approved direction rather than as separate tools applied to a product image, and motion is not metered twenty times heavier than a still.
documents.s: Coverage of the season — winner: Astria

documents.t: Stoodio's pitch is that it builds a brand's AI studio, and it is refreshingly specific about being fashion-only rather than a general image tool. The platform lists five integrated capabilities: image generation, video generation, workflows that chain prompts, models, edits, and exports into repeatable pipelines, a model database, and asset management. The model database is the strategy. As an official partner of ModelManagement.com, Stoodio offers access to over 100,000 consented digital twins with worldwide, perpetual commercial rights, and it is pointed about what that means—no composite faces, no grey zones. For a brand whose legal team is uneasy about synthetic likeness, or that operates in a market tightening around AI disclosure and personality rights, this is a materially different proposition from a library of invented faces. The company frames itself as a production partner rather than a tool, promising guided onboarding so a team integrates AI into real production from the first session. Its published evidence is a single detailed case study: a Berlin activewear brand reporting 40% lower cost per SKU, production cycles moving from three weeks to three days, and double the content output. There is no published pricing; the route in is a booked demo.
documents.s: Stoodio: licensing as the product strategy

documents.t: Astria shares Stoodio's fashion focus and diverges on autonomy and breadth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit the brand's own people edit and run. Breadth shows in two places. Categories: templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion disciplines, not variations on apparel. And casting: alongside adult models across body types, the library covers children's and extended-size casting, which are production requirements a licensed adult-model roster does not address.

documents.t: Stoodio's case study is genuinely useful—specific numbers, a named founder, a real brand—and it is one story from a small brand. That is honest early-stage evidence, and a buyer should read it as such rather than as a pattern. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and broader across brand size and contributor type.

documents.t: Consider a European brand whose counsel has flagged AI-generated faces as a risk. The marketing director wants AI production; legal wants documented consent and clear commercial rights for any human likeness used in advertising. This is Stoodio's scenario, and it answers it well. A licensed twin from a consented roster with worldwide perpetual rights is a document legal can read, and the onboarding engagement means someone from the vendor helps wire it into the brand's real production. If that constraint is genuinely binding, the rest of this comparison is secondary. Now change one detail: the brand also sells a children's line and a small jewelry capsule, and its campaign imagery is set by a freelance stylist who is not an employee. The licensed adult-model roster does not cover the children's line. Jewelry needs different lighting and macro conventions than activewear. And the stylist needs to be inside the workflow, reviewing looks with the team, not briefing a vendor. In Astria those are ordinary: children's and extended-size casting exist in the library, jewelry and beauty are first-class template categories, and the stylist joins the brand workspace and reviews on the multiplayer Board with live voice.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Stylic

documents.t: Stylic's promise is speed and price. The published workflow is three steps: upload a product image in any format, spend about a minute choosing from 500+ backgrounds and 30+ AI models, and download commercial-ready results roughly ninety seconds later. Features include single, multiple, and catalogue photoshoots, 4K and 8K output, brand watermarking, clothing colour change, custom AI models, and bulk creation. Check the vendor’s current pricing page for plans and enterprise terms. The intended audience is stated plainly: Shopify stores, Amazon sellers, Meesho brands, D2C fashion labels, fashion startups, and creative agencies. The pricing, the marketplace orientation, and the rupee-denominated savings figure all point the same way—this is a tool for sellers, not a system for brands. The published statistics deserve a sceptical read. Stylic cites 10,000+ fashion businesses in one place and 200+ fashion brands in another, alongside 2.4 million images generated, a rupee figure for photoshoot budget saved, and a claim that 94% of users replaced their photographer. No methodology accompanies any of them, and the two audience-size figures are hard to reconcile. None of this means the product is bad; it means a buyer should ask how each number was produced before treating it as evidence, and should weigh it against a company profile that is early-stage and light on named references.
documents.s: Stylic: three minutes to a listing image

documents.t: Astria's buyer list includes the people Stylic's headline claim positions against. Photographers, studios, and educators use Astria to install repeatable production workflows for brands—which is a useful signal about what the product is for. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored and reused rather than reconfigured per shoot. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct categories, casting covers ages and body types including children and extended sizes, and the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion.

documents.t: Stylic's evidence is aggregate and self-reported: user counts, images generated, savings, and a replacement statistic, with marketplace names such as Myntra and Flipkart mentioned as context rather than as customers with published stories. Astria's public materials name fashion brands—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published too, and checkable in a different way: a named brand can be looked at, and a photographer can be asked.

documents.t: Consider a label that started on marketplaces and is now launching its own site, with 70 styles, a stylist on retainer, and a founder who cares how the clothes are framed. The Stylic era made sense: cheap listing images, generated fast, good enough for a marketplace grid where every competitor's photo looks similar. What breaks is not image quality—it is everything around it. The stylist's point of view cannot be stored, so each shoot is reconfigured from menus and drifts. The site needs a lookbook and campaign imagery, which the tool is not aimed at. Motion is not on offer. And when the founder asks for a warmer, tighter crop across all 70 styles, that is 70 reconfigurations rather than one edit. With Astria, the stylist sets casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format once, the founder approves it, and the 70 styles run against that treatment imported from Shopify or Google Drive. The lookbook and campaign come from the same direction. The crop change is a single edit applied everywhere. And the stylist's judgment is now an asset the brand keeps.

documents.t: This is Stylic's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. About three minutes from upload to download, with no setup and nothing to configure beyond two menus, is a genuinely low barrier — and for a seller listing a handful of products it may be all that is required. No production system competes with that on immediacy, and there is nothing wrong with buying the simple thing when the simple thing is sufficient.

documents.t: Stylic's headline statistic frames AI as a substitute for a professional. Astria's position is the opposite, and it is not merely rhetorical: photographers and studios are among Astria's users because the product lets them encode a look and hand it to a brand's team to run. That is the difference between removing craft from the process and making craft repeatable. Brands that have paid for good creative direction generally want to keep it.

documents.t: Configuring a shoot from menus produces a result. Storing an approved treatment produces consistency, because the thing being reused is the decision rather than the operator's memory of it. Over 70 styles and three channels, that is the whole difference between a collection and a folder.

documents.t: Tellos positions itself as an AI fashion video and photo studio for ecommerce brands, with a blunt promise: no studios, no models, no production chaos. Upload flat-lay or mannequin shots, generate on-model images and video, and publish. Output is optimized for Shopify product pages, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Meta Ads, and the Shopify integration is a few clicks rather than an engineering task. Two capabilities stand out. Tellos advertises private AI models trained on a brand's style, fits, and visual language, which is a serious answer to consistency rather than a menu of presets. And its heritage in shoppable video shows: the company sells a storefront video layer priced by monthly traffic, separate from its generation studio. That heritage also produces its best evidence. Tellos publishes a customer story with Inglot reporting a 17% conversion-rate uplift and an 11% increase in average order value from shoppable video on the storefront. It is vendor-written and specific to that brand's implementation, but it is a commerce outcome rather than a production-speed claim, which makes it more useful than most case studies in this category.
documents.s: Tellos: video-first content for the storefront

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is the treatment rather than the asset. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together in a brand workspace, so an approved look becomes something the team runs repeatedly instead of something one operator recreates each time. That shows up in coverage. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work, not only standard apparel PDPs. Brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic, and Astria's Describe tool can extract usable creative direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for the products and models already loaded. Motion is an extension of the same workspace: a still the brand has already approved can be animated with a choice of current video options, so the campaign's casting and styling survive into the clip.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Tellos names brands including INGLOT, Crocs, Sereia, and Strongful, and its Inglot story quantifies storefront impact. This is first-party evidence, and it is strongest where Tellos is strongest: content that lives on a product page and moves a conversion metric. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and also an adoption signal rather than a quality proof. The two point at different rooms in the same building: Tellos at the storefront, Astria at the studio that feeds it.
documents.s: Public proof: commerce outcomes versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a footwear brand launching 40 styles. Each needs PDP stills, a detail shot, a short clip for the product page, paid-social cutdowns, and a campaign image for the seasonal landing page. Two colorways arrive late. With Tellos, the team uploads product shots and generates on-model stills and clips, then publishes them to Shopify and social with formats already sized per channel. For the video job specifically this is efficient, and the storefront layer means the clips are not just assets but merchandising. What the workflow does not carry is the creative decision. The campaign image, the lookbook treatment, and the late colorways each start again from generation choices, and the brand's visual language lives in a trained model plus whatever the operator remembers. With Astria, the team establishes casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format once and approves it. The 40 styles run against that treatment; the late colorways inherit it; the campaign image and the social crops are extensions of the same direction rather than separate jobs. When the clip is generated, it animates a still the brand already signed off, which is why the motion looks like the campaign instead of adjacent to it.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: a footwear drop with motion

documents.t: Tellos's brand-trained models are a genuine consistency mechanism, and they deserve more credit than a preset menu. But a trained model captures a look, not a process. It cannot tell the next operator that this brand crops footwear tight at the ankle, casts older than the category, and never shoots on a white sweep. Astria encodes those decisions as a reusable treatment, which is what makes an approved direction survive a new hire, a new agency, or a new season.
documents.s: Where the creative decision lives — winner: Astria

documents.t: This is Tellos's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. A video layer that installs on Shopify, plays on the product page, and comes with a published conversion outcome is a merchandising capability, not just an asset pipeline. Astria produces the video; it does not sell the storefront surface that plays it. Brands whose actual goal is on-site video merchandising should evaluate Tellos on that basis—and note that it is priced by traffic tier, which is a different commercial shape from paying for production.
documents.s: Shoppable storefront video — winner: Tellos

documents.t: Both products make fashion video, and Tellos makes it faster to publish. The question is what the clip is derived from. In Tellos the video is generated as its own asset; in Astria it animates a still that already passed creative review, using a choice of current video options inside the same workspace. For a PDP loop that distinction rarely matters. For a campaign where the film and the stills must read as one shoot, it decides whether the work holds together.
documents.s: Motion that matches the campaign — winner: Astria

documents.t: We could not verify multiplayer review, shared brand workspaces, or role-based approvals in Tellos's public material reviewed for this article. Astria combines private brand workspaces with a multiplayer Board: named cursors, live voice over the actual canvas, and review that happens on the looks instead of in an email thread. When merchandising, art direction, and an outside agency need to agree, that is the difference between resolving a look and circulating a file.
documents.s: Collaboration, review, and handoff — winner: Astria

documents.t: Tellos can turn a catalog into clips in bulk, but each asset is still an independent generation, and the commercial model reflects that: a monthly generation balance for the studio, and a separate storefront product priced by how much traffic the site receives. Neither meter tracks the thing a brand is actually buying, which is a finished collection. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work—the SKU set imports from Shopify or Google Drive and runs against the approved setup—and brand pricing is scoped to usage: pay for what you create. A monthly balance is not a production budget; model a full collection, including rework, before comparing costs.

documents.t: In Astria, products, avatars, templates, approvals, and outputs accumulate across the season, and the photographer, the in-house studio, and the social agency work from the same source of truth. With Tellos, what accumulates is a library of published assets and a trained model. Both are useful. Only one of them is a workflow another person can pick up.
documents.s: Compounding production value — winner: Astria

documents.t: Shoppable video on a Shopify storefront is the outcome you are buying. Product video for TikTok, Reels, and Meta Ads is the bulk of your content need. You want channel-sized outputs published without a separate editing step. A conversion metric on the product page matters more than a campaign that reads as one shoot.

Casting, styling, and scene decisions must survive team changes, colorways, and late additions. Review should happen on a shared canvas with voice, not through exported files. Stills, campaign, editorial, and motion should all come from the same approved treatment.

Test the second colorway, the campaign frame, and whether a teammate can reproduce the approved look without help.

documents.t: Run five representative styles through both products, including one with a difficult material—patent, mesh, or a layered upper. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for product fidelity, movement, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction from scratch.

documents.t: Tolstoy's pitch is a sequence: create AI product content, make it shoppable, help shoppers choose. AI Studio generates on-brand product images and video from photos and brand guidelines. AI Player publishes shoppable video, galleries, and interactive widgets on the storefront. AI Shopper is an assistant offering recommendations, catalog guidance, and try-on. The platform is Shopify-native and widely adopted—the company cites over 5,000 Shopify brands—and it publishes commerce outcomes such as a 24% conversion lift at LSKD and a 15% AOV lift at Pantynova. Named customers include Culture Kings, Hampden, Skin Rocks, Laura Mercier, The Ordinary, Milk Makeup, Tarte, and KitchenAid. That customer list is the most informative thing on the site. Tolstoy is a general ecommerce content and merchandising platform that fashion brands use, not a fashion platform. Skincare, cosmetics, and kitchen appliances have real content needs, and a system designed to serve all of them well is necessarily designed around what they share—a product, a page, a shopper—rather than around casting, drape, fit, and collection logic.

documents.t: Astria narrows deliberately. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces the season. The narrowing is what buys the depth. Templates cover apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories rather than as generic product photography. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting. Campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion all derive from the same approved direction, and review happens on a multiplayer Board where the photographer, the in-house studio, and the agency work on the same canvas.

documents.t: Tolstoy's evidence is strong for what it sells: named brands, a large Shopify install base, and specific conversion and AOV figures. It is vendor-published and concentrated on merchandising outcomes rather than production quality, which is the right emphasis for a commerce platform. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Tolstoy proves that its widgets sell product; Astria's evidence is about who produces fashion imagery with it.

documents.t: Consider a fashion brand on Shopify with 400 SKUs and a two-person ecommerce team. It needs four PDP images per SKU, a lookbook, campaign assets, and social content, and it is attracted to buying one platform instead of three. A 400-SKU catalog at four images requires 1,600 images before rejected frames, colorways, or campaign assets. Check Tolstoy pricing for current AI Studio, player, and assistant terms, and budget for each required service. The creative question matters more. Brand guidelines are an input Tolstoy consumes per asset; they are not the same as an approved treatment that fixes casting, crop, and styling across a collection. The lookbook and campaign work is outside what the content module is aimed at, so it still needs an answer. With Astria, the 400 SKUs import from Shopify and run against one approved treatment. The lookbook and campaign extend that direction rather than starting over, motion animates approved stills, and pricing is scoped to what the brand creates rather than to three separate meters. If the brand also wants a shoppable player and an AI assistant on the storefront, those remain available to buy—from Tolstoy or anyone else—without conflating them with production.

Fashion's hard parts—drape on a sheer fabric, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention the brand has used for six seasons—are not common-denominator problems. Astria is narrower on purpose, and that is where the depth comes from.

A shoppable player with published conversion lift, plus an AI shopping assistant, plus Shopify-native distribution, is a coherent commerce surface that Astria does not offer. The first produces assets that are roughly on-brand and individually variable; the second produces a collection that is consistent because consistency is the stored object, not an instruction repeated per asset.

documents.t: Count your real annual volume first: SKUs times images, plus colorways, plus campaign and social assets, plus a realistic rejection rate. documents.t: Start with five representative garments and produce the required product views. Approve those against the references, then ask for a campaign frame with different lighting and a wider composition. Keep the casting and garment fixed while the scene changes. This is the revealing test. It exposes whether creative direction can change without altering a hem, fastening, print scale, or face. Repeat with a layered look and then a new colourway. Record the rejected attempts and any manual correction; do not count only the successful final click. Have the person who normally reviews your brand's imagery approve the results without platform labels. Then give the saved work to a colleague and ask them to extend it. documents.s: The shortlist by job

documents.t: Astria is the most direct option here for a fashion team that has a flat-lay product photo and needs the product to move. The Astria 3D ghost packshot workflow returns one six-second 1080p MP4 rotation plus front, side, and three-quarter stills. The assets are designed for product pages, Reels, TikTok, and ad creative. The operational difference is substantial: no turntable, model, studio booking, or sample shipment. Choose a locked template for the product class, upload the flat lay, and use the resulting rotation and stills across the collection. See Astria pricing for current packshot rates and billing terms. The trade-off is equally important. Astria infers views that the one input photograph does not show. The output is a generated video, not a photographed sequence and not a model containing geometry, materials, or verified dimensions. Review prints, logos, closures, hardware, hemlines, back construction, and product color against the real SKU before publication. Choose Astria when: the product is fashion, speed and no-shipping production matter, an MP4 rotation answers the channel need, and your team can approve the inferred views. Start with one difficult SKU before scaling highly structured or sheer products. Do not choose Astria for this job when: the shopper must freely control the camera, the deliverable must be GLB or USDZ, AR scale must be dimensionally validated, or a marketplace and product-risk policy requires calibrated physical evidence.
documents.s: 1. Astria: the fast fashion rotation from one flat lay

documents.t: GoPackshot is the closest match for a buyer who means, “Take our products and return ecommerce-ready assets.” Its services page describes packshot, model, ghost-mannequin and flat-lay photography; video and 360-degree content; product logistics; retouching; quality control; and delivery into brand systems. The important word is managed. You ship physical inventory and buy an operating service, not a self-serve 3D application. That makes GoPackshot a credible choice when color, garment construction, marketplace rules, product handling, and accountability matter more than owning the capture line. GoPackshot also publishes claims about color tolerances, daily capacity, studio count, integrations, and tracked logistics. Treat those as vendor-reported claims, then put the relevant ones into the contract or test brief. A public capacity number does not establish capacity for your garment mix, revision policy, or launch window. Its public service description includes 360-degree video, but does not describe the output as a freely navigable GLB or USDZ model. If you need true 3D, ask three blunt questions: Is the deliverable an image sequence, video, web viewer, or model file? Can the shopper move to an angle that was never photographed? Do we receive geometry, materials, dimensions, and usage rights? If the answers are “sequence,” “no,” and “no,” you are buying a photographic spin. That can be an excellent asset. It is not a true 3D model.
documents.s: 2. GoPackshot: managed physical production

documents.t: Orbitvu sells automated photography systems rather than operating as your outsourced packshot studio. Its ecommerce product line covers stills, 360-degree images and video; its fashion positioning includes ghost mannequin, flat lay, on-figure work, and standardized footwear angles. This route changes the economics. Instead of paying a service per project or SKU, you own equipment, studio utilization, operators, styling, color management, maintenance, and workflow integration. The best candidate already has products moving through one facility and a team that can keep a capture recipe stable. Vendor language such as “web-ready content in minutes” is vendor-reported and should be separated into capture time, operator touch time, retouching time, rework, and publishing time. A fast turntable does not dress a mannequin, correct a crushed collar, approve color, or resolve a barcode mismatch. Choose Orbitvu when the problem is repeatable physical capture at sustained volume. Do not choose it because the word “360” appears near “3D.” Confirm the exact output your selected system produces.
documents.s: 3. Orbitvu: bring automated capture in-house

documents.t: PhotoRobot also sells hardware and workflow software for in-house or studio operators. Its public output gallery explicitly separates still images, 360 spins, “3D spins,” photogrammetry 3D models, and 360 video. That taxonomy is useful because it exposes how different outputs are often grouped under one marketing label. For fashion, PhotoRobot sells ghost-mannequin equipment and describes workflows for stills, spins, and ecommerce 3D models. Those are vendor-reported capabilities. Ask to see an output from the same product class and material as yours: a matte sneaker is not evidence for patent leather; a rigid bag is not evidence for a soft dress. PhotoRobot is the more relevant shortlist entry when you want a configurable automated studio and may need several capture modes. The procurement risk is complexity: a system that can produce five asset types still needs five acceptance standards.
documents.s: 4. PhotoRobot: automated capture with a wider output menu

documents.t: Threekit belongs in the shortlist only when the buying problem is interactive 3D rather than photography. Its platform overview distinguishes virtual photography, WebGL-based interactive 3D, and augmented reality. Its platform can create glTF and USDZ variants for web AR and supports configurable products whose visual state changes with selected options. That is a materially different deliverable. The shopper can interact with geometry and materials, and the same product definition can support many configurations. It is especially relevant to customizable bags, footwear, jewelry, furniture, equipment, or other structured products where options and spatial understanding affect purchase. The hard part is the asset system behind the viewer. Before buying, scope who creates the base geometry, materials, variant logic, dimensions, and future revisions. Threekit publishes commercial performance statistics; treat every such number as a vendor-reported result, not a forecast for your store. For a single non-configurable garment, this can be more system than the buying question deserves. For a configurable product family, it may be the only category here that actually solves the problem.
documents.s: 5. Threekit: true 3D, configuration, and AR

documents.t: VNTANA is best understood as a 3D asset pipeline. Its 3D commerce page describes taking existing CAD or 3D files, optimizing them, and distributing web-ready 3D and AR assets to commerce channels. That is valuable when product development already produces usable 3D assets. It is not the same as shipping a garment to a photography studio. Ask whether model creation or cleanup is included in your scope, because “upload your 3D file” assumes the most expensive input may already exist. VNTANA publishes performance claims for 3D commerce; those are vendor-reported. Evaluate the platform on file reduction, visual fidelity after optimization, variant handling, viewer performance, publishing integrations, and the labor saved in your actual catalog.
documents.s: 6. VNTANA: optimize and distribute models you already have

documents.t: For a Shopify merchant with a small, prioritized model list, the most direct procurement path may be a 3D-modeling partner rather than an enterprise platform. Shopify’s partner guidance says a modeler may need multi-angle photographs, dimensions in millimeters, diagrams, and CAD files where available. It also provides a practical review checklist for shape, scale, materials, reflections, textures, edges, and unwanted gaps. Shopify says the delivered model should be a GLB, approximately 4 MB and no more than 15 MB under the guidance on that page. Recheck current limits before commissioning because platform requirements change. Your theme must also support the media type; see the Shopify product media guide before approving the project. This route is strong when true 3D is needed for ten important products, not ten thousand speculative ones.
documents.s: 7. Shopify Partners: bounded custom model production

documents.t: Astria should be scored on the asset it actually delivers: a fast AI-generated rotation video and angle stills from one fashion flat lay. It should not be scored as a true 3D modeling bureau. The strongest hybrid uses an approved packshot or well-lit flat lay as Astria’s input, reviews the inferred views against the physical SKU, and publishes the MP4 where rotation communicates shape or drape. Keep calibrated photography for exact color and construction evidence. Buy true 3D only when arbitrary viewing, configuration, or AR is the requirement. That gives Astria a clear place in the buying decision rather than pretending every “3D packshot” is the same file. For the full format distinction, read 3D packshots for ecommerce. For the physical-to-generative operating handoff, continue to AI product photography vs a packshot studio.

documents.t: There is no single best service because several different purchases share the name. Choose Astria for a fast AI-generated fashion rotation video and angle stills from one flat lay, a managed studio for approved physical photography and captured spins, capture equipment for a repeatable in-house studio, a model-creation partner for a true GLB or USDZ, and a 3D commerce platform for configuration, AR, or multi-channel delivery.

Its 3D ghost packshot workflow takes one flat-lay photo and returns a six-second 1080p rotation video plus three angle stills for social and product pages. It does not return an interactive GLB or USDZ model, and inferred views still require product-accuracy review.

documents.t: GoPackshot's public services page describes packshot photography, ghost mannequin, video, and 360-degree content within a managed physical production service. It does not present those outputs as freely navigable GLB or USDZ models. Ask for the exact deliverable, viewer, and file format rather than assuming that 360 means true 3D.
documents.s: Does GoPackshot create true interactive 3D models?

documents.t: No. A photographic 360 spin is a sequence of captured angles. A true 3D model contains geometry and materials, can usually be viewed from arbitrary angles, and may support augmented reality. Some vendors use the word “3D” for a spin effect, so inspect the exported file and interaction rather than the label.
documents.s: Is a 360 spin the same as a 3D product model?

documents.t: Buy equipment when physical products already flow through one location, the shot recipe is stable, utilization will be high, and the team can own styling, color management, maintenance, and quality control. Outsource when volume is irregular or operational ownership would sit with nobody.

Search results use “AI fashion model generator” for four different purchases: Product type What the buyer expects Choose it when Do not mistake it for One-off model generator Upload one garment and receive a few people wearing it Speed and a low first-image cost matter most A collection production system Fashion production system Store products, casting, art direction, and repeatable outputs The same treatment must survive a catalog, team, and campaign A shopper fitting-room widget Virtual try-on Put a garment on a chosen brand model or an individual shopper The on-body visualization itself is the job Measured fit or sizing evidence Background and listing tool Clean, crop, relight, and format product photos Marketplace consistency is the bottleneck Full fashion art direction For a few marketplace images, the simplest generator may be the best buy. For a clothing brand producing a season, test whether an approved model, garment treatment, crop, and lighting setup can be reused across hard products and changed without rebuilding the job. Run the test on directional prints, fine hardware, sheer fabric, asymmetry, and difficult drape. Count approved images, rejects, correction time, and the operations needed to add a new colorway. documents.t: For brands producing collections. The distinguishing question: can an approved creative direction be stored and re-run against new products, by more than one person? Astria — our recommendation for collection-scale production. A brand workspace holds products, casting, references, templates, and outputs, with the approved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format — stored and reused rather than rebuilt per shoot. Category templates cover apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial; casting spans ages and body types including children and extended sizes; the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion. A multiplayer canvas with named cursors and live voice means the stylist, founder, ecommerce lead, and agency review the same work. Photographers and studios use it to install workflows for brands and keep the client relationship. Trade-off: it expects a setup investment. For a single listing image today, that is the wrong purchase. Rawshot — a dedicated AI fashion studio with substantial model, camera, and background libraries. Strong on breadth of presets. documents.t: Feature lists do not discriminate between these products; two tests do. Test one — your hardest garments. Ten pieces with directional prints, sheer panels, fine hardware, and complex drape. Not your bestsellers. A tool evaluated on easy garments tells you nothing about your catalog. Test two — change your mind. Get five products approved, then add a colorway and change the crop convention. Count the operations each platform needs. This is the single best predictor of running cost, and it is the test vendors do not design their demos around. Then ask the four questions in the AI fashion photoshoot guide: can direction be stored and reused, what happens when you change your mind, can several people work on it, and what do you own at the end.

documents.t: Dress hero shot. An off-kilter, flash-lit photograph of the referenced woman in a dynamic, almost off-balance leaning pose against a dark wooden bar counter or pillar at night. Her body creates a diagonal line. She wears the reference dress and holds the reference bag. The strong flash casts a sharp shadow. Blurred shelves with bottles and bar lights define the out-of-focus background. Cool, edgy vibe. The generation requests use the exact Articles-workspace tune tokens. documents.t: The comparison supports a few narrow observations: Sunburst pushes the diagonal, flash-led editorial direction furthest. Flare and Seedream keep the complete look easy to read. Nano Banana 2 gives the bag the strongest visual presence. GPT Image 2 remains highly competitive on direction and garment handling. Muse combines the references well but misses the requested aspect ratio. Both MAI variants now complete the reusable three-reference workflow, at lower native output resolution in this test. It does not prove a universal ranking. One output cannot estimate retry rates, and the low-resolution Sloane source limits identity conclusions. Every model changes some pleats, belt geometry, chain placement, or individual bag discs.

documents.t: Start with the model whose visible tradeoff matches the job. Use Sunburst for aggressive editorial energy, Flare for product-complete GPT Image 2.5 framing, Nano Banana 2 when accessory presence matters, Seedream for a complete 2K route, Muse when reference separation matters more than exact canvas shape, and MAI only after its native resolution is sufficient for the destination. Then rerun the actual SKU and identity. Keep the source set, semantic prompt, aspect ratio, and output count fixed, and review the original download rather than a web derivative. documents.t: "Nano Banana Photoshop plugin" now describes seven different products. Most disappointing purchases in this space are category errors, not product failures: a retoucher buys a Gemini-only script and then needs GPT Image's mask, or subscribes to a tool suite and then wants to pick the model. Decide the category first. (a) Photoshop's native Generative Fill picker. Since Photoshop 27.0, the Generative Fill bar has a model picker. As of September 2026 it lists Firefly, Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana Pro, FLUX.2 pro and FLUX.1 Kontext. Partner-model use follows the current terms of your Creative Cloud plan. Nothing to install, one bill, and Firefly output carries Adobe's commercial-safety badge. Partner output does not. Check Adobe's current terms before budgeting a job. (b) Hosted-credit or hybrid panels. The vendor hosts the billing, so you never open a Google Cloud account. Astria, Pablo, AI Lab UXP, Origin AI, Review Spaces and Varo Koneko sit here. Astria and Pablo also accept your own key, which makes them hybrids. (c) Brand-subscription plugins with no model choice. Higgsfield and Magnific (formerly Freepik) ship Photoshop panels that expose tools, not models: relight, expand, remove background, upscale. The vendor picks the model behind each tool, and you need the vendor's subscription. (d) BYOK-only panels. You buy the panel and paste your own Google, OpenAI, xAI, Replicate, fal or Kie.ai key. Medicraft's Nano Banana Generative Fill, Creator MAX, Cubby Image, Prompt Fix, Eti Image, NanoBridge, PhosGen, Erect Banana and Michael Breitung's Gemini AI Photoshop Plugin all work this way. Every generation needs a provider account configured under that provider's current terms. (e) Legacy JSX scripts. AI Vision Plugin and several Gumroad scripts run as ExtendScript: a modal dialog rather than a panel, often routed through Replicate. Their genuine merit is that they run on Photoshop versions the UXP panels cannot. The Astria plugin's own lineage started as a JSX script; legacy users can move to the CCX build, and the old script still supports Replicate-backed workflows. (f) Open-source ComfyUI bridges. comfyui-photoshop, OpenLayer and ComfyPanel connect a UXP panel to a local ComfyUI graph. Free, local models, no per-image bill, your GPU and your maintenance. The right answer for a power user who already runs ComfyUI. (g) Web canvases outside Photoshop. Magnific's web app, Higgsfield, Krea, Leonardo, Dzine and Figma all run Nano Banana with a mask. You do the edit there, export a flat file, and lose the layers, the Smart Object and the selection you spent ten minutes building. Fine for a one-off. Wrong for a retoucher with a layered PSD.
