documents.t: Astria Nano Banana plugin for Photoshop: our pick. Three things decide it. First, the panel's model list is served by the Astria platform, so a model added to Astria appears in the panel the day it launches, with no plugin update or re-download. Second, the rebuilt CCX/UXP panel runs a three-step workflow: select, prompt, generate. Mask-aware models read the selection directly, and reference images act as visual instructions. Third, each generation is placed as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned resolution, so a high-resolution result placed into a small selection can be re-transformed later without resampling. One Astria key authenticates the hosted models, or a Google AI Studio key can run Gemini models. GPT Image 2 with a mask and Seedream 5 Pro are two models Adobe does not offer inside Photoshop. The same key and balance drive Astria workspaces, templates and the API. Current terms are on the Astria pricing page. No GPU is needed. Setup is covered in the Nano Banana Photoshop guide. Adobe Generative Fill with partner models. The genuine strength is zero install and one Adobe account. Nano Banana Pro arrived the day Google launched it, and Nano Banana 2 followed in Photoshop 27.6 with several reference images. FLUX.2 pro and FLUX.1 Kontext sit beside Firefly. The ceiling is model breadth and published output detail. Partner models return one variation per generate, Adobe does not publish their returned dimensions, GPT Image lives only in the Firefly web app, and Seedream is absent from Adobe's stack. Full comparison. Pablo. The closest like-for-like: a hosted UXP panel with agency licensing, published rates, and optional Google or Replicate keys. The roster spans Nano Banana, Seedream 4.x, and GPT Image variants. Its genuine strength is transparent pricing and centralized seats. The ceiling for a retoucher: Seedream 5 is not listed as of September 2026, returned resolution and layer type are not publicly documented, and there is no production platform behind the key. Full comparison. Nano Banana Generative Fill (Medicraft, on aescripts). Gemini-only, using your own Google key. Its genuine strengths are support for older Photoshop versions, an edge-feather helper, a prompt library and recordability as Actions. The ceiling: one model family and no hosted path, so generation depends on a configured Google billing account. Full comparison. Eti Image (Pouya Eti). The widest roster of any panel here, spanning Seedream, Nano Banana, GPT Image, Flux, Qwen and WAN, plus Magnific tools and several upscalers. It runs several models in parallel on one selection. The ceiling: you bring and fund Replicate, Kie.ai and Google keys, plus a Magnific key for its tools, and returned resolution is not publicly verified. Full comparison. Creator MAX (formerly Banana MAX). The feature-richest BYOK panel: Nano Banana, GPT Image and xAI Grok Imagine, with Lock Edges inpainting, grouped variations, reference images, usage history, a spend dashboard, Actions and multi-document support. It uses your own Google, OpenAI and xAI keys, and the vendor states it does not proxy prompts or images. The ceiling: no Seedream, no Flux and no hosted path. Full comparison. AI Lab UXP (Picture Instruments). A subscription with vendor-hosted tokens and no keys, covering a standalone app as well as the panel. Models include Nano Banana, GPT Image, Flux and Seedream families. The genuine strength is that usage is shown before each generation. The ceiling: it is a subscription, there is no BYOK path, Seedream 5 is not listed, and layer behaviour is not publicly verified. Check the vendor page for current plan terms. Higgsfield Plugin for Photoshop. A different product: tools, not models. Angles, Mockup Studio, Expand, Remove BG and Relight, plus layer decomposition, face and character swap, upscaling and skin enhancement, all on Higgsfield's cloud with a Higgsfield account, on Photoshop 2024+. Its genuine strength is that an existing Higgsfield subscriber gets a lot of tool breadth at no extra cost. The ceiling: you cannot pick the model, individual-plan credits reset every billing cycle, and there is no BYOK. A note on layer decomposition. Higgsfield's plugin is the only panel on this list with a dedicated tool for splitting a flat image into editable layers, and Adobe's own Layered Image Editing, announced in October 2025, is still listed as in development. We tested what the capability delivers through an ordinary image endpoint, and where it falls short, in AI layer separation in Photoshop. Magnific plugin for Photoshop. The plugin needs a paid Magnific plan. Tools cover generate, reframe, relight, upscale, background removal, skin and stock. The genuine strength is upscale and relight inside the panel for someone already subscribed. The ceiling: Magnific chooses the model for each tool, and the panel does not preview usage before a run. Check Magnific's pricing page for current terms.

documents.t: A Photoshop panel is a thin thing. Its value is whatever sits behind the Generate button today, and that changes monthly. Three examples from this year. Google's pricing page marks the original Nano Banana (gemini-2.5-flash-image) as deprecated, with a shutdown on October 2, 2026, and Adobe removed it from the Generative Fill picker in Photoshop 27.11. Flux Kontext was retired from the Astria panel in favour of Flux 2 Pro and the mask-aware GPT Image 2. And GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare and Muse Image are already on Astria's platform as of September 13, 2026; Pablo's pricing page also lists GPT Image 2.5. For scale, Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro only reached general availability on Google's API in May 2026, and Nano Banana 2 Lite followed on June 30. Two designs handle this differently. A panel that ships models as releases needs the vendor to write code, publish an update and get you to re-download it before a new model is usable. That is every BYOK panel by construction, because a new provider means new authentication code. Several of the Exchange listings we reviewed have one release and no ratings; a vendor in that state does not ship the next provider. A panel that reads its roster from a platform gets the model when the platform gets it, and the platform's business depends on getting it early. That is the Astria plugin's design. So "six models" is the wrong number to compare, and so is "27". The question is which models the panel will have next March, and who has to do what to get them.
documents.s: Why the model list matters more than the model count

documents.t: Buy nothing on a feature list. One afternoon and one PSD settle it. One PSD, one selection, one prompt, one reference. Pick a real job: a campaign hero where the shoes must be swapped from a reference image, the background extended for a 4:5 crop, and a phone removed from a hand. Save the selection as a channel so every panel gets the identical mask, and use the same short prompt and the same reference each time. Check the returned pixel dimensions and the layer type. After each generation, look at what arrived. Is it a Smart Object or flattened pixels? Double-click it: are the embedded pixels the model's full output, or were they resampled to the selection size? A 4K result that arrives at selection size cannot be recovered later, and that matters the day the client asks for the crop to move. Run it on the cheap model first. Nano Banana 2 at 1K is where most panels look fine. Then run Nano Banana Pro at 4K, GPT Image 2 with the mask, and Seedream 5 Pro where offered. The gap between panels opens at the top of the range, not the bottom. Force a timeout. Run a 4K generation on a large selection and watch what the panel does when the upstream provider is slow. Does it retry, report, or charge and show nothing? Upstream providers time out, and every hosted panel, ours included, has to handle that in front of you. Cost a month of your real volume on each billing model. Count last month's fills, including rejects, and apply each vendor's current rates to the same model, resolution, retry rate, and seat count. Use the live Astria pricing page and each competitor's pricing page rather than fixed figures copied into an article.

documents.t: Why you are looking What to shortlist Direction drifts across the collection A production system that stores an approved treatment You need lookbook, campaign, or motion — not just PDP images A production system with channel and video coverage You sell jewelry, beauty, footwear, or children's ranges A platform with genuine category depth More than one person needs to work on it A platform with shared workspaces and review It costs more than the listings justify A cheaper listing tool, not a bigger platform That last row matters. If the honest answer is "this costs more than my marketplace listings are worth," moving to a more capable platform is the wrong direction — see the listing tools below.
documents.s: Diagnose the reason first

documents.t: Astria — our recommendation for brands producing collections. The difference that matters against Botika is that the approved treatment — casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format — is stored and re-run rather than configured per photoshoot. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in one brand workspace; templates cover beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct categories; casting spans ages and body types including children and extended sizing; and the same direction carries into campaign frames, social crops, and motion. A multiplayer canvas with named cursors and live voice means the stylist, the founder, the ecommerce lead, and an outside agency review the same work rather than trading exports. Where Botika may still suit you better: if standard adult apparel PDP images are genuinely the whole job and you are happy with the current output, there is no prize for switching. Full head-to-head. Rawshot — a dedicated AI fashion studio with large model, camera, and background libraries. Worth a look if preset breadth is what you feel is missing. Comparison. Caimera — creator-led go-to-market with published case-study material. Comparison. Ayna — fashion photoshoot production with published pricing. Comparison. Stoodio — licensed digital twins of real models. The right shortlist if licensed real-model likenesses are a hard requirement for your brand. Comparison. Lumoo — compact and focused, built around producing from a single image. Comparison.
documents.s: Production systems

documents.t: FASHN — try-on and model generation for brands and creative teams. Comparison. Aiuta — enterprise try-on delivered as a QA'd service rather than a tool you operate. Comparison. Looklet — digitised models, with a studio capture step to evaluate. Comparison. Before shortlisting any of these, check you are solving the right problem — virtual try-on for fashion brands explains why two unrelated products share that name.

documents.t: Be honest about this rather than shopping upmarket. Stylic — three-step upload-to-download at low monthly tiers, aimed at marketplace sellers. Genuinely cheaper, and for a seller producing listing images and nothing else, sufficient. Comparison. Lookgen — styled outfit generation with PIM publishing. Comparison.

documents.t: Don't switch mid-season. A catalog with two treatments in it is worse than a catalog with one imperfect treatment. Evaluate in parallel. Keep the current tool running. Take ten products — including your hardest — through the shortlist. Test the revision path. Get five approved, then add a colorway and change the crop convention. Count operations. This is the test that predicts your running cost. Check category coverage against what you actually sell, not against a demo reel. Ask what you keep. Images only, or the casting, references, and templates that produced them? This determines whether next season starts from something or from nothing. Switch between seasons, and rebuild the treatment deliberately rather than trying to replicate the old one exactly. The wider category map is in best AI fashion photography platforms, and the production process itself in the AI fashion photoshoot guide. If your shortlist starts elsewhere, use Lumoo alternatives for product-photo and catalog workflows, or StyTrix alternatives to separate visual design, technical sampling, and photography decisions.

documents.t: For brands producing a full collection across catalog, lookbook, campaign, and social, we recommend Astria. For marketplace sellers who only need cheap listing images, a listing tool such as Stylic is a simpler and cheaper answer.

documents.t: Astria Workshops · Series 1: Your first AI lookbook · Lesson 3 Cast an AI model that suits your brand’s visual direction. You’ll open Astria’s Agent, choose the unique headshot skill, and turn a clear description of the face and hair into a casting task you can review and refine. Follow workshop 1.3: Casting an AI Model. The screenshots focus on the Agent controls and written instructions you’ll use.
documents.s: How to Cast an AI Fashion Model with Astria’s Agent

documents.t: Open Astria Generate in your brand workspace. Keep your casting references and visual brief beside you so you can judge whether the face and hair fit the direction.
documents.s: Before you begin

documents.t: A prompt is the written instruction for an image. In the prompt box, you describe what you want that image to show. With the Agent, you work through a task in a conversation. The Agent can use available tools to carry out the task. Under Connectors, you can also make apps such as Google Drive or Shopify available to it.
documents.s: Step 1: Understand the prompt and the Agent

documents.t: On Generate, open Agent at the top of the page. Its chat opens on the right. Below the message box, open Skills to choose instructions for the casting task. Open the Agent. Use Agent at the top of Generate to open the chat. Video: 00:53.
documents.s: Step 2: Open Agent and Skills

documents.t: Select unique headshot from the list. The skill appears in the message box and guides the Agent’s choice of tools and how it creates the portrait. A headshot is a portrait focused on the face. Choose unique headshot. Select the portrait skill from the list below the message box. Video: 00:59.
documents.s: Step 3: Choose unique headshot

documents.t: Give the Agent a specific casting direction based on the brand references. The workshop uses long copper-red hair in loose waves, light freckles and a natural, no-makeup look. You can use that level of detail for your own direction: describe the visible features that matter, instead of asking for a model without further guidance. The Agent can use relevant material in the workspace. If the task should use a particular file or reference, type @ to point to it. This workshop starts with a written description; choosing a photo to copy is a separate decision. Send the instruction when it describes the casting you want. Give a clear casting direction. The written description makes the features to review specific. Video: 01:30.
documents.s: Step 4: Describe the face and hair

documents.t: When the portraits appear, put your casting references beside them. Check the hair, freckles and natural look against the description you sent. If something needs changing, ask for that one change in the chat. Compare the next result with the first, then keep the portrait that best fits your casting direction.
documents.s: Step 5: Compare the portraits and refine one feature

documents.t: Check the selected portrait against the references again. The face and hair should fit the visual direction you chose for the brand, including the specific features in your instruction. Continue with workshop 1.4: Create your first AI lookbook image, where you’ll bring clothing, pose and background references together. Open Astria Agent from Generate → All Astria workshops

documents.t: Astria Workshops · Series 1: Your first AI lookbook · Lesson 7 Choose poses and framing that help a shopper understand the garment. You already have a look you’re happy with; now you’ll plan the views that show its fit, shape and details. Follow workshop 1.7: Poses & Framing. The steps below keep the video’s gallery review, detail study, shot list and result check in the same order.
documents.s: How to Choose Poses and Framing for AI Product Photos

documents.t: Have your styled look open in Astria Generate. Keep the product’s original gallery available so you can check which details each view should show.
documents.s: Before you begin

documents.t: Open two product galleries from the brand. The workshop uses Bobo Choses’ shirt and trouser galleries. Look at how the models are positioned in front, back and turned views. Then notice framing: how much of the person and garment appears in the photo. A full-length photo shows the outfit together. A closer crop directs attention to part of it. Pose and framing should work together to explain the product.
documents.s: Step 1: Separate pose from framing

documents.t: Look through the shirt’s gallery for its collar and hem, the bottom edge of the shirt. Notice whether a turned pose or hair moved aside helps reveal them. For a jacket, a closed view may be important too. Choose a view for a reason. This original gallery photo isolates the hem and embroidery, details that a general full-length view may not explain. Use those observations to choose the views for your own garment. A pose that hides the collar or covers the hem will not serve the same purpose as one that keeps the detail visible.
documents.s: Step 2: Identify the details each garment needs

documents.t: List the views you want to create. This is your shot list. For the workshop shirt, it includes a back view, a roughly 45-degree turned view, and closer coverage of the collar and hem. In Lookbook, open the Pose reference square to choose a stick-figure position. The picker lets you change the model’s position while keeping your other outfit references. Use Pose to describe the position. Choose the view that serves your shot list. Video: 01:05. Check each result against the intended detail. Keep the clothes and styling consistent while changing the view.
documents.s: Step 3: Write the shot list and choose Pose

documents.t: Put the selected views next to one another. Check whether they explain both the overall fit and the details you chose to show. Front. Shows the overall outfit and fit. Back. Makes the rear shape and shirt hem visible. Turned view. Adds another view of the garment’s shape. These are the full-resolution source images used in the workshop’s final view set. Check your own set in the same way; a new pose still needs an accuracy and consistency review.
documents.s: Step 4: Review the views together

documents.t: Does each photo have a purpose in the shot list? Can you see the intended collar, hem or other garment detail? Check that the clothes, styling, background and lighting remain consistent across views, and return to any view that hides the product information you need. documents.t: Astria Workshops · Series 1: Your first AI lookbook · Lesson 8 Choose reference photos that explain your product’s shape, color and details. More references are not always better: extra images that add no useful information can make the direction less clear. Follow workshop 1.8: Troubleshooting AI. You’ll prepare the product, identify missing views, choose a shoe reference, match inputs to the crop and use a short prompt to clarify fit.
documents.s: How to Choose Product Reference Photos for AI Fashion Images

documents.t: Gather the original photos of the products you want to show. Open the look you’re working on in Astria Generate, and keep your shot list nearby. It tells you which details and products must appear in each image.
documents.s: Before you begin

documents.t: For a simple T-shirt, a clear phone photo may be enough. For more detailed garments, consider a DSLR camera with even flash lighting. Keep the white balance consistent so the colors look accurate. Iron out unwanted creases before shooting: they may appear in the generated image too. Keep the garment’s real seams and details visible. Give the AI clear product information. The workshop’s original shirt reference makes the shape, collar and small embroidery visible.
documents.s: Step 1: Make the product easy to see

documents.t: Look for details the front photo does not explain. Add a back photo when the garment has a back logo, a print or a different color. For a T-shirt with a plain back, a front photo may be enough. A distinctive back. This sweatshirt has a large back print that needs its own reference. A plain back. This is a different product: the Red Vibrant Flower T-shirt. Its back adds no print detail. If a generated back view repeats a print that belongs only on the front, state that the back is plain in the prompt. Check the next result against the real garment.
documents.s: Step 2: Add back views when they provide missing information

documents.t: When shoes support the outfit, use one clear photo from the front at about 45 degrees. It shows the toe and side together. Several similar views may not add useful information. Front and side in one reference. The workshop’s shoe photo shows the shape, laces, suede panels and sole. When shoes are the main product, extra references may help show their details. Choose them for what each one adds.
documents.s: Step 3: Choose a useful shoe angle

documents.t: Include a shoe reference in a full-length image that shows the shoes. If the shot crops them out, remove that reference. Keep the inputs focused on what you want in the image. Remove a reference that the crop does not need. The shoe reference has been removed for the closer shot. Video: 01:44.
documents.s: Step 4: Match the references to the framing

documents.t: Some information is easier to express in words. Add what the photos leave unclear and keep the instruction focused. You do not need a long description copied from another chat. For example, a flat product photo of balloon jeans may not explain how roomy they should look on the body. Add “balloon fitting” to describe the intended fit. Clarify the intended fit. The short phrase adds information that a product photo may leave ambiguous. Video: 02:08. Generate, compare the fit with the real garment and adjust the wording if it still needs work. The workshop’s balloon-jeans example is a separate FRAME product; it is not the burgundy Bobo Choses trousers used earlier in the series.
documents.s: Step 5: Use the prompt for information the photos do not explain

documents.t: Check that every reference contributes useful information. Your photos should explain the product’s visible details, and the prompt should clarify what those photos cannot show. Compare the output with the real garment’s shape, color and details before keeping it. documents.t: Look at an AI-produced catalog that has gone wrong and you will usually find the same failure: it is not one model wearing forty garments, it is forty slightly different people. The face changes. The age wanders. The build shifts between the knitwear and the outerwear. The short version: description is not identity. If your model is specified in words, you are recasting on every generation. documents.s: Consistent AI Fashion Models: One Face Across a Whole Collection

documents.t: Generate fashion visuals from your products, or start with a production-ready template. Generate→Templates gallery→

documents.t: "A woman in her late twenties, shoulder-length brown hair, olive skin, natural makeup" feels specific. It is not. It describes a category that contains an enormous number of distinct faces, and each generation is free to choose a different one. Add more adjectives and you narrow the category slightly; you never reduce it to a person. This is why prompt-only workflows produce a type rather than a model. The images are consistent in the way that stock photography is consistent — same genre, different humans. The fix is categorical rather than incremental: the likeness has to exist as a stored thing that gets pointed at, not a description that gets re-interpreted. Once a face is a reference the production can reuse, "the same model" becomes a fact about the setup rather than a hope about the output.
documents.s: Why description fails

documents.t: Teams say "consistency" and mean different things. All four are needed, and they fail independently. Identity consistency — the same recognisable person. This is what references solve. Styling consistency — hair and makeup that stay the same. A stored likeness will happily give you the same face with a different fringe. Hair, in particular, drifts more than faces do and is worth calling out explicitly in the direction. Treatment consistency — same light, same grade, same lens character, same background logic. Independent of who the person is. Framing consistency — crops and proportions that match across the set. A catalog can fail on any one of these while passing the other three, and the symptom looks similar to a non-specialist: "it looks off." Diagnosing which of the four broke is the first step in fixing it.
documents.s: Four kinds of consistency, often confused

documents.t: Store the likeness, don't describe it. Whether via a trained model from eight to sixteen varied photos or an instant reference from fewer, the point is the same: the identity becomes an asset in the production rather than a sentence in a prompt. Vary the source material. Reference images should span angles, lighting conditions, and expressions. Sixteen frames from one burst teach the system one lighting condition and one angle, and the likeness collapses the moment you ask for anything else. Separate the person from everything else. Casting, garment, pose, and scene should be independently specifiable. When they are entangled — one long prompt describing all four — changing the pose perturbs the face. This separation is the single biggest practical difference between tools that hold consistency and tools that do not. Lock the treatment before scaling. Approve light, grade, and framing on a handful of products first. Drift compounds; a slightly warm bias in the setup becomes visible warmth by image 200. Review as a set, never as singles. This is a process fix, not a technical one, and it catches more than any technical measure. Contact-sheet the whole run at a size where faces are legible. Re-anchor periodically. On long runs, check late images against the earliest approved ones rather than against the images immediately before them. Drift is a slow gradient; comparing neighbours will never reveal it.
documents.s: What actually works

documents.t: Seeds. Reusing a seed reproduces a similar result for a near-identical prompt. Change the pose, the garment, or the scene — which is the entire job — and the likeness moves. Useful for reproducibility, not for identity. Longer descriptions. Adding adjectives narrows the category but never collapses it to one person. Twenty-word casting descriptions are a symptom of the wrong approach, not a solution to it. Picking the best of many. Generating forty options and choosing the most similar is expensive, slow, and still drifts, because you are selecting from a distribution rather than fixing it. Face-swapping at the end. Pasting a consistent face onto inconsistent bodies produces a characteristic uncanny result: the head belongs to someone whose build, skin tone, and lighting do not match the body beneath it.
documents.s: What does not work

documents.t: One consequence worth stating: consistency work is what makes broad casting practical. If every image is a fresh roll of the dice, representing a range of ages, sizes, and bodies across a collection is unmanageable — you cannot hold six different people consistent when you cannot hold one. Once casting is a stored reference, a brand can run a genuinely varied cast — including children's ranges and extended sizing — with the same reliability as a single model. Whether a brand does that is a values question. Consistency is what turns it from an aspiration into an operation. For portraits of real employees, the challenge is different: preserve each person while matching the photographic treatment across people. Use the AI team photos and headshots workflow for the submission brief and approval process.
documents.s: The extended-casting problem

documents.t: Before committing to a platform, run this: Establish one model. Produce ten images: five garments, two poses each, one indoor scene and one outdoor. Contact-sheet them at a size where faces are clearly legible. Ask someone who has not seen them: "Is this one person or more than one?" Then change the scene to something quite different — night, harsh light, a different location — and repeat. Step five is where most tools fail. Consistency under similar conditions is common; consistency across genuinely different lighting is what a real collection demands. For the full production context, see the AI fashion photoshoot guide. For lookbooks specifically, where casting continuity carries the narrative, see the AI lookbook guide.
documents.s: A test that predicts real-world behaviour

documents.t: Because a text description is not an identity. Words like "woman, 28, brown hair" describe a category containing millions of faces, and each generation picks a different one. Consistency requires the likeness to be stored as a reusable reference, not re-described each time.
documents.s: Why does the same AI model look different in every image?

documents.t: Only weakly. Reusing a seed reproduces similar results for a near-identical prompt, but the likeness drifts as soon as the pose, scene, or framing changes — which is exactly what a collection requires. Seeds are a reproducibility tool, not an identity tool.
documents.s: Do seeds keep a character consistent?

documents.t: For a trained likeness, typically eight to sixteen varied images. Instant reference approaches can work from far fewer. Variety across angle, lighting, and expression matters more than volume in either case.
documents.s: How many reference photos are needed for a consistent model?

documents.t: The gradual change in a model's appearance across a long production run — subtly different face, age, or build between early and late images. It is rarely visible image-by-image and obvious when the set is viewed together.
documents.s: What is casting drift?

documents.t: Yes, when the same stored reference drives both. This is what allows a still campaign and its motion cutdowns to feature recognisably the same person rather than two similar-looking people. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.

documents.t: Astria Workshops · Series 1: Your first AI lookbook · Lesson 5 Bring the background and lighting of your first AI lookbook image closer to your brand. You’ll work through a precise color, a textured reference and lighting instructions, then compare the results with your starting image. Follow workshop 1.5: Background & Lighting. Captures below show the actual controls in the video; comparison images use the original full-resolution files. Click an image to enlarge it.
documents.s: How to Control Backgrounds and Lighting in an AI Lookbook

documents.t: Open your brand’s workspace on Astria Generate, with the outfit from your first lookbook image. Keep a brand reference photo beside the first result. Notice how the background and shadows affect the mood before changing the instructions.
documents.s: Before you begin

documents.t: Make sure Image is selected. Open the gear below the prompt and find Background color. Click the color swatch. Use the eyedropper in your browser’s color picker to sample the background in your reference image, and include the resulting HEX value in your instructions. A HEX value is a color code, such as #D8D5CF, the neutral color used in this workshop. Set the background color. The swatch and HEX input are in the gear menu. Video: 00:31. The native browser eyedropper is outside the recorded frame. A color name alone can lead to different shades. A code makes the direction more specific, but it does not guarantee an exact match. Compare the background across the generated images; exact matching may need further editing.
documents.s: Step 1: Specify a background color

documents.t: For a textured setting, choose a reference image that shows the surface and surroundings you want. Add it using the plus in the Background reference square. Inspect the texture as well as the color, then compare both with the new result. Use a visual reference for a surface. The Background square sits alongside the outfit references. Video: 00:52. Face preview hidden.
documents.s: Step 2: Add a reference for a textured background

documents.t: Look at the brand’s photos and choose words that describe their light. Include that direction in the prompt. The workshop’s examples are “strong shadows,” “light shadows” and “no shadows.” Check the actual result against the reference rather than assuming the wording produced the intended effect.
documents.s: Step 3: Describe the shadows

documents.t: For softer light and gentler shadows, try “diffused lighting.” For a different effect, try “on-camera flash,” meaning a flash on or near the camera. Compare how the light changes the clothes and the background. Diffused lighting. Notice the softer light and gentler shadows. Original source image shown in the video’s lighting comparison. On-camera flash. Compare the more defined wall shadow. The reference set, format and output count match the diffused-light run.
documents.s: Step 4: Compare diffused lighting and on-camera flash

documents.t: Put the first image beside the result after your background and lighting direction. Look at the background color, the light and the shadows. Decide which changes bring the image closer to the brand’s style. First image. Use the starting look as the comparison point. After creative direction. Assess the setting and light alongside the clothes; each result still needs review.
documents.s: Step 5: Compare the first and directed images

documents.t: Compare the selected image with both the brand reference and the product photos. Check the background’s color and surface, the direction and softness of shadows, and whether the garment remains accurately represented. Keep the direction that fits your brand before moving on to hair, makeup and accessories. documents.t: Open your brand’s workspace in Astria Generate. Have a clear product photo of each item you want in the outfit. This example uses packshots—studio photos of the products—of a cream shirt, burgundy trousers and suede shoes, plus a standing pose and a neutral background reference. If you’re still deciding what the images should look like, start with the brand’s product photography. Use its background, styling and garment views to guide your choices. documents.t: An ecommerce prompt should describe a media slot, not just a mood. “Minimal luxury product photo” does not tell the system whether you need the primary product-page image, a rear construction view, a size reference, a texture crop, or a campaign banner. The useful unit of work is the complete image family for one SKU. The short version: define the channel, lock the product facts, and prompt each required view separately. Use this guide to build front, side, back, detail, lifestyle, and campaign images from a shared production brief. Public product workspaces, packshot templates, and finished prompt examples make the pattern easier to see. documents.t: Start with a table of required outputs. A useful apparel product page might need front, back, side, fabric detail, and on-model scale. A handbag may need front, side, open interior, hardware detail, and carry context. A bottle may need a primary packshot, side label, closure detail, texture, and a lifestyle image. Give every slot a single job: Primary: identify the product immediately. Alternate angle: explain depth and geometry. Back or underside: disclose construction the hero cannot show. Detail: prove texture, closure, finish, or workmanship. Scale or use: show size and physical relationship. Campaign: attract attention without replacing factual coverage. This prevents the common mistake of asking one beautiful image to do six incompatible things.
documents.s: Write for the media slot

documents.t: A dependable prompt contains eight decisions: Channel and slot: PDP hero, marketplace primary, collection tile, email banner, or social crop. Product: the reference item, colorway, variant, and configuration. Preservation: silhouette, dimensions, materials, seams, labels, hardware, print, closure, and quantity. Orientation: front, rear, side, three-quarter, top-down, open, closed, folded, or worn. Frame: camera height, crop, negative space, and aspect ratio. Surface and background: exact color, sweep, tabletop, plinth, or location. Light and shadow: direction, softness, reflections, highlight control, and contact shadow. Exclusions: props, hands, duplicate objects, glare, horizon lines, or decorative ingredients that do not belong. Write the preservation clause from the product itself. A handbag needs handle count, gusset, closure and hardware. A bottle needs cap shape, fill level, glass color and label position. A dress needs neckline, waist, sleeve, fastening, hem and drape.
documents.s: The production prompt structure

documents.t: The same photographic language does not create the same risk in every category. Use this as the first review pass before choosing an example below. Vertical Hardest problem References to supply Notice first Fashion catalog Several garments must remain distinct while fitting one body Clean product views for every garment and any visible back construction Necklines, hems, print placement, layering and shoe contact Lookbooks Continuity across a sequence without repeating one pose Approved cast, each look, hero treatment and location family Cast drift, grade drift, styling changes and sequence rhythm Jewelry Tiny geometry changes can describe a different item Verified macro, side profile and on-body scale reference Stone count, prongs, band width, finish, reflection and scale Beauty Reflective packaging competes with exact labels and product color Straight packshot, cap or pump detail, verified label artwork Vessel shape, label placement, legibility, condensation and reflections Wedding dresses Beading, transparency, fitted construction and large moving volume interact Front, back, bodice detail, hem and fabric close-up Neckline, bead density, sleeve transparency, waist and train length Vitamins and supplements Packaging contains regulated copy and claims that must not be invented Verified packshot, every label panel, closure and product-form reference Dosage, quantity, seals, claims, ingredient copy and capsule count For vitamins and supplements, generate the scene around a verified package rather than treating generated label text as evidence. No dedicated public supplement workspace is claimed in this guide; the beauty workflow below is a visual starting point for bottles, not proof of label accuracy.

documents.t: Front view of the reference dress as a clean volumetric packshot. Preserve its silhouette, waist, seams, closures, pleats, fabric flow and hem. Center the full garment with clear negative space on a solid #F2F2F2 studio background; soft diffused light, restrained contact shadow, sharp focus, square composition. documents.t: Generated packshots can support concepting, campaigns, and variant production, but packaging requires strict review. Do not invent or silently alter label copy, quantities, seals, dosage information, claims, or regulated marks. When exact text matters, composite the verified artwork or use approved product photography.

The public Beauty workspace and Beauty template provide a starting point for campaign-oriented beauty imagery. Some finished prompt-detail pages may require sign-in, so use the public workspace or template as the durable entry point. Beauty Keep the bottle factual while the scene becomes expressive A campaign still life built around a single verified product reference. Campaign 3:4 Reflective set Reference inputs Reference · bottle and label position Generated result Public result · click to inspect the original generation Copy-ready promptReplace “reference” with your uploaded product or model. Copy prompt Still-life photograph with no person in frame. Place the reference cosmetic bottle upright on a shallow film of water over a dark reflective surface, with a soft mirrored reflection directly beneath it. Preserve the bottle proportions, pearlescent finish, cap, label size and label position. Add a cold glass pane with fine condensation immediately behind it and a seamless dusk-purple background. Low straight-on camera, one large diffused source from camera left, open shadows, faint warm haze, fine 35mm grain, gentle highlight halation, vertical 3:4. The challenge Reflective vessels, condensation, mirrored surfaces, and label fidelity all compete. The set can change; the package geometry and approved copy cannot. Things to notice Follow the cap-to-body proportion and the bottle silhouette before judging mood. Keep droplets and glare away from the label-reading area. Check that the reflection mirrors the actual bottle rather than a different container. Use verified label artwork in the final production file whenever exact copy matters. The challenge Metal is defined by reflections, and a tiny geometry change can turn one ring into another. A plausible result is not automatically an accurate result. Things to notice Trace the sculptural outline, openings, band width, and stone positions against the source. Ask whether the warm environment changed the apparent metal color. Check that fabric does not conceal the product feature the image is meant to sell. Keep the verified macro or on-hand reference beside this image on the PDP. documents.t: If a marketplace requires white, write “seamless pure-white background, no horizon line” and request clean edge separation. But prompting is not color measurement. Inspect the delivered pixel values, clipping path, transparency, margins, and file profile after generation. A visually white image may still contain a warm cast or grey corners. The same rule applies to aspect ratios. State square, 4:5, or 16:9 in the prompt, then export and validate the required pixel dimensions separately.

documents.t: Do not rewrite the entire brief per SKU. Create a matrix with rows for media slots and columns for product classes. Keep the studio block stable, then swap only the class-specific preservation clause. documents.t: Use the source product beside the generated output. Check: silhouette, dimensions and part count; front, side and rear geometry; seams, stitching, closures and pockets; labels, logos, print and packaging copy; material texture, transparency and reflectivity; hardware color and attachment points; shadows, reflections and contact with the surface; scale relative to hands, bodies, furniture or props; correct variant, quantity and product configuration; channel crop, safe margins, background and file dimensions. If a discrepancy could change what a buyer believes they will receive, revise or reject the image. The prompt is the specification; review is the release gate.

documents.t: Include the image's channel and slot, the referenced product, the geometry and materials that must remain accurate, camera angle, product orientation, background, light, shadow behavior, crop, and aspect ratio.

documents.t: PDP prompts prioritize truthful coverage, repeatable angles, clean edges, readable construction, and consistent scale. Campaign prompts can use props, atmosphere, unusual crops, and stronger shadows, but should still state the product features that cannot change.

documents.t: No. Keep verified photography where exact label text, regulated information, fine material claims, gemstone details, safety-critical features, or precise color are essential. Generated images are strongest when the product reference and review standard are both clear.

documents.t: Specify a seamless pure-white background, clean product edges, neutral color balance, a restrained contact shadow, no horizon line, no props, and the required crop. Verify the exported pixels and marketplace requirements separately.

documents.t: Build prompts around the media slots the page needs: usually a hero, alternate angle, back or side view, construction detail, scale or use context, and one or more campaign crops. The exact count depends on product complexity and channel requirements.

documents.t: Ask what a fashion photoshoot costs and you will get answers ranging across two orders of magnitude, all of them true. The word covers a photographer with one light in a rented room and a full production unit on location with a crew of fifteen. The short version: the shoot fee is rarely the biggest line. Post-production, usage rights, and the cost of scheduling are what actually determine the invoice. documents.s: Create your next campaign with Astria

documents.t: Every fashion shoot budget is assembled from the same components. Rates vary enormously by market — a day in London, New York, or Milan is not a day in a smaller city — so treat what follows as a structure to fill in rather than a price list. Photographer. Quoted as a day rate, sometimes with a separate creative fee for campaign work. The single most variable line: an experienced commercial photographer with a name commands a multiple of a competent working professional, and both may deliver what your brand needs. Assistants. Usually one or two, at a fraction of the photographer's rate. Non-optional on anything with real lighting. Model. Booked through an agency, at a day rate plus agency commission — commonly around 20% — plus usage. The usage line is the one that surprises people; see below. Hair and makeup. One artist for a single model; two if you are shooting several looks against the clock. Stylist. Day rate plus prep days, which are real and frequently forgotten. Pulling and returning samples takes as long as shooting them. Studio or location. A studio day, or a location fee plus permits, plus a scout day if the location is not already known. Equipment. Often included in the photographer's rate; specialist lighting, grip, or digital capture is not. Production. A producer, catering, transport, and shipping samples both ways. Small productions absorb this into someone's job. Large ones cannot. Post-production. Quoted per image, and this is where volume bites. Retouching 20 editorial images is a project; retouching 600 catalog variants is a different business entirely. Usage rights. Frequently the largest hidden line. Talent and location licensing is scoped by territory, media, and duration. Extending a campaign, or reusing an image in a market you did not license, means renegotiating — often at a worse rate, because you have already committed creatively.
documents.s: The line items

documents.t: Rather than invent precise figures, here is how the proportions typically fall — which is more useful for planning than any single number. Small ecommerce day. Photographer, one assistant, one model, one hair-and-makeup artist, studio, standard retouching. Crew is the majority of the cost; post scales with SKU count and often overtakes the shoot fee. Usage is usually limited and cheap. Lookbook. Adds a stylist with prep days, a location, and more considered post. Styling and location can rival the photographer's fee. Deliverable count is low, so cost per finished image is high — by design. Campaign. Adds a producer, a larger crew, casting with a recognisable face, and broad usage rights. Talent and usage frequently dominate everything else, and the shoot day becomes a minority of the budget. The consistent pattern: as ambition rises, the photography becomes a smaller share and the rights and people become a larger one.
documents.s: Three realistic shapes

documents.t: Reshoots. Something arrives late, a sample is wrong, the light was not there. Ask explicitly who pays. Sample logistics. Shipping a collection to a location, insured, and back again. Your own time. The hours your team spends briefing, attending, selecting, and revising are real cost. On small teams they are the largest uncounted line by a wide margin. The calendar. The most expensive item on this list and the one that never appears on an invoice: a product that cannot be listed for three weeks because the shoot is booked for the 14th. For a seasonal business that delay has a direct revenue number attached. Revision. Deciding after delivery that the grade should be warmer means a grading session, or a reshoot, or living with it. Most brands live with it, which is its own kind of cost.
documents.s: The costs nobody quotes

documents.t: The honest framing is not "cents versus thousands," though that comparison is technically accurate and endlessly repeated. Generation cost per image is genuinely a rounding error. The fully-loaded comparison has to include: Setup time to reach an approved creative direction — real, and typically a day or two Review cycles with whoever owns the brand Rejected variants, which nobody publishes but everybody produces Correction time on garments that do not convert cleanly The salaried hours of whoever runs the process Counted properly, the per-image gap narrows considerably. It remains large — but the more defensible arguments are structural rather than arithmetic: Scheduling disappears. No model availability, no studio booking, no sample shipping, no three-week wait. Revision becomes cheap. A change of mind after approval is an edit, not a reshoot. For most teams this is the biggest practical difference. The long tail becomes affordable. Products that could never justify a shoot day can be presented properly — which is where the revenue argument usually lives. Direction is retained. The approved treatment is reusable next season rather than expiring with the shoot. The side-by-side model is worked through in AI versus traditional photoshoot cost, and the per-variant view in product photography cost per SKU. For a figure against your own catalog rather than a worked example, the photoshoot calculator counts the products in your store that need imagery and prices the coverage from there.
documents.s: How the AI comparison actually works

documents.t: Ask every supplier the same six questions: What is included — crew, studio, equipment, catering, transport? How many finished, retouched images, and to what standard? What usage rights, for which territories, media, and duration? What happens if we need a reshoot, and who pays? What is the revision policy after delivery? What do we own at the end — final files only, or raws and layered files too? Question three is where most budget overruns originate. Question five is where most disappointment does.
documents.s: How to compare two quotes properly

documents.t: A single-day commercial fashion shoot commonly lands somewhere between a few thousand and several tens of thousands, depending on crew size, location, talent, and usage rights. The range is wide because "photoshoot" describes anything from one photographer in a rented studio to a full production unit.
documents.s: How much does a fashion photoshoot cost?

documents.t: Usually post-production and usage rights. Retouching is quoted per image and scales with volume, and licensing for a model or location often costs more over time than the shoot day itself — particularly when a campaign is extended or reused.
documents.s: What is the biggest hidden cost in a photoshoot?

documents.t: Because quotes bundle different things. One may include retouching, licensing, and a producer; another may cover the shoot day alone. Compare quotes line by line, and specifically check usage rights, retouching volume, and who pays for reshoots.
documents.s: Why do photoshoot quotes vary so much?

documents.t: Highly variable, but a well-run ecommerce day produces far more usable frames than an editorial day, because the setup is fixed. Editorial days may yield only a handful of finished images. Always agree deliverable counts rather than shooting hours.
documents.s: How many images does a shoot day produce?

documents.t: Per image, dramatically. Fully loaded, the gap is smaller than headline figures suggest once setup, review, rejected variants, and staff time are counted. The larger practical saving is usually the removal of scheduling and sample logistics rather than the per-image price. Price your catalog with the photoshoot calculator, or explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.

A beautiful campaign cut can do the first job while leaving the other two unfinished. Start with one product proposition and two opening hooks. Keep the evidence, offer, destination, and closing action the same. This gives the production team a small deliverable and the marketing team a question it can actually test. documents.t: A campaign film builds a world. A product-page demonstration helps someone inspect an item. An acquisition ad has to connect an interruption in a feed with a useful next step. Write that connection in one sentence before choosing footage: “Show the jacket's removable collar, then take interested shoppers to that jacket.” The AI fashion film guide covers the broader motion production. Here the unit of work is an ad variant with a defined hypothesis. If your main need is a faithful demonstration for an existing shopper, start with apparel product-video production. A complete brief names the audience, product or collection, proposition, evidence, destination, placement, offer, and primary success metric. An ad for a single jacket should land where that jacket is immediately identifiable. If the selected color is unavailable, fix the brief or destination before producing more variants.
documents.s: Give acquisition creative its own brief

documents.t: Collect an approved hero frame, an accurate detail view, any real demonstration footage, product names, current offer copy, and the destination URL. Store the SKU and colorway with each visual. Add the approved logo, type treatment, audio permissions, and final copy as separate editing assets. Astria's ecommerce workflow describes creating imagery from product inputs and creative templates. Those reviewed stills can form the visual source kit for an ad. They still need product approval before they become motion, and the final cut needs editing, audio, and placement review. Use generated scenes to explore framing or extend an approved visual treatment. Use real product footage when the ad claims something demonstrable, such as a detachable part or pocket capacity. Keep text, prices, and end cards in the edit so a commercial revision does not require regenerating the garment. Record what is permitted for the assets you use, including paid advertising and the planned channels. For a creator-led ad, obtain the creator's agreed usage scope; do not turn a synthetic presenter into an invented customer testimonial. These are production checks, not a substitute for reviewing the applicable platform and campaign requirements.
documents.s: Build a small source kit

documents.t: Consider a jacket with a genuinely removable collar. The following brief is illustrative: confirm the product feature before using this copy. The timing is an editing target, not a claim about the ideal length of every fashion ad. Time Visual Job 0–3 seconds Hook A: full jacket with collar; Hook B: close-up of collar being removed Test product-first versus detail-first opening 3–8 seconds The same filmed removal and reattachment demonstration in both versions Establish that the feature is real 8–12 seconds Two approved styling views of the exact jacket Show how the feature changes the look 12–15 seconds Stable jacket hero and edited “Shop the jacket” end card Give a clear next step matching the destination Keep the audio, text treatment, total duration, and all footage after the opening the same across A and B. If you change the first image and the opening copy together, call the test an opening-package test. It cannot isolate which of those two changes drove the result. Design speech and music deliberately, but make product identity and the action understandable with sound off. Caption speech that carries the proposition. Watch the actual export on a phone: a neat desktop layout can still make a product name or fastening too small to see.
documents.s: A 15-second edit with a clear job for each beat

documents.t: Generating three hooks, four offers, three avatars, and two soundtracks creates 72 combinations before any evidence tells you which variation matters. It also spreads review effort and media spend across many different questions. For the first test, produce two exports of the same proposition: Element Version A Version B Opening Full product in the first frame Feature detail in the first frame Demonstration Same approved footage Same approved footage Offer and CTA Same wording Same wording Landing page Same product destination Same product destination Audience and delivery settings Held steady within the test Held steady within the test TikTok's split-testing documentation describes separating the audience into exclusive groups for a controlled comparison. Its testing-variable guide lists creative assets, including opening hooks, and permits one selected variable per split test. Check compatibility with your objective and campaign setup before promising a particular experiment. Use the platform's experiment tool when available. Two ads placed in an ordinary optimized ad group are not automatically a balanced experiment: unequal delivery can reflect the delivery system's choices as well as the creative. Treat that result as directional unless the setup supports the comparison you intend to make.
documents.s: Two useful variants beat an unplanned matrix

documents.t: Make a 9:16 master for a vertical-feed brief, with enough room to reposition copy for the destination's actual interface. Do not use one fixed “safe zone” for every platform, language, and ad format. As checked on September 5, 2026, TikTok recommends 9:16 for Non-Spark in-feed ads, with a minimum of 540 × 960 pixels. Its safe-zone guidance varies with dimensions, caption length, and additional formats, and it warns that preview and live display can differ. Use the current downloadable templates and verify your specific placement in the TikTok in-feed ad specifications. An editorial delivery target of 1080 × 1920 gives this brief a practical full-HD master; it is not the quoted platform minimum. Confirm accepted encoding, duration, file weight, and account-specific options at upload. For Reels or another placement, use its own current Ads Manager specification and preview rather than assuming TikTok's rules apply. Keep hems, footwear, product names, and the call to action clear of visible controls. Reframe a wide campaign shot if the vertical crop removes the product feature. Make a separate end card for another ratio when necessary; squeezing the whole composition into a smaller box usually weakens legibility.
documents.s: Export for the placement, then inspect its overlays

documents.t: Approve the ad and destination together. The product, color, feature, price, availability, and promotion should agree. If the ad opens on one jacket and lands on an unrelated collection, a low purchase rate may be a destination problem rather than an opening-hook problem. Inspect generated motion for changing prints, logos, fastenings, silhouettes, and accessories. Review the transitions as carefully as the hero frames. A collar cannot disappear before the demonstration removes it, and a bag cannot gain capacity during a packing shot. Have the product owner sign off the merchandise, the creative lead sign off the cut, and the marketer sign off the destination and test setup. Preview the final uploaded file rather than approving only the editing timeline. Compression, player overlays, or a misplaced caption can change what the viewer understands.
documents.s: Review every claim through the landing page

documents.t: Select the primary metric from the campaign objective before launch. For an acquisition test, that might be cost per purchase or purchase conversion under a consistent attribution setting. Set the test budget, duration, and sample requirements from baseline volume and the difference worth detecting. A handful of orders is not a universal stopping rule. Use attention and click measures to investigate the result: Observation Next thing to inspect Weak early retention Whether the opening identifies a relevant product quickly enough Good retention, few destination visits Proposition clarity and the reason to take the next step Many clicks, few purchases Destination match, load time, stock, price, and product information Strong commerce result, high production cost Whether the concept can be repeated economically across products These are diagnostic hypotheses. They do not prove that the hook, page, or price caused the result. Compare metrics using the same definitions and attribution window; a “view” on one platform is not necessarily the same event elsewhere. Keep the full test record, including inconclusive results. Avoid declaring a winner from a single early spike or silently changing the offer midway. If both edits fail, revisit the proposition and destination before commissioning ten more openings.
documents.s: Measure the commercial result, then diagnose the edit

documents.t: Track concept development, source production, all generation attempts, product review, editing, audio, captions, and delivery. Keep media spend separate so you can distinguish an expensive production process from an expensive acquisition channel. Divide your production spend by the number of approved creative variants. Cropping two variants into three ratios each gives six files, not six independent creative ideas. Budget for both the underlying concepts and the additional finishing work. Use Astria pricing for current generation rates. A promising concept should survive a second SKU without losing its logic. Reuse the shot structure and editing treatment, but replace the evidence with footage of the actual new product. A removable-collar ad is not a template for a jacket whose collar is fixed. For planning across a collection, connect this record to the AI lookbook workflow. If the open question is which production suite fits the team, the Astria vs Higgsfield comparison covers that buying decision. The ad test should decide the creative question, not serve as an unmeasured comparison of tools.
documents.s: Price a repeatable concept, not a folder of exports

documents.t: Include a clear product opening, evidence for the proposition, a legible next step, and a matching destination. A short sequence can do all four jobs. Choose its duration around the message and placement rather than assuming one length is always best.
documents.s: What should a fashion video ad include?

documents.t: Start with two versions that differ in one defined element, such as the opening hook. Keep the product evidence, offer, destination, and other delivery conditions steady so the result answers a useful question.
documents.s: How many fashion ad variants should a first test use?

documents.t: Reviewed product photos can supply the visual basis for generated motion and an edited ad. Check every shot for garment changes, keep commercial text editable, and use filmed evidence when demonstrating the actual behavior or function of the product.
documents.s: Can AI create fashion video ads from product photos?

documents.t: Reuse the approved source assets, then adapt framing, text, audio, and end cards to each placement. Check the current upload specification and preview overlays. A common vertical ratio does not guarantee that the same layout is safe everywhere.
documents.s: Can the same fashion video run on every social placement?

documents.t: Choose a primary metric that matches the campaign objective, with consistent attribution and a planned sample. For acquisition, commerce outcomes matter more than views alone. Use retention and clicks to diagnose the edit, and retain an inconclusive result when the evidence is insufficient. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.

documents.t: FLUX.1, launched in August 2024 by Black Forest Labs, represents a significant advancement in the field of generative deep learning. This innovative model is designed to push the boundaries of creativity, efficiency, and diversity in media generation, particularly focusing on images and videos. With a mission to develop state-of-the-art generative models, FLUX.1 leverages advanced architectures such as flow matching and Denoising Image Transformer (DIT), similar to the technologies employed in Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3).
documents.s: Introduction to FLUX.1

documents.t: FLUX.1 is built on a robust foundation of 12 billion parameters, allowing it to deliver exceptional image fidelity and controllability. This model excels in generating high-quality images that cater to a wide range of applications, from artistic creations to detailed photorealistic outputs. The architecture combines the strengths of transformer models and diffusion techniques, enabling FLUX.1 to outperform its predecessors, including SDXL and SD1.5, in terms of image quality and prompt adherence.
documents.s: Key Features and Innovations

documents.t: FLUX.1 comes in three distinct variants, each designed for different use cases:
documents.s: Variants of FLUX.1

documents.t: Performance: This is the flagship model, offering state-of-the-art performance with exceptional image quality, detail, and diversity. Access: Available exclusively via API, making it suitable for commercial applications. System Requirements: High system requirements, not suitable for consumer hardware.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Pro]

documents.t: Purpose: A distilled version intended for non-commercial use, ideal for research and development. Features: Provides similar quality and prompt adherence as the Pro version but is more efficient and can run on consumer hardware. Availability: Open-weight model, downloadable for local use.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Dev]

documents.t: Speed: Optimized for fast image generation, making it suitable for local development and personal projects. Performance: While it sacrifices some image fidelity for speed, it is designed for quick outputs. License: Released under the Apache 2.0 license, allowing for broader usage. Each variant caters to specific needs, from high-performance commercial applications to efficient local development and rapid prototyping.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Schnell]

documents.t: Fine-tuning FLUX.1 on Astria is easy: you just need a handful of images to get started.
documents.s: Fine-Tuning FLUX.1 on Astria.ai: Step-by-Step Guide

documents.t: Before you can start fine-tuning FLUX.1, you'll need to generate an API key on Astria.ai. Here's how: 1. Login to Astria.ai: Visit Astria.ai and log in using your Gmail ID. 2. Access the API section: Once logged in, navigate to the API section of your account. 3. Generate the API Key: Click on the 'Generate API Key' button. This will create your unique API key, which you can use for all API requests. 4. Check current pricing before creating fine-tunes and generating images using FLUX.1.
documents.s: Generate Your API Key

documents.t: Here, we'll walk you through fine-tuning FLUX.1 using the API, specifically focusing on creating a model that excels at generating human face images. We'll use images of a woman from the free stock photo website, Pexels, to fine-tune our model. Prepare your data: Gather around 8-16 high-resolution images. Upload these images to PostImages to get the image URLs. Ensure that the images are diverse in terms of lighting, angles, and expressions to capture the full range of features you want the model to learn. Initiate fine-tuning: Replace YOUR_API_KEY and YOUR_MODEL_ID with your generated API key and Tune ID. Use the following code to fine-tune FLUX.1 for human faces: import requests from io import BytesIO # Replace with your actual API key API_KEY = 'YOUR_API_KEY' # Function to download images and convert them to binary def download_image(url): response = requests.get(url) if response.status_code == 200: return BytesIO(response.content) else: print(f'Error downloading image: {url}, status code: {response.status_code}') return None # Fine-tune a model using Flux.1 def fine_tune_flux_model(api_key): fine_tune_url = 'https://www.astria.ai/tunes' image_urls = [ 'https://i.postimg.cc/9fThRXgx/pexels-sound-on-3756747.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/dttwHYD1/pexels-sound-on-3756750.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/fysTTSwj/pexels-sound-on-3756752.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/prPRtNZs/pexels-sound-on-3756917.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/fRVZsfcQ/pexels-sound-on-3756944.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/0yhvyKnM/pexels-sound-on-3756962.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/LXKmNgZK/pexels-sound-on-3756993.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/ZqyT8xnx/pexels-sound-on-3760859.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/RF748Cc3/pexels-sound-on-3760918.jpg' ] images = [] for url in image_urls: image = download_image(url) if image: images.append(('tune[images][]', ('image.jpg', image, 'image/jpeg'))) fine_tune_data = { 'tune[class_name]': 'woman', 'tune[name]': 'woman', 'tune[title]': 'Flux Tune Model 1', 'tune[base_fine-tune]': 'Flux.1', 'tune[model_type]': 'lora', 'tune[branch]': 'flux1' } fine_tune_headers = { 'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}' } fine_tune_response = requests.post(fine_tune_url, headers=fine_tune_headers, data=fine_tune_data, files=images) if fine_tune_response.status_code == 200: tune_id = fine_tune_response.json()['id'] print(f'Fine-tuning started for tune ID: {tune_id}') return tune_id else: print(f'Error fine-tuning model: {fine_tune_response.status_code}, {fine_tune_response.text}') return None # Main execution flux_tune_id = fine_tune_flux_model(API_KEY) 6. Monitor the progress: Fine-tuning typically takes about 30-60 minutes. You can monitor this through the provided URL. 7. Generate the images: Once fine-tuning is complete, use the following code to generate images: import requests API_KEY = 'YOUR_API_KEY' MODEL_ID = 1504994 # The hardcoded ID for the Flux model # Generate images def generate_images(api_key, model_id): generate_url = f'https://www.astria.ai/tunes/{model_id}/prompts' generate_data = { 'text': '<LoRA:`MODEL_ID`:1.0> sks woman In the style of TOK, a photo editorial avant-garde dramatic action pose of a person wearing 90s round wacky sunglasses pulling glasses down looking forward, in Tokyo with large marble structures and bonsai trees at sunset with a vibrant illustrated jacket surrounded by illustrations of flowers, smoke, flames, ice cream, sparkles, rock and roll', 'num_images': 4, 'model_type' :'lora', 'model': 'flux.1_dev' } generate_headers = { 'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } generate_response = requests.post(generate_url, headers=generate_headers, json=generate_data) if generate_response.status_code == 200: prompt_id = generate_response.json()['id'] image_url = generate_response.json()['image_url'] print(f'Images generated for prompt ID: {prompt_id}') print(f'Image URL: {image_url}') else: print(f'Error generating images: {generate_response.status_code}, {generate_response.text}') # Main execution generate_images(API_KEY, MODEL_ID) # Main execution generate_images(API_KEY, MODEL_ID)
documents.s: Guide to Fine-Tuning Human Faces

documents.t: Prompt 2: A woman dressed in ornate, golden armour, holding a sword, standing on the battlefield at sunrise, with a determined expression. Prompt 3: A woman driving a classic pink convertible with a shiny finish, reminiscent of a Barbie car, cruising down a candy-coloured boulevard lined with palm trees. documents.t: FLUX.1, especially when fine-tuned, provides a powerful tool for creators and developers. Whether you're looking to generate human portraits, artistic renditions, or even specific pet images, fine-tuning FLUX.1 using Astria's API opens up new possibilities. It is important to remember that Flux image prompting tends to give better outputs with a more narrative-style prompt rather than the traditional comma-separated tags. Also, what’s truly unique about Flux is its ability to render text – not just single words, but entire sentences – with great clarity. This feature alone opens up a universe of possibilities for businesses looking to integrate text into their images.

documents.t: This guide still describes the fine-tuning flow accurately — you upload images, POST a tune, and generate against it — but the model landscape moved on considerably. Read it for the API mechanics, not the model recommendations. The FLUX line advanced. FLUX.1 [Pro], [Dev], and [Schnell] have been joined by newer releases, including FLUX.2 Pro. The branch and model parameters shown below still work; check the current list before hardcoding one. Gemini-branch references removed the training wait. For many use cases you no longer need to train a LoRA at all — a reference can be created instantly from a handful of images and used the same way in prompts. Editing models joined the line-up. Nano Banana and Seedream handle instruction-based edits (background swap, object removal, colour change) that previously required inpainting or a second pass. Check current terms. Use current pricing for API rates and any available offers. Always discover models programmatically rather than hardcoding a name — see the API reference for the current endpoints and parameters. If you are producing fashion or ecommerce imagery rather than building on the API, the AI fashion photoshoot guide covers the production side of the same platform.

documents.t: An AI clothing-on-model generator can turn a flat lay, ghost mannequin, or garment photo into an image of a person wearing the product. That makes on-model coverage possible for catalog items that would not justify another model-and-studio day. The short version: use a complete, evenly lit garment reference; tell the workflow what must not change; and check product truth before judging the model or scene. A convincing person does not prove that the clothing is accurate or that it will physically fit a customer. Reviewed September 7, 2026.
