documents.t: Several search terms describe overlapping jobs: Term Usually means What to verify Flat lay to model Turn a garment photographed from above into a person wearing it The full garment is visible and unfolded Product-to-model Combine a product reference with a selected or generated model Which parts of the product and person the workflow preserves Clothing-on-model generator A tool-led name for either of the above Whether it accepts your real clothing image rather than generating a similar outfit from text Model swap Replace the person in an existing fashion image Garment, pose, crop, and lighting remain unchanged Brand-side virtual try-on Generate merchandising imagery of a product on selected models This is not the same as a shopper fitting-room widget or measured fit prediction If the immediate goal is to put your clothes on an AI model, the operation is product-to-model. If the goal is to let each shopper upload a selfie, that is a different product and privacy workflow. The virtual try-on guide separates the two.
documents.s: Flat lay to model, product-to-model, or virtual try-on?

documents.t: Still choosing a format? The ghost mannequin alternatives comparison covers when to use flat lay, a hanger, live-model photography, or AI on-model. This guide covers the conversion after you have chosen on-model output. The economics are brutal and familiar. Your top sellers get the full treatment — model, studio, stylist, retouch. Everything below the top 20% gets whatever is cheapest, which means a flat lay or a ghost mannequin, because the marginal revenue does not justify a shoot day. So the long tail is presented worse than the head, which suppresses its performance, which confirms the decision not to invest in it. The loop is self-sealing, and it is the single clearest place where cheap on-model conversion changes something material about a business.
documents.s: Why the long tail stays flat

documents.t: This is the part that gets skipped, and it causes most disappointing results. Good source material: The entire garment visible, unfolded, nothing cropped off Even, diffuse lighting with no hard shadow Accurate colour — if your source is warm, every output inherits that warmth Resolution high enough to resolve weave, texture, and stitching Ghost mannequin shots, which are frequently the best input available because the garment is already holding a human shape Problematic source material: Styled flat lays with sleeves folded or the hem tucked — folded areas have to be invented Partial crops Hard directional shadow, which gets baked in as if it were fabric colour Garment on a hanger, distorting the shoulders Screenshots, or images compressed so far that texture is gone A brand with clean, consistent product photography gets clean, consistent on-model output. A brand whose product shots were taken by six different people over three years gets exactly that variance back, amplified. If your outputs are inconsistent, audit your inputs before blaming the tool.
documents.s: Your source image decides everything

documents.t: Converts reliably: solid-colour knits and jersey, tees, simple dresses, structured outerwear, tailored pieces with clean lines. Anything where drape is predictable and the surface is uniform. Needs per-item review: directional prints and stripes, which can mirror or misalign across a seam; logo scale and placement; sheer and semi-sheer fabric; complex gathering, pleating, and ruching; fine hardware — buckles, eyelets, zip pulls, chain straps. Expect to intervene: garments whose construction is the product. Technical outerwear with visible seam-sealing, structured tailoring, performance wear with panel logic. The output will look plausible and be wrong in the ways your customer specifically cares about. The pragmatic approach is triage rather than uniform treatment: batch the easy categories with spot checks, and route the hard ones to individual review. Treating all 600 variants identically means either over-reviewing the simple ones or under-reviewing the difficult ones — usually both.
documents.s: What survives conversion, and what needs watching

documents.t: Running a large batch introduces a second-order problem: the individual images are fine and the set is not. Same causes as everywhere else in this work — light and grade creeping, crops shifting, casting wandering across a long run. For a catalog this matters more than for a lookbook, because the grid view puts thirty products side by side and every inconsistency is on display simultaneously. Two habits prevent nearly all of it: Fix the treatment — model, light, background, crop, grade — before running volume, and store it rather than re-specifying it. Review in grid view at the size the customer sees, not one image at a time at full resolution. The mechanics of holding casting fixed are covered in consistent AI fashion models.
documents.s: Where drift creeps in

documents.t: Per product, and quickly — this should take seconds once you know what you are looking for: Colour matches the actual garment, not the source photo's white balance. This is the most common cause of returns from imagery. Print alignment across seams, and print scale relative to the body. Logo correct in size, position, and orientation. Closures — buttons on the correct side, zip direction, buckle threading. Fabric behaviour — does it drape like the material it is? Silk that hangs like denim is instantly wrong. Length and proportion — a cropped jacket that renders hip-length is a returns problem, not an aesthetic one. Anatomy, especially hands and any hand-to-garment interaction.
documents.s: The pre-publish checklist

documents.t: It solves presentation for the long tail, colorway coverage without reshooting, consistent framing across a catalog, and the ability to change your mind about the treatment without re-booking anything. It does not solve fit information — no image tells a customer whether a size 12 will fit them — and it does not replace the photography of your hero products, where the real thing photographed properly still carries weight that a conversion does not. For the wider production picture, see the AI product photography guide and AI fashion photoshoot guide. For the garment-on-body question specifically, see virtual try-on for fashion brands. For what the whole exercise costs per variant, see product photography cost per SKU.
documents.s: What this does and does not solve

documents.t: Yes. The garment is analysed from the product image and rendered on a model with plausible drape, fit, and lighting. Quality depends heavily on the source image: an evenly-lit, complete, unfolded garment shot converts far better than a styled or partial one.
documents.s: Can you turn a flat lay into an on-model photo?

documents.t: The whole garment visible and unfolded, even diffuse lighting, no heavy shadow, accurate colour, and enough resolution to resolve texture and detail. Ghost mannequin shots are usually the best starting point because the garment already holds its shape.
documents.s: What makes a good source image for on-model conversion?

documents.t: On-model imagery is widely regarded as helping shoppers judge fit and scale, which flat lays cannot convey. The size of the effect varies by category and price point, so it is worth measuring on your own catalog rather than assuming a published figure applies.
documents.s: Do on-model images convert better than flat lays?

documents.t: Directional prints across seams, sheer and semi-sheer fabrics, complex drape and gathering, fine hardware, and garments whose construction is the selling point. These need per-item review rather than batch acceptance.
documents.s: Which garments do not convert well?

documents.t: No. A ghost mannequin shows the garment holding a human shape with the mannequin removed — no person. On-model conversion puts the garment on a rendered person, which communicates fit, scale, and styling that a hollow shape cannot.
documents.s: Is this the same as a ghost mannequin shot?

documents.t: Yes. A product-to-model or brand-side virtual try-on workflow uses your garment photograph as a reference and generates a person wearing it. The result must still be checked against the real garment for color, cut, print, closures, texture, and any detail hidden in the source image.
documents.s: Can AI put my clothes on a model?

documents.t: A model-swap workflow is designed to change the person while preserving the photographed garment, pose, and composition. Treat preservation as a testable requirement rather than an automatic guarantee, and compare every result with the approved clothing reference before publishing it. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.

documents.t: FLUX 3 Image is the strongest new option when composition control and targeted editing matter as much as the first render. Black Forest Labs gives it up to ten references, native 4K output, web grounding, and bounding-box controls that place or edit individual elements without rebuilding the whole frame. It does not automatically replace Nano Banana 2 as our general fashion default. In our first matched Astria test, FLUX 3 produced the most naturally photographic frame, but Nano Banana 2 followed the requested off-balance diagonal pose more aggressively and completed faster. GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst was the fastest tested endpoint, while Seedream 5 Pro remains the specialist we would start with for difficult color and fabric texture. This is a one-brief qualification of the current endpoints, not a universal ranking. documents.s: The short comparison

documents.t: FLUX 3 is Black Forest Labs' multimodal foundation-model family. FLUX 3 Image is the image-generation and editing part of that family, released on October 1, 2026. It is separate from FLUX 3 Video, even though both share the FLUX 3 name and underlying multimodal direction. The image endpoint has five useful production ideas: one prompt can generate a new image or describe an edit; one request can combine up to ten image references; an element table with coordinates can place subjects, products, panels, or type inside explicit bounding boxes; the same boxes can target several local edits while leaving unmentioned elements locked; output runs from a quick square preview through 1K, 1.5K, 2K, and 4K, with web and image grounding available. Black Forest Labs also offers commercial-weight licensing for companies that want to fine-tune and deploy FLUX 3 Image on their own infrastructure. That makes the family relevant beyond a hosted creative tool, although licensing, serving, and workflow costs need a separate procurement review. In Astria, FLUX 3 appeared as public partner model 5811585 on October 2. It was available in the partner gallery at review time, but not yet in the curated popular-model selector returned by the live catalog. Browse the current FLUX 3 gallery.
documents.s: What FLUX 3 Image actually is

documents.t: We reused the reference set and semantic prompt from the published GPT Image 2.5 qualification. All four models received the same Sloane portrait, pale-yellow sleeveless belted dress, circular-detail gold bag, 16:9 aspect ratio, 2K request, and one-output count in Astria workspace 896 (Articles). SloaneFixed identity reference DressFixed color, two buttons, waist ring, and silhouette BagFixed chain and circular metal construction The dress and bag sources exceed 2K on the long edge. The supplied Sloane portrait is 679×722, below our preferred 1600-pixel source gate, and was not upscaled. Identity observations are therefore directional.
documents.s: The matched reference test

documents.t: Dress hero shot. An off-kilter, flash-lit photograph of the referenced woman in a dynamic, almost off-balance leaning pose against a dark wooden bar counter or pillar at night. Her body creates a diagonal line. She wears the reference dress and holds the reference bag. The strong flash casts a sharp shadow. Blurred shelves with bottles and bar lights define the out-of-focus background. Cool, edgy vibe. Reference tokens are omitted above for readability. The generation records contain the exact Articles-workspace tune IDs.
documents.s: Prompt

documents.t: FLUX 3 ImagePrompt 47065867 · 2K · strongest natural editorial realism Nano Banana 2Prompt 47065878 · 2K · strongest diagonal pose adherence GPT Image 2.5 SunburstPrompt 47065876 · 2K · fastest completion in this run Seedream 5 ProPrompt 47065877 · 2K · coherent look with weaker bag-handle interaction All four outputs pass the article-size visual gate. Every model preserved the pale-yellow sleeveless dress, two-button front, circular waist hardware, recognizable Sloane identity, gold chain bag, and dark bar setting. None should be treated as an exact SKU reconstruction: folds, belt wrap, bag-disc count, bag scale, and hand contact vary.
documents.s: The four outputs

documents.t: FLUX 3 looks the least staged. The worn wood, background clutter, restrained skin texture, direct flash, and slight lens imperfection create a convincing location photograph rather than a perfectly cleaned campaign render. The face remains recognizable and the dress construction stays unusually legible. This is the frame we would choose when the art direction calls for candid editorial realism. Nano Banana 2 produces the most forceful fashion composition. Its long diagonal body line, stretched arms, shadow, and bag placement make the “almost off-balance” instruction visible immediately. GPT Image 2.5 delivers a polished, product-legible frame but settles the pose against the pillar rather than pushing the requested instability. Seedream keeps the face, color, and overall campaign mood coherent, but the raised strap and the way it crosses the hand need retouching.
documents.s: Image quality

documents.t: There is no runaway winner in one image. Nano Banana 2 follows the pose and diagonal request best. FLUX 3 balances the scene instructions with the strongest naturalism and retains both dress buttons, the waist ring, the bag's circular surface, and the flash-lit bar. GPT Image 2.5 gives the bag and garment a clear commercial read, but interprets the pose more conservatively. Seedream preserves the key references while introducing the most distracting contact error. For production, judge two questions separately: Does the image express the brief? Does the product remain accurate enough to approve? The most attractive answer is not always the most faithful one.
documents.s: Prompt adherence and reference fidelity

documents.t: FLUX 3's meaningful advantage is not that other frontier models lack image inputs. All four can generate from references and edit images. The difference is the control surface.
documents.s: Editing and reference-image support

documents.t: Use FLUX 3 when a brief contains explicit spatial relationships: a product in the lower-right, a headline in a reserved area, several people in fixed positions, or a multi-panel editorial. Its native layout prompt carries a global caption plus named elements and bounding boxes on a 0–1000 coordinate grid. Those same elements can be recolored, moved, replaced, resized, or removed while unmentioned elements remain locked. That is more deterministic than asking a general conversational editor to “move the bag slightly left” and hoping the face, garment, and background do not drift. The matched Astria run above tests reference composition, not the separate bounding-box workflow; box precision remains a provider capability to qualify on the exact interface you plan to use.
documents.s: FLUX 3 Image

documents.t: Nano Banana 2 is the most flexible generalist here. Google's current API supports multi-turn generation and editing, web and image-search grounding, and up to 14 references across documented object and character roles. It remains the model we would start with when a team needs one endpoint for ordinary campaign, catalog, product, and iterative editing work without designing a coordinate layout first.
documents.s: Nano Banana 2

documents.t: GPT Image 2.5 is the strongest route when the work behaves like design: edit precision, readable type, flexible custom dimensions, transparent output, or an image built through several explicit changes. Sunburst is the higher-capability variant; Flare is the smaller option. OpenAI exposes low through max quality levels, so a fair speed or pricing comparison must hold quality and dimensions fixed.
documents.s: GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst

documents.t: Seedream 5 Pro combines multi-image fusion with point, lasso, box, sketch, color, and material controls. Its provider also documents separating a finished design into independent layers. In our own October 15 test the endpoint did not return transparent layers from a single request, though it did extract individual elements cleanly one pass at a time; see AI layer separation in Photoshop for what that workflow delivers. Either way the model is especially relevant for posters and dense design work, while our wider Astria benchmark still gives it a specialist role for saturated garments, woven texture, skin, and repeated identity.
documents.s: Seedream 5 Pro

documents.t: FLUX 3, Nano Banana 2, and GPT Image 2.5 all offer native 4K paths. Their limits are not identical: FLUX 3 describes 4K as roughly 16 megapixels, Google's dimensions vary with aspect ratio, and OpenAI constrains custom dimensions by edge length, aspect ratio, and total pixels. Seedream 5 Pro currently tops out at the 2K tier in its official image API. Do not buy 4K as a label. Test whether the extra pixels preserve product geometry, typography, skin, and small accessories after export. A larger hallucination is still a hallucination. In this single simultaneous Astria run, GPT Image 2.5 completed first, followed by Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5 Pro, and FLUX 3. FLUX 3's result justified the wait for this editorial brief, but the gap matters in live exploration. Use lower-resolution drafts when the endpoint offers them, approve composition early, and reserve the largest render for finalists.
documents.s: Resolution and speed

documents.t: The vendors use different billing units and quality controls, so a raw “price per image” comparison is easy to misread. Black Forest Labs prices FLUX 3 Image by output-resolution tier, with a materially larger step for 4K. See BFL pricing. Google meters Nano Banana 2 image generation through model input and image-output tokens, with output usage tied to resolution. See Gemini API pricing. OpenAI meters text, image input, and image output tokens; output dimensions and quality affect the practical total. See OpenAI API pricing. Volcengine prices Seedream 5 Pro outputs by resolution band and separately accounts for additional input images after the first. See Volcengine model pricing. For the Astria route used in this comparison, use current Astria pricing. The useful budgeting formula is: approved-asset cost = total generation and editing spend ÷ number of outputs that pass reference, legal, and creative review A slower or nominally higher-priced endpoint can still be cheaper if it removes retries and retouching. A fast draft model can still be the right first step when the team is exploring composition rather than approving a SKU.
documents.s: Pricing: compare approved outputs, not sticker rates

documents.t: the composition contains several elements with strict spatial relationships; local edits must leave the rest of the frame stable; you want candid, natural editorial realism rather than a highly cleaned render; up to ten references need to become one deliberate composition; web-grounded real-world context or a self-hosted commercial-weights path matters.
documents.s: Choose FLUX 3 Image when

documents.t: you need the safest general starting point for fashion and product work; speed, volume, references, editing, and 4K output all matter at once; the workflow is conversational and iterative rather than box-directed; the brief mixes creative art direction with product preservation.
documents.s: Choose Nano Banana 2 when

documents.t: precise editing, beauty finish, typography, or a designed layout is central; transparent output or custom pixel dimensions matter; quality can be tuned explicitly against latency and budget; text and image inputs need to become a polished campaign asset.
documents.s: Choose GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst when

documents.t: saturated color, embroidery, weave, sheen, or skin rendering is the risk; point-, region-, or sketch-guided edits fit the design workflow; multi-image fusion or layer separation is more valuable than 4K delivery; a fashion brief has already shown that Seedream handles its material or safety constraints reliably.
documents.s: Choose Seedream 5 Pro when

documents.t: FLUX 3 Image earns a place in the production shortlist immediately. Its combination of references, spatial layout, targeted editing, grounding, natural photographic character, and native 4K is genuinely differentiated. For ordinary reference-led fashion work, start with Nano Banana 2 and add FLUX 3 when composition control or a less polished, more believable editorial surface is the opportunity. Add GPT Image 2.5 for design precision and Seedream 5 for difficult color and material. Then approve the model on your hardest real SKU rather than on a general leaderboard. The exact prompt IDs, model IDs, timings, source provenance, delivered dimensions, and selection notes for this qualification are recorded in the repository benchmark manifest. Read the broader fashion image-model comparison, GPT Image 2.5 review, Seedream 5 guide, and benchmark methodology.

Dressing forms, waiting for neck composites, and showing clothes without a person are three different problems. They do not need the same replacement. The short version: use flat lay when you need a simpler product-only view, a live model when the worn garment needs to be documented, and AI on-model when you have approved product references and need more styling options. If you already know you want to keep the hollow garment format, use the ghost mannequin capture and compositing guide. If you have chosen AI on-model and need source preparation, use flat lay to on-model.
documents.s: Choose the alternative by the work it removes

documents.t: A queue of unfinished collars is a capacity problem. Changing the entire catalog to on-model imagery introduces casting, styling, and gallery decisions before it fixes that queue. Pixelz describes its ghost mannequin service as combining multiple supplied product images in post-production, with manual, FTP, and API upload options. That is a concrete alternative to making every composite in-house. It still needs the source photographs. Before switching formats, ask a retouching provider to process a representative set using your existing crop, garment shape, and color standard. Compare revision time and accepted results with the current process. If the catalog presentation is already useful, moving the joining work may be enough. An AI tool that produces another hollow garment image is also preserving the format. Ask which visible areas come from supplied photographs and which are generated. A plausible invented lining is a different deliverable from a composite of the photographed lining.
documents.s: When the bottleneck is editing, keep the format

documents.t: Flat lay is the clearest alternative when chest or hip volume is not the point of the image. A graphic tee may need its print shown without folds crossing the design. A matching set may need both pieces visible together. There is no reason to create an invisible torso for every such view. Shopify's clothing photography guide describes flat lay as an overhead view on a surface and distinguishes it from model, mannequin, and lifestyle photography. It also recommends planning the angles and detail views needed for each product. A simpler setup does not eliminate the shot list. A hanger is another option when the suspended garment reads well and fits the brand's presentation. Judge the actual sample: if the shoulders collapse, the neckline stretches, or the body hangs like a narrow tube, the hanger has removed information you needed. Keeping the hanger visible can be more straightforward than retouching it out and reconstructing the area behind it. Our recommendation: choose these formats for their useful product view, then account for any missing view elsewhere in the gallery. Do not treat a single flat lay as an equivalent replacement for a front, back, and volume set.
documents.s: When you need simpler product-only capture

documents.t: Live-model photography is the strongest choice when the buying question concerns the actual garment on a body: where a sleeve ends, how a skirt falls when standing, or what an open jacket reveals. The photograph records one sample, one wearer, one pose, and any styling adjustments. It does not prove how every size fits every shopper. Record the model's measurements and sample size, and avoid pinning that changes the feature you are trying to show. For a dress whose appeal is its drape, a short, controlled shoot may be a more useful investment than perfecting a hollow silhouette. Keep separate detail views for features that hair, hands, or styling obscure. This is a decision about what to document. A brand can still use ghost mannequin for the clean front view and a real wearer for the side profile or movement. There is no requirement to make every gallery slot use the same format.
documents.s: When a person is the missing information

documents.t: AI on-model is worth testing when the missing asset is a styled presentation and the product has already been photographed clearly. It can make an existing reference library useful in more contexts. It also introduces a new approval task: checking that the rendered garment still describes the item being sold. Pixelz's August 2026 synthetic-model workflow starts with real product imagery, prepares it before generation, reviews the generated result, and sends selected outputs through final post-production. Its description supports the practical boundary: generation is one stage of production, and convincing outputs can still contain product errors. This is a vendor-described process, not evidence of an approval rate. Astria's ecommerce workflow lets brands select creative templates, upload product photographs, and generate imagery for lookbooks, social, and campaigns. For a team moving beyond product-only presentation, that provides a route to test an on-model treatment using existing inputs. Our recommendation is to start with a garment whose identity you can verify from the references. Approve the neckline, sleeve length, print placement, seams, closures, and opacity before judging whether you like the model or background. If the generated image supplies a back view that you never photographed, it has not established what the back looks like. Keep a physical worn view when drape or fit is the selling point and the generated result cannot be checked adequately. AI on-model is a visual interpretation, not a measurement-based fit test. The virtual try-on guide covers that distinction in more detail.
documents.s: When AI on-model is a useful replacement

documents.t: A practical replacement brief names a gallery slot and the information it must retain. “Replace ghost mannequin” is too broad. Example brief Sensible decision Condition for making the switch Basic tee needs a clearer graphic view Test flat lay as the product-only front Full graphic and garment proportions remain readable Tailored blazer needs its structured shape shown without a person Keep ghost mannequin; improve or outsource the composite The existing format serves the requirement Dress needs evidence of worn length and fall Add or prioritize a live-model view Sample size, wearer, and styling are documented Existing ghost images are accurate, but the gallery needs outfit context Add an approved AI on-model image Styling does not hide or alter product-defining features New drop has no usable product photographs Capture references before selecting an AI route The actual colorway and construction can be verified These examples are recommendations for a pilot, not claims that a garment category always succeeds in one format. An old ghost mannequin image does not become obsolete when an AI model arrives. If it still gives shoppers a clearer view of the product, keep it. The alternative may replace the next shoot's presentation work while leaving useful existing assets in service.
documents.s: Decide what leaves the gallery, not just what enters it

documents.t: A price per composite and a price per generation buy different things. For this decision, use the cost per SKU with its required gallery approved. Count sample preparation, capture, outside fees, generation, retouching, operator time, reviewer time, and corrections. Include a physical shoot fallback for products the alternative cannot handle. For planning, allocate shared setup across the expected batch and value internal time at the same rate in each route. Then count coverage. A cheaper front image is not a saving if it requires a new side image to recover information the original showed. Conversely, keeping an approved ghost image and adding one useful on-model view may cost less than replacing the entire set. For a numeric costing framework, use product photography cost per SKU. For the broader allocation of studio and AI work across campaigns, see AI product photography versus a packshot studio.
documents.s: Compare the cost of a complete approved gallery

documents.t: Choose two routine items, two recurring production problems, and two difficult products from your own range. This is a suggested operational sample, not a statistically representative experiment. Name the bottleneck. Record whether you want to reduce dressing time, composite revisions, shoot scheduling, or missing on-model coverage. Fix the gallery brief. Require the same product information, output dimensions, and deadline for the current route and the candidate alternative. Preserve the approved physical references. Set acceptance rules before production. Product-changing errors are failures. Name who checks them, and set a revision limit after which the SKU returns to physical capture or the existing workflow. Record the whole job. Track elapsed time, human minutes, outside spend, rejected outputs, missing views, and whether each complete gallery passes. Count failed attempts and fallback work. Switch only the passing group. If basics pass and patterned items do not, use separate routes. Keep the current gallery available until the replacement is approved. Check the destination channel's current image requirements before making a candidate your main image. For Amazon, start with the apparel image guide and the category-specific source it points to. Production approval and sales performance are separate questions. After the accuracy review, test gallery presentation with your own traffic. Do not attribute a sales change to on-model imagery if the same launch also changed pricing, promotions, or assortment.
documents.s: Run a six-SKU replacement test

documents.t: Choose flat lay for a simple product-only view, hanger photography for a suspended presentation, live-model photography to document the garment worn by a real person, or AI on-model imagery for styling variations from approved references. Keep ghost mannequin when isolated body volume is the requirement. The best choice depends on the job of the image.
documents.s: What is the best alternative to ghost mannequin photography?

documents.t: AI can replace some new presentation work when suitable product references already exist and the outputs pass review. It does not remove the need to document the garment. If a generated image changes seams, print placement, opacity, or proportions, use a corrected output or physical photography instead.
documents.s: Can AI replace a ghost mannequin shoot?

documents.t: It is an alternative to doing the composite in-house, but it keeps the ghost mannequin format and source-photography requirements. Consider it when editing capacity is the bottleneck and the existing product presentation already works.
documents.s: Is outsourcing ghost mannequin retouching an alternative?

documents.t: Flat lay can avoid mannequin dressing and interior compositing, but styling, capture, retouching, and approval still take time. Compare the total cost of an approved product gallery with the same required views, including any extra images needed to explain volume or worn appearance.
documents.s: Is flat lay cheaper than ghost mannequin photography?

documents.t: Keep accurate existing images while testing the new format. A product-only view and an approved on-model image can serve different gallery roles. Remove a ghost mannequin view only when its replacement covers the same information and the remaining gallery still represents the product accurately.
documents.s: Should I remove existing ghost mannequin images when adding AI models?

documents.t: Ghost mannequin photography is not a one-click cutout. It is a small composite: the garment is photographed while holding body volume, the support is removed, and separately captured hidden areas are joined back in. The short version: the result lives or dies on the source views. A clean neck join comes from photographing the inside neck, not asking a retoucher or model to guess it. documents.s: From a dress photo to a packshot

documents.t: If you are deciding whether to keep this format, start with ghost mannequin alternatives. That comparison weighs replacement workflows; this guide covers capturing and finishing the hollow garment image. A flat lay documents a garment on a surface. A hanger shot suspends it from the shoulders. A ghost mannequin gives it the chest, waist, sleeve, and hip volume of a worn object, then removes the visible support. It is sometimes called invisible mannequin or hollow-man photography. That makes it useful for ecommerce because the product remains the only visible subject while construction is easier to read than in a flat lay. It does not prove fit. The volume comes from one mannequin form, pinning choices, steaming, camera position, and retouching. The usual production is: Style and photograph the garment on a mannequin. Photograph the back and any hidden interiors separately. Mask out the mannequin. Composite the inside collar, neck, hem, or other hidden areas into place. Rebuild only real edges, then normalize background, crop, and shadow. Review the composite against the garment before export. The neck is where weak work reveals itself. A collar that is too deep, an impossible lining, or a rear label floating at the wrong angle means the hidden view was missing or the join was rushed.
documents.s: What the technique actually does

documents.t: Front on mannequin, full garment visible Back on mannequin, matched camera height and distance Inside neck and collar with the garment reversed or supported separately Front and back detail references for closures, labels, trims, and texture Color target or approved reference under the same light
documents.s: Every garment

documents.t: Hood: inside hood, hood attachment, and back fall Open jacket or shirt: inside front edges, facing, lining, and under-collar Dress or top with deep neckline: inside front and back necklines Trousers or skirt: inside waistband and any area revealed by the intended hollow opening Rolled or turned cuff: inside cuff and sleeve opening Asymmetric garment: both sides and every fastening state used in the final The rule is simple: if the mannequin currently hides an area that will appear in the finished image, photograph that area. “Repair in post” is not a source plan.
documents.s: Add views when the construction needs them

documents.t: Use a mannequin close to the sample size. A garment stretched across a form does not become truthful when the form disappears. If the sample is larger, pin from positions that will remain hidden and keep tension symmetrical. If it is smaller, use the correct form rather than forcing closures or changing silhouette. Steam or press deliberately. The objective is not to erase every wrinkle; it is to show the material as it should arrive while retaining believable fabric behavior. Over-clipping and heavy retouching produce a hard paper silhouette that no longer describes the garment. Fix the camera, focal length, height, lighting, and garment centerline across the set. Front, back, and insert views need to agree geometrically. A collar insert shot from above cannot be dropped convincingly into a body frame photographed straight on. Use soft, even light that resolves texture without a hard shadow crossing the garment. Keep exposure and white balance fixed across colorways. Shopify recommends consistent aspect ratios for featured images because collection grids display them side by side; that consistency begins in capture, not in the final crop. See Shopify's product media guidance.
documents.s: Setup before the shutter

documents.t: Strong candidates: shirts, simple tops, tailored jackets, coats, knitwear with stable edges, dresses with clear construction, trousers, and skirts. These benefit from visible volume and have interiors that can be captured predictably. More demanding: sheer fabric, lace, fringe, open knits, reflective materials, complex layering, very loose drape, deep gathers, and garments with many ties or straps. Removing the support through transparency can become a pixel-level job, and reconstructing hidden layers can turn into invention. Often better on-model: garments whose central question is fit, movement, stretch, or proportion on a body. Ghost imagery can show the product cleanly, but a shopper may still need a real or reviewed on-model view. Flat lay to on-model covers the source and review requirements for that derivative.
documents.s: Which garments work best

documents.t: The base silhouette comes from the dressed frame. The hidden interior comes from the insert frame. Use cloning or generation only for small continuity repairs where the underlying construction is known. A plausible lapel or seam is not necessarily the sold lapel or seam.
documents.s: Build from evidence

documents.t: Do not mirror one sleeve, pocket, or lapel over the other unless the garment is actually symmetrical and the duplicated details remain correct. Logos, embroidered marks, button sides, zipper pulls, and directional prints expose mirroring immediately.
documents.s: Preserve asymmetry that is real

documents.t: The garment should hold volume where the form supported it, then fall according to its material. Removing every tension cue leaves an object floating in a vacuum. Retain controlled depth and a restrained grounding shadow if the channel permits it.
documents.s: Keep fabric physics believable

documents.t: Review twenty outputs together. Shoulder width, hem height, scale, crop, background, and shadow should stay fixed across the catalog. A beautiful individual composite can still damage the collection grid if it is 8% larger than every neighboring product.
documents.s: Match the set, not just the frame

documents.t: AI is useful for segmentation, background cleanup, small edge reconstruction, shadow normalization, and applying a reviewed treatment across many products. It can also create alternate packshot or contextual assets from an approved reference set. The risky part is hidden geometry. If only a front view exists, a model may invent the inside collar. If a sleeve is folded behind the torso, it may generate a plausible cuff position. Those are generated derivatives, not product evidence. Use a three-level review queue: Low risk: solid, simple, opaque garments with complete source views; batch and spot-check. Medium risk: prints, hardware, layered collars, open fronts; review every output. High risk: sheer fabric, intricate construction, asymmetric details, or missing inserts; capture again or send to manual retouching. The point of automation is to spend human attention where construction makes it valuable, not to remove the approval gate.
documents.s: Where AI belongs

documents.t: Shopify accepts product images alongside video and 3D media, and its image service creates sizes for different storefront contexts. A ghost mannequin frame can be the featured image when it is the clearest representation of the product, followed by back, detail, on-model, scale, and motion views in the order that answers buying questions. The Shopify product media guide covers ordering and technical limits. Keep the ghost master uncropped, then make the storefront crop from it. Do not permanently destroy sleeve, hem, or whitespace just to fix one theme breakpoint.
documents.s: Shopify

documents.t: Do not transfer the Shopify choice automatically. Amazon's public advertising guidance recommends a plain white background, at least 80% product fill, four or more views, and a minimum 1,000-pixel dimension for zoom. But Seller Central category rules decide whether a particular apparel main image must be on a human model or off-model, and those rules can differ by garment type and marketplace. Check the live category style guide first. Use the ghost image as a supporting view when it clarifies construction and the category permits it. The main-image workflow is detailed in Amazon product images for apparel.
documents.s: Amazon

documents.t: Check the final image against the physical sample, not against the retoucher's previous export: Neck and collar depth are anatomically and structurally plausible Inside label, facing, lining, and seam positions are correct Shoulder width and slope match the garment Sleeves are equal only where the garment is equal Buttons, buttonholes, zipper, pockets, and hardware are complete Directional prints cross seams correctly Fabric transparency and edge softness are believable Hem is level where intended and retains real drape Color matches the approved photographed reference Shadow is allowed by the destination and consistent across the set Scale, crop, and whitespace match the catalog standard Front, back, and detail files map to the correct SKU and colorway If the reviewer cannot tell whether an odd join is a real feature or a composite error, return to the sample. Do not resolve ambiguity by making the image prettier.
documents.s: The pre-publish QC gate

documents.t: At collection scale, name and track the views. A minimal row needs: Field Example SKU / variant JK-104-NVY-M Source view front_dressed, inside_neck, back_dressed Product source of truth Sample version or approved photo set Output role Shopify featured, Amazon alternate, wholesale line sheet Retouch method Manual composite, AI-assisted cleanup Accuracy checks Color, collar, hardware, print, hem Approver / status Named reviewer, approved or reshoot That manifest is what turns a retouching trick into a production system. It also makes cost per SKU honest: capture, insert views, retouch, review, and rework all belong in the model. See product photography cost per SKU.
documents.s: A reusable file manifest

documents.t: Ghost mannequin photography shows a garment holding three-dimensional body volume without a visible person or mannequin. It is usually made by photographing the garment on a mannequin, capturing hidden areas such as the inside neck separately, and compositing the views into one clean product image.
documents.s: What is ghost mannequin photography?

documents.t: At minimum, capture the dressed front and back plus separate insert views for every area the mannequin hides: commonly the inside neck and collar, and sometimes the inside hem, hood, sleeves, or waistband. Complex garments need more inserts, not more invention in retouching.
documents.s: What photos are needed for a ghost mannequin image?

documents.t: No. Ghost mannequin photography isolates garment shape and construction without a visible person. On-model photography shows styling, scale, and one fit state on a particular body. Most apparel catalogs benefit from using each for the question it answers.
documents.s: Is a ghost mannequin image the same as an on-model photo?

documents.t: AI can help remove a mannequin, reconstruct simple hidden regions, normalize backgrounds, and create controlled derivatives. It can also invent a plausible but wrong neck join, seam, lining, or shape. Use supplied insert views and require visual approval against the actual garment.
documents.s: Can AI create ghost mannequin images?

documents.t: Do not assume so. Amazon main-image rules vary by category and marketplace, and some apparel rules require adult clothing to be shown on a human model while other product types must be off-model. Check the current category style guide in Seller Central before producing the main-image set. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.
documents.s: Can ghost mannequin photography be used as an Amazon main image?

In our first matched fashion test, both produced polished, reference-led campaign frames. Sunburst pushed the diagonal pose and direct-flash tension harder; Flare kept the complete bag more legible. That is a first production read, not a universal ranking. We ran one controlled brief with one output per model so you can inspect the actual difference without a hand-picked winner. documents.t: Dress hero shot. An off-kilter, flash-lit photograph of the referenced woman in a dynamic, almost off-balance leaning pose against a dark wooden bar counter or pillar at night. Her body creates a diagonal line. She wears the reference dress and holds the reference bag. The strong flash casts a sharp shadow. Blurred shelves with bottles and bar lights define the out-of-focus background. Cool, edgy vibe. The model-specific reference tokens are omitted above for readability. documents.t: GPT Image 2.5 SunburstPrompt 46636365 · 4K requested / 3792×2160 actual · stronger diagonal tension; fine bag-disc geometry changes GPT Image 2.5 FlarePrompt 46636364 · 4K requested / 3792×2160 actual · complete bag and steadier framing; belt geometry varies Both outputs pass the article-size visual gate and preserve the central reference relationships: Sloane remains recognizable, the dress stays pale yellow with the sleeveless belted construction and two gold buttons, and the bag retains its gold chain and repeated circular metal texture. Neither result is a literal product reconstruction. Pleat placement, the belt wrap, individual bag discs, and crop differ from the supplied images. For campaign work, those shifts may be acceptable. For a PDP or catalog asset, compare every construction detail against the product before approval.
documents.s: Sunburst vs Flare

documents.t: Sunburst is the more aggressive editorial interpretation in this pair. The body line is strongly diagonal, the flash contrast is harder, and the crop feels closer to a magazine campaign. The tradeoff is that the bag reaches the frame edge. Flare is more product-complete. It keeps the bag fully visible, gives the dress more breathing room, and still holds the direct-flash nightlife brief. Its pose is less precarious and therefore slightly less surprising. Our routing rule from this one brief is simple: start with Sunburst when shot energy and art direction are the approval risk; start with Flare when garment and accessory visibility are the approval risk; run both when one extra comparison is cheaper than guessing which interpretation the client meant.
documents.s: What the variants do differently

documents.t: We also ran the identical Articles-workspace references, semantic prompt, 16:9 request, and one-output count through Nano Banana 2, MAI-Image-2.6-Flash, and Muse. The resolution switch stayed at 4K where the endpoint supports it. MAI and Muse do not expose the same 4K selector; that incompatibility is recorded instead of silently changing the GPT Image 2.5 settings. Nano Banana 2Prompt 46636366 · 4K requested / 5504×3072 actual · strongest accessory scale; bag-disc and belt details vary MAI-Image-2.6-FlashPrompt 46636367 · native request / 1365×768 actual · graphic tilt with simplified surface and bag-disc detail Muse ImagePrompt 46636363 · native request / 1920×1280 actual · complete styling, but returned 3:2 from the 16:9 request The wider context does not produce a new universal winner. Nano Banana 2 remains a strong general fashion default. Muse keeps the product relationships coherent but misses the requested canvas ratio. MAI Flash gives a usable campaign frame at lower output resolution. The new GPT Image 2.5 variants are immediately competitive when a polished, flash-led fashion treatment is the goal.

documents.t: Before anything visual. A lookbook made for wholesale buyers and one made for customers are different documents wearing similar clothes. Wholesale buyers need to place an order. They want clear garment views, style numbers, colorway ranges, fabric composition, price points, and delivery windows. Mood matters, but a beautiful lookbook that omits the style numbers will be sent back. Press need one striking image and a clear story, delivered in a format they can drop into a layout. Customers need desire and context — the world, the styling, the sense that this collection is for someone like them. Trying to serve all three in one document produces something that serves none of them. Decide, then build a variant if you must.
documents.s: Stage 1 — Decide who it is for

documents.t: One page. If it runs longer, it is not a brief. The collection in a sentence. What is this season about? The reference points. Three to five images that are not fashion photographs — a film still, a building, a colour, a painting. Fashion references produce imitation; non-fashion references produce direction. The casting. Described as a person, not a demographic. The world. Place, season, time of day, quality of light. What this collection is not. The most useful line in any brief and the one most often missing.
documents.s: Stage 2 — Write the brief

documents.t: The line sheet is every piece with style number, colorways, fabric, and price. Boring and non-negotiable. The shot list is what you will actually produce, and it must be shorter than the line sheet. A working ratio for a season: 12–24 full looks 4–8 detail shots — fabric, hardware, trim, the things a buyer wants to see up close 2–3 hero images for the cover and press Optionally 1–2 group shots, which are disproportionately expensive to produce well Include every SKU and you have made a catalog. That is a different, also-necessary document.
documents.s: Stage 3 — Line sheet and shot list

documents.t: Give each planned image a job before booking production. Here is a sample for three looks; expand it to fit the collection. Image Look and products View Where it goes 01 Look A: jacket J01, trouser T01 Hero with space for the collection title Cover and opening web section 02 Look A: J01, T01 Full length, clear silhouette First look page 03 Look B: knit K02, skirt S02 Three-quarter, showing the layering Second look page 04 Look B: K02 Close detail of the knit Detail page beside the full look 05 Look C: dress D03 Full length, a different pose Closing look page Add colourway, sample readiness, orientation, and approval owner as columns in your working sheet. A missing back view is easy to request here and expensive to discover during layout.
documents.s: A shot list you can copy

documents.t: The three decisions that determine whether the result looks like anything. Casting — a specific presence, not a checkbox. Whether this is a booked model or a stored reference does not change how carefully it should be chosen. Location — specific beats generic. "A coastal town in October" gives a photographer something to work with; "outdoors" does not. Styling — pull the looks and photograph them on a hanger before shoot day. Every stylist knows some combinations that read beautifully on paper fall apart on a body.
documents.s: Stage 4 — Casting, location, styling

documents.t: Traditionally: book the crew, ship the samples, shoot for one or two days, select, retouch. The dominant cost is scheduling — everyone and everything in one place on one date — and the dominant risk is that samples arrive late. With AI production: build one hero look completely and get it approved, then derive the rest against that approved treatment. The calendar changes shape rather than simply shrinking: creative direction still takes days, but sample logistics and scheduling largely disappear, and revisions stop being reshoots. Either way, the discipline is the same — approve one look completely before producing twenty. The mechanics of the AI route are in the AI lookbook guide, and casting continuity specifically in consistent AI fashion models.
documents.s: Stage 5 — Produce

documents.t: The stage almost everyone skips, and the one that separates a lookbook from a folder. A lookbook is read in order. Which look opens? Which closes? Where does the rhythm shift from wide to close? Where does colour arrive, and where does it rest? Lay every image out small, all at once. Then: Cut the weakest three. Eighteen strong looks beat twenty-four with six passengers. Check the rhythm — three wide shots in a row is monotonous; alternating every frame is agitated. Group by story, not by product category. "Knitwear" is a merchandising unit, not a narrative one. Read it back to front. Weak endings are more common than weak openings and less often noticed.
documents.s: Stage 6 — Sequence

documents.t: For a first edition, use this page order as a starting point: Cover: brand, collection or season, and one strong image. Opening: a short collection note and a look that establishes the direction. Look pages: give the clothes enough space; keep captions and look numbers in consistent positions. Detail pages: place fabric or construction close-ups beside the looks they explain. Closing page: a final image, contact or order link, and the next action for the reader. In the wholesale edition, connect each look to its style numbers and line sheet. In the consumer edition, link to the relevant products. Keep buying information as editable text so a price or delivery change does not require altering the photography. You can assemble this in a slide editor, page-layout tool, or your site's content system. Choose the tool by what must remain editable and who will update it next season.
documents.s: A simple lookbook page layout

documents.t: From one production, derive: PDF for buyers and press. Aim for a compact download, and send a link if the file is too large for the recipient's attachment limit. Style numbers and delivery windows on the wholesale version. Web for the site, in the correct aspect ratios, optimised, with real alt text. Vertical crops for social, planned from the start rather than salvaged afterwards. Print, if you are producing one, at the right colour profile and resolution. Planning these formats before production is the difference between four deliverables and four productions.
documents.s: Stage 7 — Format and deliver

documents.t: Read the document at the size the recipient will use. Check that captions remain legible on a phone, image crops preserve the garments, and each product link opens the correct style or colourway. Match wholesale codes and dates against the current line sheet. Open the exported PDF itself: a correct working file can still produce clipped text or broken links. Use descriptive image filenames and keep a master with editable text, full-size images, and a version date. Have someone who did not build the layout check it before delivery.
documents.s: Before you export the lookbook

documents.t: Send to buyers with a clear subject line, order deadline, and delivery window. Send to press with a short note and a link, not a 40 MB attachment. Roll out on-site and on social over weeks rather than in one dump. Archive everything — the brief, the approved treatment, the selects — so next season starts from something.
documents.s: Stage 8 — Distribute

documents.t: These are planning allowances for a small seasonal brief, not measured industry averages. Replace them with your team's estimates and supplier commitments. Stage Traditional With AI production Brief and references 3–5 days 3–5 days Line sheet and shot list 2–3 days 2–3 days Casting, location, styling 1–2 weeks 2–4 days Production 1–2 shoot days + 1–2 weeks post 2–4 days including revisions Sequencing and layout 3–5 days 3–5 days Formats and delivery 3–5 days 1–2 days The pattern is worth reading carefully: the creative stages barely move, because they are judgment. The logistical and revision stages compress hard. Any vendor claiming a lookbook in an afternoon is quoting the render time and ignoring the job.
documents.s: An example production calendar

documents.t: A curated selection of styled looks in a deliberate order, usually twelve to twenty-four for a season, with enough detail shots to convey fabric and construction. Wholesale lookbooks additionally carry style numbers, colorways, fabric composition, and delivery windows.
documents.s: What should a lookbook include?

documents.t: For the small seasonal production outlined here, allow roughly four to eight weeks as a planning example, not a guaranteed turnaround. Sample availability, approvals, revisions, and layout can take longer than the shoot itself.
documents.s: How long does it take to make a lookbook?

documents.t: A wholesale lookbook is a buying tool: it needs style numbers, colorways, composition, price points, and delivery dates alongside clear garment views. A consumer lookbook is a mood piece and carries almost none of that.
documents.s: What is the difference between a wholesale and a consumer lookbook?

documents.t: Usually several: a PDF for buyers and press, a web version for the site, and vertical crops for social. Deriving all of them from one production is far cheaper than treating each as a separate deliverable.
documents.s: What format should a lookbook be delivered in?

documents.t: For anything beyond single-product shots, yes. Styling is knowledge about clothes — proportion, layering, what goes with what — and it is the part that most visibly separates a considered lookbook from a grid of garments. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.

documents.t: We benchmark public image models with inputs a fashion team can inspect: one identity, one garment, one accessory, one semantic prompt, one canvas request, and one predetermined output per endpoint. The current public comparison covers GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare, GPT Image 2, Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5 Pro, Muse Image, MAI-Image-2.6, and MAI-Image-2.6-Flash. All compatible requests ran in Astria workspace 896 (Articles). documents.t: A text-only image can demonstrate taste, but it cannot show whether a supplied person, garment, or accessory survived generation. A useful fashion benchmark asks questions that have visible ground truth: Does the person remain recognizable? Does the dress retain its color, neckline, buttons, belt, and silhouette? Is the bag still a separate product with its chain and circular construction? Did the requested composition and canvas survive? Is the result attractive only after it is accurate enough for the intended use? No text-to-image-only result is used as public evidence in the current article family.
documents.s: Why reference-led evidence matters

documents.t: The source assets came from Maison Urban prompt 46557199 and were copied into workspace 896 so article work did not run in a customer workspace. SloaneMaison Urban tune 3904080 · Articles tune 5639061 · 679×722 DressMaison Urban tune 3907553 · Articles tune 5639041 · 1440×2160 BagMaison Urban tune 3907242 · Articles tune 5639043 · 1440×2159 The dress and bag pass the preferred 1600px long-edge source gate. Sloane is the explicit exception: the supplied identity portrait is 679×722 and was normalized to a valid JPEG without upscaling. Identity conclusions are directional.
documents.s: The complete source set

documents.t: Dress hero shot. An off-kilter, flash-lit photograph of the referenced woman in a dynamic, almost off-balance leaning pose against a dark wooden bar counter or pillar at night. Her body creates a diagonal line. She wears the reference dress and holds the reference bag. The strong flash casts a sharp shadow. Blurred shelves with bottles and bar lights define the out-of-focus background. Cool, edgy vibe. The live request inserts <faceid:5639061:1> woman, <faceid:5639041:1> dress, and <faceid:5639043:1> bag in the corresponding semantic roles. Phrases such as “comparison article brief” are not part of the prompt.
documents.s: The semantic prompt

documents.t: Control Rule Workspace 896 (Articles) Aspect ratio 16:9 requested for every model Output count One per endpoint Selection The only returned output; no choice among alternates Resolution Highest exposed endpoint setting: 4K for GPT Image 2.5, GPT Image 2, and Nano Banana 2; 2K for Seedream 5 Pro; native when no shared selector exists Reference incompatibility Record it; never replace the cell with text-to-image Public asset Optimized WebP derivative made from the downloaded original Muse returned 1920×1280 (3:2) from the 16:9 request. MAI flagship and Flash expose no shared resolution selector and returned 1365×768. Those differences are disclosed rather than normalized away.
documents.s: Controls and selection rule

documents.t: For each output, the benchmark record stores: model and live tune ID; prompt ID and workspace; full semantic prompt and source-tune provenance; requested aspect ratio, resolution, and output count; actual master dimensions and original media URL; public derivative path and dimensions; the fixed selection rule; visual-quality, fidelity, and exclusion notes. The machine-readable record is benchmark/image-models-2026-09/reference-comparison.json in the article repository.
documents.s: What we record

documents.t: Every selected result is opened at its original dimensions before publication. It must look good at article size and keep all three reference roles legible. Reviewers inspect identity, dress construction, color, bag geometry, composition, artifacts, and actual canvas shape separately. The full-resolution downloads remain the masters. WebP files under static/img/ are delivery derivatives. A smaller derivative is never reported as the generation's actual resolution.
documents.s: Visual review gate

documents.t: An earlier synthetic garment source was rejected for poor reference quality. Its outputs, public claims, and dependent covers were removed from the article family. The historical September pilot remains an internal audit trail in runs.json; it is not the evidence presented on the current public pages. Other limitations remain: one output per endpoint cannot estimate retry rates; one identity, dress, and bag do not represent every product or cast; the Sloane source limits high-resolution likeness conclusions; garment folds, belt geometry, chain placement, and individual bag discs vary in every output; model behavior and endpoint controls can change after capture.
documents.s: Exclusions and limitations

documents.t: Use rights-cleared source images and record their original dimensions. Put all editorial generations in workspace 896. Use the same reference tunes and semantic prompt for every compatible endpoint. Fix the aspect ratio and output count. Request the highest exposed resolution without inventing a control for endpoints that lack one. Download the original output and record its true media type and dimensions. Review visual quality and source fidelity before creating a web derivative. Publish the only output or record the incompatibility; do not substitute text-only evidence. Read the full reference-matched comparison or the shorter Astria model-selection guide.

documents.t: Jewelry is a geometry problem disguised as a lighting problem. A beautiful result is unusable if it changes the prongs, stone count, chain pattern or scale. Strong prompts therefore lock the piece first, then specify how metal, stones and skin should respond to light. documents.t: A flattened design is a dead end. The export looks finished, the working file is gone or was never yours, and the next request is always the same: move the headline, swap the product, extend the background for a different crop. Layer separation is the idea that a model can hand those parts back to you, and the capability is real. ByteDance documents it for Seedream 5.0 Pro: one request returns a base image plus up to 16 transparent layers, each tagged with its stacking order and position. Whether you can reach it depends entirely on how you call the model. In our own testing on October 15, 2026, the Astria endpoints returned a single flat image rather than layers, so this article covers the route that does work today: extracting one element per request and assembling the returns yourself. That route is slower than the promise. It is also good enough to rebuild a poster as an editable document, which is what we did below, failures included.
documents.s: AI Layer Separation in Photoshop: Pulling a Flat Design Apart

documents.t: Worth knowing before you judge any workflow against it. ByteDance's image generation API exposes a layer_decomposition flag on Seedream 5.0 Pro and 5.0 Flash. When set, the documented behaviour is: one base image plus up to 16 layers, each returned as a PNG with a real alpha channel placement metadata per layer: a stacking index and a bounding box in both pixel and normalised coordinates, so a caller can reassemble the stack a single input image only, at 1K, 1.5K or 2K, with no 4K path in this mode an optional prompt that targets specific elements, or no prompt at all to let the model pick them no partial success: if one layer fails, the whole request fails ByteDance's launch material also describes the background behind a removed subject being reconstructed. That claim appears in its product blog rather than the API specification, so treat it as the vendor's description. Two things follow. The output is separate PNGs plus coordinates, not a PSD — reassembly is the caller's job either way. And layered mode is capped at 2K, so a layer-separation asset is never a 4K hero.
documents.s: What the model can do natively

documents.t: Every image below comes from one supplied photograph of a skincare tube at 4000 by 6000 pixels. Nothing here is text-to-image. First we built something worth pulling apart. Seedream 5 Pro composed a finished campaign poster from that product reference: product on a stone pedestal, foliage behind it, a lilac gradient, a headline and a subtitle. That composite became the input for every separation attempt that followed. Supplied referenceThe only source material The flattened compositeSeedream 5 Pro, 2K, built from the reference Then six requests against that composite. Request Model What came back Transparency The documented layer flag, set explicitly Seedream 5 Pro One flat image. The flag had no effect on the response None Split into independent transparent layers, in words Seedream 5 Pro One flat image, the poster re-rendered largely unchanged None Isolate the product only Seedream 5 Pro Product cleanly isolated on a flat white field, label intact None Reconstruct the background with every element removed Seedream 5 Pro Clean plate, gradient and floor rebuilt, no trace of the objects None Isolate the headline and subtitle type Seedream 5 Pro Lettering on a flat white field, typeface and spacing preserved None Return a PNG with a real alpha channel GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst A PNG container with no alpha channel, RGB only None The first row is the one that matters. The documented capability is not reachable through the endpoints we tested, and nothing we ran returned an alpha channel, including the model whose provider documents transparency support. The PNG arrived as a PNG and carried no transparency once inspected.
documents.s: What we tested, and what came back

documents.t: The per-element results are the reason to carry on. ProductLabel, gold cap and sun motif preserved TypographySame typeface, weight and spacing Clean plateObjects gone, gradient and floor rebuilt The typography result is the surprise. Asked for the lettering alone, the model reproduced the same geometric sans at the same weight and letter spacing rather than paraphrasing it into a lookalike. That is the difference between a layer you can reposition and a layer you have to rebuild. The clean plate is the quiet workhorse. Once the background exists as its own image with nothing standing on it, every other element is free to move.
documents.s: What the extractions actually look like

documents.t: Four passes, in this order, each one request against the same flattened source. Pass one, the clean plate. Remove everything and rebuild what was behind it. Name the objects you want gone, and say explicitly that the surface and gradient must be reconstructed where they stood. Do this first: it is the layer everything else sits on, and if the model cannot rebuild the background convincingly, the rest of the exercise is not worth running. Pass two, the hero element. Isolate the product, the subject, the single thing the layout is about. Ask for a flat, even field behind it rather than transparency, because that is what you will reliably get and it masks cleanly. Pass three, the type. Request the lettering alone, and name what must survive: the exact typeface, weight, spacing and position. Vague requests here produce a plausible headline in the wrong font, which is worse than no layer at all. Pass four, the props. Foliage, pedestal, secondary objects, one request each. Resist the urge to batch them. Every element you add to a single request raises the chance the model reinterprets the whole frame instead of extracting a part of it. Then assemble: clean plate at the bottom, props, hero, type on top, masking the flat field behind each extraction. What you have at the end is the thing the flat export denied you, a layout where the headline can move, the product can be replaced and the canvas can extend for a different aspect ratio. Working inside the Astria Photoshop plugin, each pass returns into the open document as its own layer, which removes the four browser round trips and the registration drift that comes with them. The plugin guide covers the panel itself.
documents.s: The working sequence

documents.t: Be honest with yourself about what this is before you promise it to a client. It is not one click. Four or five requests per design, plus masking. For a single hero layout that is a good trade. For two hundred SKUs it is a staffing problem, and that work belongs in a production pipeline instead. It is reconstruction, not recovery. The model is not reading hidden layer data out of a flattened file, because there is none. It generates a plausible version of each part. The product that comes back is a very good likeness, not the original pixels. For a visual, a mockup or a layout study that is fine. For a regulated label, a legal mark or print artwork it is not. Keep the approved artwork. Expect flat fields, not cutouts. Nothing we tested returned a transparent layer or a layered file, so plan to mask. Fine detail degrades. Isolated elements come back at the model's own resolution and interpretation. Check small type, edge quality and any geometry a customer would recognise before the layer reaches a deliverable. One element per pass. Both all-at-once attempts failed in our test, and we would not plan around that changing.
documents.s: The limits, stated plainly

documents.t: Useful context, because this capability is moving quickly and the marketing runs ahead of the shipping. Photoshop does not do this yet. Adobe announced Layered Image Editing, described as automatically separating objects in an image onto different layers, at MAX in October 2025, and still labels it in development. No current Photoshop or Firefly feature list documents the capability. Generative Fill is a different tool: it writes a generated result for the selection you made, rather than taking a finished composition apart. Affinity shipped it first among the big editors. Canva announced AI-assisted Scene Decomposition for Affinity in September 2026, described as splitting a flattened image back into editable layers, unlocked with a Canva premium plan. Seedream is not the only model that can do it. Alibaba's Qwen-Image-Layered, released as open weights in December 2025, decomposes an image into RGBA layers with the layer count set by the prompt. Plugins are ahead of hosts. Higgsfield's Photoshop plugin has carried a Layer Decompose tool since June 2026, offering 1K to 2K output and an adjustable layer count. Its own pages describe its web Layers editor as powered by Seedream 5.0, while the plugin documentation names no engine. The direction is clear even if the dates are not. Treat any single result, including ours, as a snapshot.
documents.s: Where the field stands

documents.t: The working file is gone. An agency folded, a freelancer moved on, or all that survives is a JPEG from a sign-off email. One layout, many crops. A campaign image has to become a 4:5, a story, a banner and a PDP tile. With the background as its own layer, the recrop is composition rather than a new shoot. Market and seasonal variants. The typography changes per language or promotion while the photography stays. Posters, layouts and design studies. Dense work with several discrete elements is exactly where pulling parts out beats painting them out. Our packaging mockup guide covers the generation side of related work.
documents.s: Where it earns its place

documents.t: Short and specific beat long and descriptive in every pass we ran. Name the elements to remove individually rather than saying "remove everything". Say what must be reconstructed, not only what must go: "rebuilding the surface and gradient where the objects used to be". For type, list the attributes to preserve: typeface, weight, spacing, position. Ask for a flat, even background behind an isolated element instead of requesting transparency. Keep one element per request.
documents.s: Prompt patterns that worked

documents.t: Taking a finished, flattened design and recovering its parts as separate editable pieces: the subject, the typography, the props and the background behind them. The goal is a document you can restyle, recrop and re-version without rebuilding the artwork from scratch.
documents.s: What is AI layer separation?

documents.t: ByteDance documents layer decomposition for Seedream 5.0 Pro and 5.0 Flash, producing one base image plus up to 16 transparent PNG layers with placement metadata, at up to 2K. Alibaba's open-weights Qwen-Image-Layered also decomposes images into RGBA layers. Google's Gemini image models and OpenAI's GPT Image do not document layered output.
documents.s: Which models can decompose an image into layers?

documents.t: Only where the integration passes the parameter through. In our October 15, 2026 test the Astria endpoints did not return layered output, with or without the documented flag, so the practical route today is extracting one element per request and assembling those returns as layers in Photoshop.
documents.s: Can I get layered output through any image API?

documents.t: Not yet. Adobe announced Layered Image Editing, automatic separation of objects onto layers, at MAX in October 2025 and still lists it as in development. No current Photoshop or Firefly feature list documents the capability. Affinity shipped an AI-assisted Scene Decomposition feature in September 2026, behind a Canva premium plan.
documents.s: Does Photoshop separate a flat image into layers?

documents.t: Recovering editability you have lost: a flattened export with no working file, a campaign layout that must be recropped for another channel, a design whose typography changes per market, or a subject that has to move to a new background.
documents.s: What is layer separation actually useful for?

documents.t: All generations ran through Astria on October 15, 2026, in the Articles workspace, from one supplied product photograph at 4000 by 6000 pixels. The composite was built with Seedream 5 Pro at 2K. Check Lumoo pricing for current rates, allowances, workflow templates, and integration access.
