documents.t: WearView's plan page lists product-to-model, consistent model generation, and pose control on Lite. Pro adds model swap, ghost mannequin, video, and five team members; Advanced lists fifteen team members. API access is presented under Enterprise. These make WearView a relevant candidate for a team concentrating on garment presentation. The evaluation: choose one recurring face and a fixed pose brief. Produce several garments, then add a new colorway. Compare face continuity, garment silhouette, and how much manual correction the operator needs. Test your own inputs; product-page examples do not establish performance on sheer fabric, unusual sleeves, or small prints. The tradeoff: check the feature tier you actually need before comparing price. Use WearView pricing for current credit requirements for your resolution and workflow; our WearView comparison supplies the wider buying context.
documents.s: WearView: compare the on-model workflow

documents.t: FASHN offers a web app and a developer API. Its API documentation covers try-on, product-to-model, model creation, editing, and image-to-video endpoints. This is useful when the job includes integrating generation into a service, rather than operating only a visual editor. The evaluation: give the developer and creative reviewer the same test set. Require a successful garment transfer, a useful response to an invalid input, retrieval of the output, and a repeat run without losing the product identifier. An attractive manual result alone does not prove the automated workflow is ready. The tradeoff: API integration requires someone to own input preparation, error handling, output storage, and review. If no one will maintain those parts, evaluate the app first. Its pricing page distinguishes app and developer pricing, and notes that tool costs rise with settings. Daily credits expire within their daily window, so they should not be treated as a single allowance available on launch day. If “try-on” means a shopper-facing experience rather than images prepared by your team, read virtual try-on for fashion brands before comparing plans. The FASHN comparison covers its overlap with Astria.
documents.s: FASHN: evaluate try-on and integration separately

documents.t: Astria's fashion workflow combines product references and templates for lookbook, campaign, and social imagery. It belongs on the shortlist when the buying question is whether one approved direction can produce a useful set across your collection. The evaluation: agree a treatment for casting, crop, lighting, and setting. Run five products, including the difficult ones. Then change the output format and add another SKU. Ask the reviewer whether the collection still reads as one production, and record the operator time needed to make that happen. The tradeoff: creative direction and product review still need an owner. A brand satisfied with its current catalog images may not benefit from adding a more elaborate campaign workflow. This guide does not establish that Astria is cheaper or more accurate than Lumoo. For automated work, review Astria's API documentation as well as the creative trial. Account balance, callbacks, error handling, and storage terms affect a production integration. Do not assume keeping a URL in a spreadsheet is the same as archiving an output.
documents.s: Astria: test the collection's creative direction

documents.t: Use one fixed brief across all shortlisted tools: ten products, two catalog views per product, and five campaign frames. That is 25 accepted images. State the output resolution and which garment details must remain accurate before anyone starts generating. Track each tool's actual attempts, charged credits or balance, editing minutes, and accepted files. Do not mix euros and dollars without a stated exchange rate, and do not mix monthly subscriptions with an annual price advertised as a monthly equivalent. For a simple illustration, a run that spends 60 currency units to deliver 20 accepted images costs 3 units per accepted image before labor. If only ten pass review, it costs 6. Those are hypothetical numbers, not results from Lumoo or any competitor. The purpose is to expose the effect of rejection and rework. The cost-per-SKU guide explains how to extend this to a collection budget. Check your launch calendar too. A plan sufficient for a steady trickle of images can behave differently when the whole collection is due on one day. Ask about additional usage and scheduling against that actual deadline.
documents.s: Price an accepted set, not a credit allowance

documents.t: Use representative references. Include a simple garment, a patterned item, a difficult material, and an unusual construction. Supply front, back, and detail photographs where required. Agree rejection criteria. Wrong fastenings, invented seams, altered print placement, and changed product proportions should fail even if the picture looks attractive. Test revisions. Add a colorway and request a new crop after the first set is accepted. Record what must be repeated. Test handoff. Have another team member find the correct source product, approved result, and reusable setup without help from the original operator. Move a small batch first. Retain source photography, SKU mapping, exports, and approval notes. Expand only when the new process produces a better outcome for the stated requirement. A generated back view deserves particular care. If the reference never shows the back closure or seam construction, the tool cannot establish those facts from appearance alone. Publish only after checking the view against the actual product.
documents.s: A migration test that catches product errors

documents.t: Muse is worth testing when a brief contains several supplied assets with different roles. A good prompt should say which reference is the person, which is the garment, which is the accessory, and which properties must survive. Use a checklist after generation: Is the person still recognizable? Did the garment retain color, neckline, buttons, belt, and silhouette? Is the bag still a distinct product with the right material language? Did the requested crop and aspect ratio survive? Is the result good enough at article or campaign size after it passes those checks?

documents.t: Nano Banana 2.1 is a strong candidate for commercial reference-based image work: it ranks third in Arena's multi-image-edit Product, Branding & Commercial Design category as checked on October 7, 2026. In our 31 reference-led samples, it preserves the jacket's main features and produces convincing on-model portraits, but does not win every identity, label, or campaign constraint. It belongs on a production shortlist alongside Sunburst and Flare, with product-specific approval before use. For a fashion brand, a prettier picture with the wrong embroidery is a failed asset. For an ecommerce team, readable copy cannot compensate for a changed product shape. For a marketing team, composition, product fidelity, and copy accuracy need separate approvals. Nano Banana 2.1 · separate native 4K cover render · supplied cast and garment references. This cover is outside the matched 2K comparison. Tested October 7, 2026. Five original briefs across five models, plus a clean-packshot-to-real-scene brief across six models, one output per cell. We show reviewed selections and report the rejected cells in text; there are no replacement runs in the comparison.
documents.s: Nano Banana 2.1 for Fashion, Ecommerce, and Marketing: Comparison

documents.t: Google's released model ID is gemini-nano-banana-2.1. Its predecessor, called Nano Banana 2 or 2.0 in this comparison, is gemini-3.1-flash-image. Nano Banana Pro is a separate model. Google describes improvements to realism, instruction following, text rendering, and character consistency through successive edits. Outputs support 1K, 2K, and 4K; wide-image tiling fixes target panoramic ratios at higher resolutions. It supports up to 14 reference images, with documented consistency roles for up to four characters and ten objects. These are provider capabilities to qualify on a real brief, rather than proof of exact garment reconstruction. See Google's model documentation. Google Cloud dates the generally available release to October 6, 2026. Its technical specifications also rule out provider-level seed and sampling controls. An identical seed is therefore not a fair-control promise for this comparison.

documents.t: We selected Sunburst and Flare because they lead this specific Arena category, and Seedream 5 Pro because it ranks fifth and offers a relevant material-and-fashion alternative. The direct predecessor is required to isolate the practical upgrade question. Muse remains a useful multi-reference challenger; Ideogram 4.5 and Reve 2.0 are not interchangeable with the different versions currently exposed in Astria's catalog. The five original cases use the same supplied images, exact semantic prompt, 4:3 requested aspect ratio, 2K requested resolution, and one requested output per model in Astria workspace 896, Articles. Face inpainting and film grain are disabled. The only returned image is the predetermined comparison candidate; there are no selective reruns. We use 2K as the common resolution supported by Seedream Pro and the other selected endpoints. Actual dimensions differ between providers. The cover is a separate native 4K render with the supplied portrait and jacket. No source or output was enlarged to meet the resolution gate. The synthetic jacket and serum references come from our earlier benchmark assets. The jacket source has four teal cranes, four brass buttons, two lower floral motifs, orange leaf-pattern jacquard, a pointed collar, and a scalloped hem. The serum source supplies the bottle, pump, carton, palette, and label design. These are fictional products made for testing, not customer SKUs. We checked the deployed integration before submitting 2.1: production release v4821 contains the routing update. Tune 4180298 now targets gemini-nano-banana-2.1; separate tune 5850983 targets gemini-3.1-flash-image. The two product-only 2.0 baselines were generated before the upgrade, with the verified former mapping; all later 2.0 cases use the separate legacy tune. Spicy Mayo is deprecated and excluded. The curated MCP catalog still carries an older display label, which is why we verified release history and committed provider mappings instead of relying on names. Attempt-level transport telemetry is not exposed by the tool.

documents.t: The brief asks for a complete front view on an invisible mannequin, with the referenced jacket's construction, motif counts, color, and weave preserved. This tests a catalog transformation before adding the complexity of a person or location. The exact brief supplied to all five models was: Create a product-only ecommerce photograph of <faceid:5851059:1> jacket on an invisible mannequin, front view with sleeves hanging naturally, against a warm ivory seamless studio background. Preserve the exact burnt-orange silk jacquard leaf weave, all four teal crane motifs and lower floral details, four brass dome buttons, pointed collar, cropped length and scalloped hem. Show the complete garment without clipping. Soft even catalog lighting, realistic material detail. No person, no accessories, no added text, no new logos. Jacket — four reviewed comparison selections The same supplied jacket and brief. The 2.1 output is withheld because it changes the collar label; its result is reported below. Side by sideScan line Source productSupplied synthetic jacket Nano Banana 2.0 — pre-upgradeRetains four cranes and four buttons; recognizably follows the source collar and hem. Cloth relief and feather details are redrawn. GPT Image 2.5 SunburstClear hanging-garment presentation and strong motif counts. Jacquard relief is more pronounced; the source collar label is omitted. GPT Image 2.5 FlarePreserves the recognizable color, cranes, buttons and scalloped outline. Texture and embroidery are reinterpreted; the collar label is omitted. Seedream 5 ProStrong warm color and recognizable weave, four cranes and four buttons. The collar label is omitted and the lower flowers are simplified. These images preserve the main garment features well enough for this editorial comparison. They are not pixel-identical product reproductions. We would check embroidery close-ups and trim placement against an actual SKU before approving ecommerce use. The source includes an invented collar label; its removal by Sunburst and Flare is another reason to keep packaging or brand-label fidelity separate from general visual quality. Seedream also completed and retained the main garment structure, with simplified floral details and no collar label. The 2.1 sample also retains four cranes, four brass buttons, lower flowers, leaf-pattern cloth and a scalloped hem. However, it replaces the invented source collar label with different lettering. We keep that image internal rather than presenting it as an approved branded product asset. This is a specific miss on this run, not evidence that every 2.1 product edit fails. The five single-output cells do not establish a general winner for fabric fidelity. No missing or incompatible output is replaced with a text-only example. documents.t: The second brief turns a supplied serum bottle and carton into a rose-and-ivory campaign layout. It requests three exact copy lines: “LUMEN SERUM”, “A daily ritual.”, and “DISCOVER THE COLLECTION”, with the product on the right and copy on the left. All five models render those three lines legibly in the completed baseline outputs. Sunburst adds an outlined call-to-action treatment; Flare uses an italic middle line; 2.0 uses a simpler sans-serif layout. Nano Banana 2.1 uses a restrained sans-serif headline and serif middle line. The copy pass therefore does not isolate an upgrade advantage on this brief. Seedream renders the three marketing lines too, but duplicates “30 mL” near the bottom of the carton. That is an unrequested packaging change, even though the large ad copy reads correctly. Product fidelity still needs a stricter judgment. Bottle and pump proportions differ, and the upright carton creates a new label presentation. The source bottle omits the “04” printed on the carton, while our prompt explicitly requests “No. 04 ROSE” on both. This tests controlled text normalization as well as preservation. Nano Banana 2.1 retains the source bottle's “No. ROSE” instead of applying the requested “No. 04 ROSE” normalization. We keep all five images internal because exact packaging and geometry did not pass. The typography findings remain useful, but none is an approved SKU advertisement. Model Three requested ad lines Specific packaging or layout observation Nano Banana 2.1 Correct and legible Bottle omits requested “04”; carton includes it Nano Banana 2.0 Correct and legible Carton text remains sideways despite upright presentation Sunburst Correct and legible Adds an outlined CTA treatment; product proportions differ Flare Correct and legible Italic middle line; pump and bottle proportions differ Seedream 5 Pro Correct and legible Adds an extra “30 mL” near the carton bottom For marketers, approve the product first, then check spelling, hierarchy, contrast, and room for channel-specific crops. For ecommerce teams, retain approved product photography when an AI transformation changes the SKU's defining shape or hardware.
documents.s: Marketing copy: readable headlines are only half the job

documents.t: Nano Banana 2.1, Pro, Sunburst, Flare and Seedream tie at 11 / 11 preserved text lines. Nano Banana 2.0 scores 10 / 11. With a clearly readable source, the leading group reproduces even the small blue French copy. There is no single text-fidelity winner in this round. We start with one real product in a clean studio packshot: a white La Roche-Posay Effaclar Mat tube on a plain background, photographed by Cosmin Ursea on Unsplash, used under the Unsplash License. Every front-label line is readable in the original, including the small blue wording above the cap. Each model gets that unchanged packshot and the same brief: put the product in an adult hand beside a bathroom window, keep the label uncovered, and reproduce all packaging text. The prompt does not supply the wording; models must read it from the image. One output per model, no reruns. Nano Banana Pro is included in this round only. We manually checked the 11 source lines against each full-resolution output. A line passes only when its complete wording, accents and punctuation remain correct and legible; letter case, spacing and apostrophe styling do not affect the score. This measures copy reproduction in these six images, not exact typography or product geometry. The models still redraw type weight and cap details. For this brief, 2.1 joins the leading group and avoids the predecessor’s small-copy error. A clear packshot makes this a useful test of text preservation when moving a product into a real scene; one sample per model cannot establish a general accuracy ranking.

documents.t: For identity ground truth we adopted a detailed, synthetic portrait from our earlier GPT Image 2 benchmark: 1792 × 2304 pixels, not an enlarged casting thumbnail. Its wavy dark bob, green eyes, facial proportions and skin marks are the visual anchors. It already includes the jacket, so the separate garment reference reinforces that cue. This tests one supplied identity across views, not independent casting or every possible garment assignment. A source created by GPT Image 2 may also favor related models; a wider production study needs more casts and source styles. CastFixed synthetic portrait, adopted as this test's identity ground truth JacketFixed construction, color, weave, motifs and trim Campaign accessoryNine green stones, white separators, rose-gold settings and cable chain The first brief asks for a front-view waist-up portrait including the complete jacket and hem. The second changes only the pose: a 30-degree turn to camera-left, with the face looking back at camera. Both request the same facial and garment features, ivory background, soft light, no jewelry and no added text. Front view — identity versus pose compliance Same cast, jacket, semantic prompt and requested settings. Use the source references above to assess identity and garment detail. Side by sideScan line Source productSupplied synthetic cast; jacket reference above Use this face and the separate jacket reference above to check each output. Nano Banana 2.1Upright front pose, recognizable bob and face, four cranes and four buttons. Skin is smoother than the supplied portrait; a matching orange lower garment is invented. Nano Banana 2.0Upright front pose with recognizable facial anchors and main garment features. Face appears narrower; a matching orange lower garment is invented. GPT Image 2.5 SunburstStays close to the source skin detail, face and head tilt; four cranes and buttons. Hands-in-pockets styling and ivory trousers are added. GPT Image 2.5 FlareClose facial resemblance and strong garment detail. Retains the source head tilt rather than a strictly upright front pose; adds dark trousers. Seedream 5 ProRecognizable cast and upright pose with the main garment attributes intact. Skin, embroidery and surface texture are redrawn. Nano Banana 2.1 and 2.0 follow the upright front-pose direction more clearly. Sunburst and Flare retain more of the supplied portrait's skin texture and head tilt, which helps likeness but weakens strict pose compliance. All five preserve the recognizable bob, eyes and face alongside the main jacket features. These are human visual judgments, not biometric similarity measurements. Three-quarter view — the same identity and garment Same cast, jacket, semantic prompt and requested settings. Use the source references above to assess identity and garment detail. Side by sideScan line Source productSupplied synthetic cast; jacket reference above Use this face and the separate jacket reference above to check each output. Nano Banana 2.1Clear body turn and direct gaze; recognizable cast, four cranes and four buttons. Skin and embroidery remain somewhat simplified. Nano Banana 2.0Clear body turn and gaze, retaining the cast and garment anchors. Smooths skin and adds a matching orange lower garment. GPT Image 2.5 SunburstStrong source resemblance and material detail with the requested body turn. Adds hands-in-pockets styling and ivory trousers. GPT Image 2.5 FlareRecognizable face, detailed cloth and a clear turn. Retains a stronger head tilt and adds pocket styling. Seedream 5 ProRecognizable cast, clear body turn and garment structure. Facial finish and fabric relief differ from the source. The pair does not reveal a decisive 2.1-over-2.0 identity win. Both Google versions create a coherent cast across these two views, while the supplied facial texture stays closer in the GPT variants. Skin smoothing, tiny marks, weave and crane feathers still change. A campaign can tolerate more variation than a casting approval or a product detail page; decide that tolerance before reviewing outputs.

documents.t: The fifth brief combines the same cast, jacket and nine-stone necklace in a pale limestone gallery, with ivory trousers, warm side light and a relaxed walking pose. The references have explicit roles; the necklace should stay separate from the teal embroidery. We supplied this identical brief to every model: Create a full-length fashion campaign photograph of <faceid:5851882:1> woman wearing <faceid:5851059:1> jacket with plain ivory trousers and <faceid:5851884:1> necklace, in a pale limestone gallery. Brand direction: restrained ivory, burnt orange and teal, warm late-afternoon side light, relaxed walking pose, premium editorial realism. Preserve cast identity, jacket construction, four teal crane motifs, four brass buttons, leaf weave and scalloped hem. Preserve the necklace's nine green stones, white stone separators, rose-gold settings and cable chain; wear it visibly at the neckline without merging it with embroidery. Plausible anatomy and garment contact, no extra people, no additional jewelry, no invented product, no added text. All five combine the three reference roles into a coherent fashion scene. None passes every strict campaign constraint. We keep these images internal and report the observations rather than featuring a compromised product example. Model What works Why this cell needs revision Nano Banana 2.1 Complete walking figure, plausible hands, warm limestone setting, recognizable cast and four cranes Open neckline leaves only three buttons clearly visible; tiny necklace settings and stone geometry are not verified as exact Nano Banana 2.0 Complete walking pose and strong warm directional light Introduces a cream collar that changes the jacket; necklace geometry is reinterpreted Sunburst Strong likeness, rich cloth detail and convincing warm architecture Clips the top of the head, opens the neckline and shows three buttons; necklace settings change Flare Close likeness, four visible buttons and polished garment-and-jewelry separation Crops below the knees instead of a full-length frame; necklace stone geometry changes Seedream 5 Pro Recognizable cast, four visible buttons, coherent architecture and lighting Crops the lower legs; tiny necklace settings cannot be approved as an exact accessory reproduction The useful distinction is between assembling the references and preserving every product constraint. The models manage the first more consistently than the second. For a brand campaign, review the neckline, closures, jewelry settings, hands and crop before judging the atmosphere. For a full catalog, qualify additional identities and garments, then inspect repeated edits for drift.
documents.s: Three-reference outfit and brand-direction test

documents.t: For this cast and garment, Nano Banana 2.1 is a credible starting point for pose-directed, reference-led fashion portraits. It maintains the main garment anchors and produces a coherent identity pair. The product-only label miss and uncertain campaign accessory detail mean we would not approve every output automatically. Sunburst and Flare deserve the same brief when close source likeness and editorial material detail matter. In these samples they retain more facial texture, while occasionally retaining the source pose too strongly or choosing a crop the brief did not request. Their Arena lead is relevant shortlist evidence, not a substitute for product review. Nano Banana 2.1, Pro, Sunburst, Flare and Seedream all preserve the 11 measured lines in the clean-packshot-to-real-scene round. Nano Banana 2.0 misses one small-copy line. Seedream 5 Pro remains a useful fabric-and-color alternative at 2K. It keeps the principal jacket features and coherent casting here, but the packaging duplication and campaign crop need correction. Nano Banana 2.0 remains competitive on these small samples; we did not measure a consistent upgrade advantage in identity or three-line ad copy. These are 31 qualification samples, including six packshot-to-real-scene results, not a statistically reliable model ranking. They use provider defaults rather than matched internal inference budgets: Google's 2.1 default thinking is medium, while its predecessor defaults to minimal. Actual delivered ratios also vary slightly. We did not test long editing chains, wider real-product catalogs, wider cast diversity or a matched latency distribution. Keep aesthetic, identity, product and copy approvals separate.
documents.s: Which model would we start with?

documents.t: Grokbot was unavailable in this session. We used web search and checked the following short quotations against the original posts. Both pages displayed “2h ago” when checked on October 7, 2026; the October 7 posting date is inferred from that relative timestamp. These are community anecdotes, not Astria measurements. u/TimeCounty7878, posting in reAPI's official subreddit, wrote: “2.1 kept the exact wording, and the layout is cleaner.” Their comparison used one run per prompt and different models' default thinking settings. The vendor-affiliated venue and small sample matter when assessing the claim. Original post, checked October 7. u/mementomori2344323, describing a recursive FLUX 3 versus 2.1 edit test, qualified its metric as measuring “only preservation of untouched regions.” The test used different model-specific interfaces and three source images. It raises a useful concern about drift through repeated edits, but does not measure overall commercial-image quality. Original post, checked October 7. Those reports suggest useful qualification tests: exact-copy layouts, repeated local edits, and settings-aware latency checks. They do not replace our controlled reference comparison.
documents.s: What the community is saying

documents.t: Standard is available; Nano Banana 2.1 does not support Flex. Google's Cloud pricing page explicitly says so in the Nano Banana 2.1 footnote, even though a combined table heading mentions Flex/Batch/Off-peak. Batch support is separate and should not be mistaken for Flex availability. See Google Cloud pricing and Gemini API pricing, checked October 7, 2026. For an interactive creative review, plan around Standard and measure the complete round trip. For an asynchronous approved catalog batch, check whether your chosen interface exposes Google's supported Batch path. The Astria generation tool used here does not expose a service-tier selector; we make no claim that these runs used Batch or Flex. Priority availability differs across Google's documented surfaces, so confirm the specific API before designing a deadline-critical workflow around it. Budget with current rates for input, reasoning or text output, image output at the chosen resolution, and any search grounding. Divide total generation and review effort by the number of approved assets. A lower output component does not guarantee a cheaper completed campaign when references, reruns, and manual correction change. Get current Astria rates from Astria pricing. For reproducibility, archive the source images and provider model ID, not just the interface's model name. Use approved reference packs for production, and requalify them after a provider upgrade. Our benchmark methodology explains how we separate material fidelity, identity, copy, and aesthetic judgments. Test your own reference pack Run one brief across your shortlist Supply approved cast and product images. Compare identity, garment detail and copy before choosing the campaign treatment. documents.t: An architect needs to explain a facade option. An interior designer needs to compare finishes in the same room. A development manager needs an image that makes a proposed project understandable to stakeholders. Each needs a visual of a specific change, with the existing design still legible. The Astria Nano Banana Photoshop plugin lets you start with a sketch, a photograph or an exported model view, describe the change, and review the result in a layered Photoshop document. Use it to explore materials, atmosphere and presentation while keeping the underlying design in your modeling application.
documents.s: Nano Banana Architecture in Photoshop for Design Teams

documents.t: The architecture demonstration starts with a line drawing of a modern house and pool. It creates a daylight interpretation, then explores night lighting, blue pool illumination, outdoor dining and a different viewpoint. The source is already an image in Photoshop. Before 00:00 — The source sketch establishes the house, pool and camera view. After 00:12 — The generated daylight interpretation adds materials, glazing, planting and reflections. Select an image to enlarge it. Frames are cropped from the original video. Photoshop layers 00:12 — The generated image and its mask sit above the original sketch on Layer 0. This is the actual panel from the recording. Watch the original Astria demonstration. The recording shows an earlier plugin interface; use the current panel for the selection, reference-image and returned-layer workflow. Illustrations are stills from that recording.
documents.s: Watch a sketch become a realistic concept

documents.t: Team role Decision to support Photoshop workflow Building architect Explain the character of an early design Materialize a sketch or a clay-render export using the intended palette Interior designer Compare flooring, cabinetry and upholstery Select one surface or furnishing group and attach finish references Visualization artist Improve the realism of a model export Work on material appearance, reflections, planting and atmosphere Lighting designer Discuss day, evening and pool lighting Keep the source view fixed and compare separate lighting interpretations Development manager Communicate alternative schemes or project phases Export each designed option first, then apply a consistent visual treatment Design director or project lead Review options with the client Keep alternatives in named layers and show the same crop for each Developer marketing team Explain the planned experience of an amenity Prepare clearly labeled concept images from approved project views
documents.s: Match the image to the project decision

documents.t: Lighting option at 00:30. Night atmosphere and pool illumination are visual treatments of the source scene. Viewpoint exploration at 00:53. Generate presentation ideas here; export precise camera views from the project model. A viewpoint change reveals surfaces the original drawing never supplied. For a client presentation that must match the design, set the camera in Blender, SketchUp or CAD and export that view first. This also lets a project team compare several angles against one authoritative model. For surface shades, begin with Photoshop adjustment layers when the geometry and texture already work. Use generation when a change needs a new material appearance or reconstructed reflections. Keep lighting variations separate from material comparisons so the brighter image does not become the accidental favorite.
documents.s: Explore lighting and viewpoints separately

documents.t: A useful architecture image answers a question. Decide what can change and what must remain fixed before generating. Level Typical question Starting image Photoshop approach City or district How would this approved development sit in its surroundings? Oblique view exported from a site model Select the development area; retain surrounding context Neighborhood or campus What character should the public spaces have? Massing view with paths and courtyards established Edit ground treatments, planting, and street furniture Road or street How would a proposed street redesign look at eye level? Street photograph with a designed intervention composited into it Select the proposal footprint; keep buildings and junctions fixed Building How could this clay model read as a finished building? Neutral render from the architect's model Apply a material palette across the full view Renovation What can change while keeping the existing shell? Site photograph or proposed-model render Edit finishes or a separately modeled addition Interior Which finish and furniture combination suits this room? Room photograph or render Change one surface or furnishing group at a time Detail Would a different screen, handle, or joint treatment work visually? Close view of the relevant assembly Make a small selection and inspect at full size These are presentation workflows. A realistic image does not establish dimensions, buildability, or performance. Keep the surveyed information, geometry, and technical decisions in the project model and drawings.
documents.s: Start with the decision, then choose the size of the edit

documents.t: Export a clear view from your modeling or rendering application, or open a project photograph you have permission to use. For a clay render, make window recesses, slab edges, entrances, and ground levels legible. A featureless white block gives the model little evidence about the intended facade. Keep an untouched base layer. Save selections for recurring edit areas, and put each alternative in a named group: Facade — brick, Facade — limestone, or Kitchen — oak fronts. Hide earlier alternatives before generating the next one so they do not become part of its input. Open the Astria panel through Photoshop's Plugins menu. The current plugin requires Photoshop 2025, version 26 or later, on macOS or Windows. Its documented workflow accepts selections and reference images and returns an edit as a new layer. See the plugin and installation page. In version 2, references can come from an image file or the current Photoshop layer. The panel exposes model-dependent controls and handles contextual capture and blending around the selection. Those conveniences still need a visual check at building edges and material boundaries. Astria's version 2 release notes describe the changes. For each edit: Select the intended area. Use a polygonal selection or a path for planar surfaces. Exclude windows, reveals, fixtures, and other elements that must stay. Attach relevant references. Use a material sample for a material edit, a furniture photograph for a furniture edit, or a palette board for a full-view treatment. Name each reference's role in the prompt. Choose the model and output settings. Start comparisons at the same supported resolution, with the same output count. Choose a supported resolution suited to the final presentation and inspect the returned pixel dimensions. Describe the change and the constraints. State what to alter, which reference governs it, and what to preserve. Review the returned layer. Toggle it against the base; inspect the mask, perspective, repeated elements, and neighboring pixels. Refine the mask in Photoshop before showing the option to a client. For material alternatives, keep camera and lighting consistent. For intentional lighting changes, check whether your panel's Generate menu offers Generate with the prompt only: this omits the added preservation instruction in builds that expose it. Put the geometry and camera constraints in your own prompt, while explicitly allowing the lighting change.
documents.s: Set up the Photoshop document

documents.t: Decision: can the client understand the architectural character before the full material setup is complete? Start with a courtyard building rendered in neutral gray. Include the actual openings, balcony edges, paving levels, and roofline. Add a reference board containing the intended limestone, bronze metalwork, and paving. Use the whole view as the selection for this first treatment. Turn the supplied clay render into a realistic architectural concept image. Use the clay render as the authority for geometry and camera position. Use the attached material board only for material appearance: pale limestone on the opaque facade, bronze metal on the existing frames, and warm gray paving on the existing courtyard surface. Keep the building outline, number and position of openings, floor count, balcony depths, roofline, ground levels, crop, and perspective unchanged. Retain the direction of the source shadows. Introduce realistic surface texture and reflections without adding architectural elements. Try Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro on the same input. Compare the result by counting windows and checking slab edges before judging atmosphere. Add Seedream or another reference-capable model only with the same source, references, prompt, and framing. The useful before/after shows the clay view beside the materialized view, with matching crops. A more dramatic image that adds a floor or moves the entrance is a failed interpretation of this brief. “Clay to real” here means visual interpretation. For sun, wind, daylight, or microclimate evaluation, use tools that calculate those quantities from the project data; Autodesk's Forma analysis documentation illustrates that separate workflow.
documents.s: 1. Building architects: turn a clay render into a realistic concept

documents.t: Decision: should the same facade use brick, stone, or metal? Select the opaque cladding on one elevation. Subtract glazing, mullions, balcony rails, soffits, and neighboring buildings. Save that selection. Generate each option from the original view, with its corresponding material reference. Replace only the selected opaque facade cladding with the terracotta brick shown in the material reference. Follow its warm red-brown color variation and matte surface. Use horizontal running-bond courses with a consistent module across the elevation. Preserve the existing facade plane, all window openings, frames, sills, balcony rails, roofline, perspective, lighting, and everything outside the cladding selection. For the limestone option, change the material instruction and reference while keeping the remaining brief fixed. Distinguish this design-option comparison from a model comparison, where even the requested material stays identical. Look closely at corners and window returns: does the treatment wrap convincingly, or does the model paint a flat texture across the openings? Exact bond dimensions, panel sizes, and fixing details belong in the facade design. If a joint must land precisely, draw it or model it and use that as the next reference.
documents.s: 2. Facade designers: compare materials without redesigning the building

documents.t: Decision: what can the homeowner achieve by changing finishes, and what requires a physical alteration? For a finish refresh, use the existing photograph. Select cabinet fronts and end panels, keeping the countertop, appliance openings, sink, and wall geometry outside the selection. Change only the selected kitchen cabinet fronts and exposed end panels to the natural oak finish in the supplied sample. Keep grain direction vertical on the doors. Preserve every door and drawer division, handle position, appliance opening, countertop, sink, backsplash, room boundary, camera position, and existing light direction. Keep the countertop edge and cabinet shadow gaps clearly defined. For an extension, first model the proposed volume and openings, then export the same camera view. Use that view to explore cladding and atmosphere. Asking the image model to invent an extension from a photograph leaves roof junctions, heights, and internal relationships unresolved. Present the existing photograph, finish-only proposal, and modeled-extension visualization as separate options with explicit labels. That helps the client understand the scope of each decision.
documents.s: 3. Home renovation architects: show a finish refresh and an extension separately

documents.t: Decision: which material palette works in the actual room? Begin with one surface. Select the visible floor while excluding furniture, skirting, and door thresholds. Attach a flooring reference that shows several boards or tiles, rather than an ambiguous close-up. Replace the selected floor finish with the pale oak flooring in the reference image. Run the boards toward the far window, following the room's perspective. Preserve the room dimensions, walls, skirting, door thresholds, furniture positions, and camera. Retain contact shadows under the furniture and the original direction of daylight. Do not change any wall or furniture finishes. Next, make a separate furniture edit with a product reference. Include the object's footprint and contact shadow in the selection. Inspect legs, seams, proportions, and occlusion; reference-based generation does not guarantee an exact catalog match. Composite the actual product cutout when exact product identity is required. A convincing comparison uses the same room and exposure for both palettes. Otherwise, clients may prefer the brighter picture rather than the better material combination.
documents.s: 4. Interior designers: change a floor, then furniture, then the mood

documents.t: Decision: how does a local detail affect the composition? For an entrance screen, start from a view where its frame and opening are already designed. Select the infill and supply a photograph or drawing of the proposed screen pattern. Replace only the selected entrance-screen infill with the vertical bronze fins shown in the reference. Fit the fins inside the existing frame and follow the perspective of that frame. Preserve the frame outline, adjacent door, glazing, wall finish, ground, camera, and light direction. Do not extend fins across the doorway or alter the entrance width. Compare a mask-aware model such as GPT Image 2 with a reference-capable Gemini model. The question is whether the edit stays local and respects the frame. If exact fin count or spacing matters, place a drawn pattern first and ask for a material treatment of that pattern. For a paint color, handle swap, or minor alignment correction, a conventional adjustment layer or transformed product cutout may be sufficient. Reserve generation for changes that need a new material appearance, reflected environment, or contextual reconstruction.
documents.s: 5. Detail designers: test a screen, balustrade, or hardware change

documents.t: Decision: what would the spaces between the buildings feel like? Use an oblique site-model view with the building volumes, streets, paths, and courtyards already established. Select one public-space area and provide a landscape palette. Work on one block or courtyard before trying to reinterpret an entire district. Develop the selected courtyard into a realistic public-space concept using the supplied paving and planting references. Keep all building footprints, heights, entrances, street edges, paths, and camera position as shown in the source model. Add planting only inside the existing planting beds and benches only within the designated seating areas. Keep the central walking route open. Preserve the surrounding blocks. Prepare more than one view from the same underlying model if the proposal needs both an aerial explanation and a pedestrian experience. Treat each generated image as a separate interpretation and check materials and features across views. For development phasing, export each phase from the model first, then apply a consistent visual treatment. Keep phase colors, boundaries, labels, and legends on ordinary Photoshop layers so the presentation remains unambiguous.
documents.s: 6. Neighborhood and campus planners: make a massing study legible

documents.t: Decision: how can a proposed street change be explained to residents or stakeholders? Start with a licensed street photograph and a perspective overlay of the designed curb, path, and planting geometry. Select the intervention footprint. The overlay supplies the spatial arrangement; the image model supplies a possible material and landscape appearance. Render the proposed street intervention shown in the supplied composite. Use the overlaid curb and cycle-track geometry as the authority for the layout. Replace the marked parking strip with the shown cycle track and planting islands. Keep the existing building facades, junction positions, crossing locations, horizon, camera, and all unmarked street areas unchanged. Use the attached paving and planting references. Do not add traffic lanes, move intersections, or invent signs and road markings. Check continuity through the image: does the cycle track disappear behind a tree, jump across a crossing, or narrow unexpectedly? Keep required markings and labels as deliberate overlays when generation cannot reproduce them reliably. NACTO's neighborhood-street guidance is useful background for the design conversation. A Photoshop visualization can communicate a proposal; the road layout still needs its normal design and engineering review. At city scale, use district views to explain an established massing strategy. Retain the authoritative land-use map, transport network, and annotations separately rather than asking the model to redraw them.
documents.s: 7. City planners and road designers: visualize an approved street proposal

documents.t: Decision: should a courtyard feel open and meadow-like, or more structured and shaded? Start from the same landscape model or photograph. Select the established planting beds, keeping paths, levels, drainage features, and entrances fixed. Supply references for the intended planting character. Change vegetation only within the selected planting beds to the meadow character shown in the reference photographs: fine grasses and low flowering perennials. Keep path edges, paving, retaining walls, ground levels, existing tree positions, and building entrances unchanged. Keep planting clear of the visible walking routes. Preserve the camera and the original lighting. Make a second seasonal interpretation from the same source, with a season-specific reference. Label it as an illustrative seasonal view. Check species appearance and planting scale against the actual planting schedule; the picture does not establish growth, survival, water use, or cooling performance.
documents.s: 8. Landscape architects: compare planting character and seasonal appearance

documents.t: Decision: how would a new use read inside an existing structure? Use a measured-model view or a project photograph with protected fabric clearly identified. Select only the proposed furniture, freestanding partitions, or new finish area. Attach references for the intervention. Within the selected area, visualize the freestanding reception desk shown in the design reference. Preserve the existing masonry, columns, beams, window openings, floor levels, and all visible historic surface detail. Keep the desk separate from the existing columns and retain the camera and light direction. Do not restore, clean, replace, or invent details on the existing building fabric. Show the original next to the proposal and identify the added elements. For restoration studies, use archival or measured evidence for missing features; stylistic plausibility is insufficient evidence of what was originally there.
documents.s: 9. Conservation and adaptive-reuse teams: explore reversible interventions

documents.t: Decision: how would a different interior identity work within the same shell? A hotel lobby, office reception, or cafe can share the same method: retain the approved layout and change a defined palette or furnishing group. Use a reference board with clearly labeled materials and objects. Restyle only the selected cafe banquette and wall panels using the reference board: muted olive upholstery on the existing seats and natural walnut veneer on the existing panels. Preserve the seating layout, table count and positions, aisle boundaries, windows, ceiling, camera, and light direction. Keep upholstery and veneer assigned to their specified surfaces. Do not introduce signs or lettering. Place logos, wayfinding, and exact text as editable Photoshop artwork after the edit. For lighting mood options, work from a separate copy of the approved view and explicitly allow lighting to change. Evaluate illumination levels with the lighting-design workflow, rather than reading them from the generated image.
documents.s: 10. Hospitality, workplace, and retail designers: compare fit-out concepts

documents.t: Nano Banana is Google's name for a family of image models, not one fixed model. Google's image-generation documentation distinguishes Nano Banana 2 from Nano Banana Pro and describes image-guided editing and resolution options. The table below is a testing plan, not an architecture benchmark or a ranking. Confirm the current models and controls in your installed panel. Model to test Architecture task What to compare Nano Banana 2 Clay-to-real and initial material options Openings, silhouette, perspective, and material assignment Nano Banana Pro The same clay view or a detailed multi-reference brief Whether constraints and reference roles survive the edit GPT Image 2 A selected cabinet, screen, or facade detail Locality of the edit, edge quality, and surrounding pixels Seedream 5 / 5 Pro The same facade or interior material brief Texture scale, repeated patterns, and unintended redesign Flux 2 Pro The same photographic material or landscape edit Surface appearance, shadows, and preservation of the source Astria lists these model families on its Photoshop plugin page. Resolution and reference support vary by model and integration; verify the selected model's controls instead of assuming every model supports the same settings. Photoshop's native Generative Fill also supports partner models and reference images, as Adobe documents. Evaluate Astria around its actual panel workflow and available models, rather than the outdated claim that Photoshop only offers Adobe models.
documents.s: Choose a model for the architectural edit

documents.t: Choose one base image and one edit. Keep the reference files and their order, prompt, selection, source-layer visibility, aspect ratio, resolution, and output count fixed across compatible models. Record any model-specific control or input-path difference. For local editing, distinguish what the model returned from what the Photoshop mask reveals. A good final composite can conceal changes elsewhere in the returned image. Review both before claiming that a model preserved the geometry. Use four checks: Geometry: building outline, openings, slab edges, perspective, and repeated elements. Reference fidelity: material color, pattern, grain direction, object shape, and scale cues. Edit boundaries: unintended changes, halos, broken shadows, and seams. Presentation quality: credibility and clarity at the size the client will actually see. Record manual cleanup separately. documents.s: Every current model, inside the layers panel

documents.t: Make a selection, describe the edit, and the result comes back into the document. The plugin handles the export, the API call, and the re-import, and it returns generations as layers so the rest of your normal workflow — masks, blend modes, adjustment layers, non-destructive corrections — still applies. The panel currently carries six models: GPT Image 2 (mask-aware, at 1K, 2K or 4K), Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 5 Pro, Seedream 5 and Flux 2 Pro, with the current line-up shifting as new releases land. Results land as Smart Objects holding the model's full returned resolution, so a 4K result dropped into a small selection still carries every pixel. The panel reads its model list from Astria, so a new model appears in the dropdown on launch day with no plugin update. That is deliberate: the plugin's usefulness is partly that you do not have to migrate your workflow every time a better model appears.
documents.s: What it does

documents.t: The models are not interchangeable, and having several in one panel is most of the value. Instruction-following edits — "remove the object", "change the wall to sage green", "make it evening" — are where the Gemini-line models are strongest. Natural-language editing against an existing image is what they are built for. Photographic generation — new content that has to sit convincingly alongside a photograph — is where the Flux line has generally been strong. Mask-aware surgical replacement — swap the shoes from a reference, take the phone out of a hand — is where GPT Image 2 earns its place. It reads a brushed selection directly, so the edit stays inside the mask and the rest of the frame is left alone. Long, structured prompts — a multi-clause brief for a packaging variant or a full re-light, with materials, light direction and framing spelled out — are where Seedream 5 tends to hold together. Speed and throughput — some models return in seconds; others are slower and better. For a hundred small corrections, the fast one is the right call. The practical habit is to try the cheap fast model first and escalate only when it fails. Most edits do not need the best available model, and running everything through the most expensive option is how a plugin subscription starts feeling expensive.
documents.s: Why model choice matters

documents.t: Select generously. Give the model context around the edit — a tight selection produces edits that do not know what they are sitting next to, and the seam shows. Keep generations on their own layers. Then mask rather than erase. The best result is frequently a blend of two attempts, and that is only possible if you kept both. Prompt the change, not the scene. "Change the wall behind her to sage green" beats a full re-description of the image. Describing everything invites the model to reconsider everything. Fix colour and grade in Photoshop. Generated regions often come back very slightly off. A curves adjustment clipped to the layer is faster and more controllable than re-prompting for a colour shift. Work at sensible resolution. Because each result arrives as a Smart Object holding the model's full returned pixels, generating a hero at 4K and transforming it later costs nothing in resolution: scale it down, scale it back up, re-mask, and the original pixels are still there. For volume the old rule still applies. Run the cheap, fast model at a working size first, and reserve 4K for the frames that will carry the campaign.
documents.s: Working with it properly

documents.t: For fashion and product work the division tends to fall out like this: Bulk production — a whole collection against one approved treatment — belongs in a production workspace, not in Photoshop. That is a throughput problem, and doing it one document at a time is the wrong shape. See the AI fashion photoshoot guide. Hero images belong in Photoshop. The shot that carries a campaign gets individual attention, and this is where generative editing inside a real editing environment beats a web app. Corrections — a distracting object, an awkward shadow, a background that needs extending to a different aspect ratio — belong in the plugin. These are the everyday tasks that were never worth a browser round trip. Client work where layered files are a deliverable belongs in Photoshop, because the layers are the point.

documents.t: The demonstration includes ground cleanup, warm lighting, dress-train changes, hand and phone removal, hair refinement, makeup, and creative pose or setting changes. Those edits serve different purposes: cleaning an obstruction preserves the intended photograph, while changing the dress or setting creates a new interpretation for the client's review. Before 01:38 — Hands interrupt the bridal profile and hair detail. After 02:05 — The hands are removed, revealing a cleaner profile. Compare the hair, earring and neckline. Select an image to enlarge it. Frames are cropped from the original video. Watch the original Astria demonstration. The recording shows an earlier plugin interface; use the current panel for the selection, reference-image and returned-layer workflow. Illustrations are stills from that recording.
documents.s: Watch distraction removal and bridal refinements

documents.t: Keep an untouched copy of the photograph. Select the unwanted phone, hand or background object with enough surrounding context to reconstruct what it covers. Avoid including the face or dress unnecessarily when they are already satisfactory. The editing brief should identify the obstruction and what must remain: the person's facial features, pose, dress construction, crop and existing light direction. Generate a correction, toggle it against the source, and inspect the region at full size before continuing. Hair, fingers, jewelry and lace deserve particular attention because their fine shapes can become convincing but incorrect substitutes. If the covered area contains a meaningful detail, another photograph from the same sequence can provide reference evidence. A dress button, ring or embroidered panel is easier to restore from the real event than to reconstruct from a generic description.
documents.s: Start with one distraction

documents.t: For a small exposure or skin-color adjustment, use a normal Photoshop adjustment layer. Use generation when removing an obstruction or changing a scene requires content that the photograph does not already contain. Make a warm evening treatment in a separate group from the cleanup. Compare the original light and the new atmosphere at the same crop. A golden treatment should still retain natural skin color and distinguish the dress from the background. The video also explores a longer dress train, a veil and changes to pose or background. Present those as creative alternatives. A client who wants an accurate record of the day should be able to choose the corrected original without also accepting an invented garment or setting.
documents.s: Keep retouching and creative restyling separate

documents.t: Judge the finished image both at full size and in the actual album layout. A clean edge on screen can become a distracting halo around hair in print. Look at the transition into the unedited photograph, contact shadows, and any detail that was hidden by the removed object. Save a layered master and export the approved version. Naming groups by the decision, such as cleanup or evening treatment, makes later client feedback actionable. Keep the original available when a revision should undo only the creative treatment. documents.t: Select the phone and the area it obscures, describe its removal, and review the reconstructed region on the returned Photoshop layer. Supply another event photograph as a reference when a hidden dress, hand or jewelry detail matters.

documents.s: Before you begin

documents.t: Choose poses, framing and prompts—the written instructions for each image—that suit the product. A dress may need a full-length image to show its shape. documents.t: Save styling directions that you expect to reuse with the category. For a jacket, specify whether it should be shown open or closed, alongside the chosen poses and framing. documents.t: Ecommerce teams talk about photoshoot budgets. Catalog operations run on a different number: what it costs to get one product photographed, approved, and live. That number is the one that scales with the business, and most brands have never calculated it honestly. The short version: divide the full production cost by the products that actually received an approved image set. A cheap per-image quote can still produce an expensive catalog if it leaves out views, retouching, revisions, or your team's time. documents.t: Most teams compute cost per image, which flatters the number, or divide the photographer's invoice by the SKU count, which understates it badly. The honest formula: Total loaded cost ÷ SKUs that shipped usable imagery Total loaded cost includes: Crew — photographer, assistants, stylist, hair and makeup Studio or location, plus permits Sample logistics — pulling, shipping both ways, returns, insurance Post-production, per image, at your actual approval standard Your team's hours — briefing, attending, selecting, revising, uploading Reshoots and rejects A share of any usage licensing Two denominators matter. Use SKUs that shipped, not SKUs photographed — the ones that got dropped still consumed budget. For this calculation, use a style-colourway as the imagery unit. If your inventory assigns a SKU to every size, group sizes that share the same image set; count them separately only when they need different imagery. Use that same denominator in every quote. Run this once on your last production. Compare the invoice-only figure with the loaded figure to see which omitted costs matter in your workflow.
documents.s: Calculate it properly

documents.t: Assume 50 style-colourways need four final images each. That is 200 required images. Add photography, studio, styling, sample handling, retouching, internal review, and revisions using your own quotes. For AI generation rates, use Astria pricing. Divide the total by the number of complete, approved SKU sets. If only 40 sets ship, divide by 40 SKUs or 160 approved images. Rejected frames still consume budget, but do not count as deliverables. For a per-image quote, multiply the quoted rate by the required views per SKU, then add any separately billed setup, logistics, licensing, and internal work.
documents.s: Calculate cost per SKU with current quotes

documents.t: Send every supplier the same brief: number of style-colourways, required views, background, styling, output size, retouching standard, usage, and deadline. Ask whether the quote is per image, per product, per hour, or per day, and whether minimum charges apply. Then fill the gaps: who prepares samples, who handles difficult surfaces, how many revision rounds are included, and what happens to an unapproved image? For AI production, also count reference preparation, paid attempts, manual corrections, and human review. A credit buys an operation; your catalog needs a usable result. Use fashion photoshoot cost for the shoot budget and AI versus traditional photoshoot cost for the production-method comparison. Keep this page's calculation at the product level.
documents.s: How to compare product photography quotes

documents.t: Here is the structural problem, and it is not a failure of anyone's judgment: When products need similar handling and views, much of the per-item work repeats. Batching spreads setup costs, but it does not remove styling, checking, and retouching for each item. Expected sales need not follow that pattern. If a few styles carry most of your revenue, the same image spend takes a larger share of the margin on lower-volume products. So there is a crossover point where imagery cost exceeds any defensible share of a product's expected margin. Below it, the rational decision is the cheapest possible treatment — a flat lay, a ghost mannequin, or the supplier's own photo. That can leave the lower-volume products with less useful coverage. Before cutting it further, test whether the missing views are needed to explain the product; low sales alone do not tell you which images are expendable.
documents.s: Why the long tail stays ugly

documents.t: A typical apparel PDP set: Image Purpose Front, on-model or ghost The primary listing image Back Fit and construction Detail ×1–2 Fabric, hardware, trim Lifestyle or in-context Scale, styling, desire Additional colorways Accuracy per variant For this planning example, allow four to eight images per style-colourway. Do not multiply by colourways again if your SKU count already includes them. A 200-style collection in three colorways is 600 variants and, at six images each, up to 3,600 individual assets per season. That multiplication is the whole reason per-SKU thinking matters. Budgets are approved per shoot; costs are incurred per variant.
documents.s: What each SKU actually needs

documents.t: Batching. More SKUs per setup amortises the fixed cost. Real, and limited by attention — quality degrades late in a long day. Simplifying the standard. Fewer images per SKU, less retouching. Cuts cost directly and visibly. Offshoring post. Reduces the per-image retouch line. Adds turnaround time and a review burden that partly offsets it. Shooting less often. Fewer, bigger productions. Amortises well and hurts speed to listing — new products wait for the next shoot. Compare these choices against turnaround time and the coverage customers need. The lowest production invoice is not necessarily the lowest cost of getting the catalog live.
documents.s: What actually moves the number

documents.t: The reason AI production is interesting here is not that it is cheap per image — it is that it decouples per-SKU cost from crew time. The AI product photography workflow shows where reference preparation, review, rejects, and channel delivery enter that calculation. Once an approved treatment exists, the next SKU needs reference preparation, generation, and review. Some products will also need manual corrections or conventional photography. Measure those costs in a pilot rather than assuming they fall to the generation fee. If that combined cost is lower while the approved coverage stays useful, the budget can reach more products. Whether this improves sales is a separate test; cheaper production does not establish a revenue lift. Two honest caveats. First, the up-front direction work is real and should not be skipped; a bad treatment scaled across 600 variants is worse than no treatment. Second, review does not scale to zero — the hard garments still need looking at, per item. Budget for both, and see flat lay to on-model for which garments need the attention.
documents.s: What changes the shape

documents.t: For your own catalog, work out: Loaded cost of last season's production (all lines above, including your hours) SKUs that shipped usable imagery Current cost per SKU = 1 ÷ 2 Expected gross margin per SKU over its life — for a median SKU, not a hero Imagery as a share of margin = 3 ÷ 4 If step five is uncomfortable for the median product, you have quantified why your long tail looks the way it does. Then model the alternative honestly: up-front direction cost, plus per-variant generation and review, divided across the same SKU count. Use your approved-image ledger for the denominator. The photoshoot calculator is another starting point for planning coverage; reconcile any estimate with the style-colourway counting rule above. The full side-by-side is in AI versus traditional photoshoot cost, and the traditional line items are broken down in what a fashion photoshoot costs.
documents.s: A model you can fill in

documents.t: Take the fully-loaded cost of a production — crew, studio, post-production, sample logistics, and your own team's hours — and divide by the number of SKUs that shipped usable imagery. Not by images produced, and not by SKUs photographed.
documents.s: How do you calculate product photography cost per SKU?

documents.t: A working apparel set might contain four to eight images: front, back, details, and on-model or lifestyle views. Set the count from the product and sales channel. Count each style-colourway once when its size variants share those images.
documents.s: How many images does each SKU need?

documents.t: When low-volume products require the same production work as bestsellers, imagery can consume a larger share of their expected margin. Check that relationship in your own catalog before reducing coverage.
documents.s: Why is the long tail of a catalog photographed worse?

documents.t: Each colourway needs an accurate reference and approved coverage. A digital colour edit must be checked against the actual product, including trims, patterns, and fabric appearance. Budget separately when a colourway needs its own image set.
documents.s: Do colorways need separate photography?

documents.t: There is no universal figure — it depends on price point, margin, and expected units. The useful test is relative: your imagery cost per SKU should be a defensible fraction of the gross margin that SKU is expected to generate over its life. documents.s: Bottom line

documents.t: Shopify product media is one ordered set, not three separate feature checklists. The first item may represent the product in collections and cart; the last item may never be reached. Images, video, and 3D only work when the sequence answers the shopper's questions in order. The short version: lead with a product-identifying still, earn each richer format with a distinct job, and test the live theme on mobile. Shopify's upload maximum is not your performance budget.
